#10140. Anthropic's IPO prospectus is big on promises, short on answers to tough questions

Pity Sam Altman: He's going to have a lot more explaining to do when OpenAI follows this work of abstract legal art

It's official: Anthropic is going public, and boy, are our eyebrows tired from poring over hundreds and hundreds of pages of questionable claims.

Anthropic is going to need to do a lot to make its massive IPO more than just a flash in the pan, as systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn tell host Brandon Vigliarolo on this week's episode.

For one, the company has nearly a trillion dollars in compute commitments to pay for, which is going to mean it'll be burning through more cash than a datacenter gas turbine turned up to 11. In addition to its massive spending for the foreseeable future, there's also the fact that much of its computing power relies on customers who are also competitors.

In short, we're skeptical, but you probably already knew that. It's El Reg, after all, and we're not just taking what the AI industry claims at face value - if it looks like a house of cards, it probably is.

Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and this week we're focusing on what I think our contributor Carly Page aptly described as the peak of the AI hype cycle we've been in for the past few years, and that's the public release of Anthropic's initial public offering filing. With me to talk this over is our systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn, both of whom I'm sure have plenty to say about this matter.

So, I'm sure we've got a lot to cover. 614 pages is a lot to go through. Tobias, I understand you were combing through this thing with a fine-toothed comb. Talk us through the hard numbers before we get into some of the more wobbly parts of this IPO.

Sure. At face value, going into any S-1 filing, it is a kind of mess of risk mitigation, kind of covering your butt. They all pretty much read like a doomsday prophecy.

The S-1 definitely did that. But on the numbers side of things, the takeaway for the market was kind of interesting because there were some people looking at the numbers and going, "OK, this actually seems reasonable." Their operating losses were only about 700 million dollars.

I think on 16.3 billion net [revenues], right? That was what they reported.

Now they also mentioned, I think, and I was going to ask you about this, $80.7 billion total losses, but I understand that was an accounting adjustment of some kind. Did they mention in the IPO what that meant specifically?

Not specifically. It's a little fuzzy, and it's always kind of like this.

Anthropic's business is extremely cash heavy, and so they had to go to partners and say, "Hey, we need capital in order to pay for compute to train these models. We can either take it in debt or you could also get repaid in valuation, our equity." And so I believe a large part of that loss is they're trying to write off a lot of the equity that they're going to have to pay off when they do go public. And so I do believe that's the lion's share of that loss. Because it does look huge, but when you think about how companies go public and how they raise capital as startups, it's not really that surprising. It's just a huge number because Anthropic is arguably the largest IPO in US history at this point.

Right. But bottom line is their actual day-to-day business losses were $693 million....It was $1.2 billion, I think, for the first half of the year or same time last year or something like that. So it's gone down.

And they're trying to go out at two trillion now? Is that the number?

Well, the number kind of depends on whether they're going to be able to sustain this. I was going to mention for the first time ever, their revenues outpaced their compute expenses two to one. This has never been true in the company's history, and it's one of the reasons that people are feeling more confident about this. The issue that really comes from all of this, and what has gotten missed somewhat in the more rosy interpretations of the S-1, is that they also are signed up to have to repay upwards of 800 billion dollars and counting of compute commitments out through the next two decades or so.

You outlined in your story just a whole host of people they owed billions of dollars to for compute. Like you said, it would be great. That $16.3 billion in [revenue] would be great if those compute costs were going to hold steady, right? But they're not. They're going to keep climbing and there are a lot of bills that are going to be due. So, profitability is relying on making more than that nearly trillion dollars in compute obligations, and that's a big if.

I mean, the big question mark is in terms of what the technology does for inference costs, because I think a lot of this is betting on being able to get the same hardware that is much more efficient down the road and maybe not drop your prices proportionately and profit on the difference. But it remains to be seen whether there will be enough competition to just have the price go do with the increasing cost. And you see that a lot. I think the inference costs have dropped pretty significantly over the year, on average. I mean, it's really hard to calculate inference costs because there are so many different factors and it's really situational depending on the workload and how much caching is going on and things like that. But overall it's a lot cheaper to do inference now than it was a few months ago.

But again, I feel like if you're betting this $2 trillion IPO on the fact that we're going to keep getting better and cheaper at inference, right? I mean, I know Moore's Law is kind of a thing of the past, but at this point, what if we run up against another compute bottleneck and inference stops getting cheaper before they need it to?

Obviously any IPO prospectus is one big document about risk, right? Like, "Hey, you might make a ton of money investing in this company, or we might go complete belly up and you lose everything," right? That's always a possibility.

Right. And they still haven't demonstrated that the use case for AI is wide enough at volume that they claim it is. I mean, in certain sectors it's pretty obvious now there's going to be AI for a long time. Coding, everyone kind of agrees that works and we know how to manage that. And then there will be adjacent fields to that. But once you start getting into more general office work and regular business tasks that are not super-compute heavy, I don't know. It's a good question. We'll see if people are going to use it that broadly, but I just see it being overly optimistic.

The big question I have right now is: Is there enough user demand to support even a $200 billion a year revenue stream? Because even going off just commitments that they can't get out of made in the first half of this year, that's $417 billion running out through about 2033 to 2036.

I think the upper end of your estimate was a total, including newer commitments, of about $807 billion. At the lower end, $782 billion at the lower end. That's not that much of a difference when you're looking at hundreds of billions of dollars.

But if they can't make a profit with a two to one revenue-to-compute ratio — if they have to make twice as much in revenue in order to pay for their compute and still not break even — you extrapolate this out and they're going to have to be making $200 billion plus, assuming no additional compute contracts are made during that period over the next year, which is definitely not going to happen. They've already said they're going to keep making compute contracts. So this number just keeps getting more absurd the further out you go, unless inference magically gets dirt cheap, which we haven't seen.

Right. And it could cap. You know, I think also you made a really good point in your story, Tobias, when you mentioned that some of their biggest customers are also some of their biggest competitors. They're leasing space from hyperscalers, they're making deals with people to host their compute. But these are also companies that are operating their own AI models. And you might end up in a situation where they're like an MVNO, which, if anyone's not familiar with a mobile virtual network operator, is cell phone companies that are not T-Mobile, Verizon, or AT&T. Anyone who's not those big three in the United States is operating a virtual network that piggybacks on someone else's infrastructure. And when that infrastructure is busy, you get less priority. So we could see them run into a similar situation there, I imagine.

There's an interesting trend that another piece I'm working on later today touches on. Some of the AI gateways like OpenRouter are now starting to move away from just focusing on price metering and looking towards things like fastest time to tokens and all the quality of service metrics in terms of the way that they price and deliver the models, because inference pricing has become very commoditized in terms of what they're dealing with. They're not necessarily serving all the frontier models at very high prices. They're dealing with a lot of open weight models. And if you just focus on the lower end of the market, there's not a lot of margin there. So it makes sense to go, "Well, maybe if we deliver this faster or have better reliability or service, we can move up the price and get a little profit." And I think everyone in the industry is starting to realize that the music is stopping and they have to take a seat at some point and make the business model work. So there's going to be a lot of pressure on that. And that's also showing up in things like the licensing of models. A lot of those open weight models have seen their licenses get more restrictive over time as companies realize, "Well, maybe we don't want someone competing with us with this thing that we've made." So I think there's a lot..

That reminds me of Mistral just releasing the open weight version of Large 4, "Le Chonk". And the licensing model basically said if you intend to use this for any down-market purposes, you've got to sign a fairly restrictive agreement with us so that you're not just using this open weight model without us benefiting from it, right?

A lot of the big Chinese models, like Kimi K3, I believe were among the first to move back in this direction, basically saying, "Hey, if you're just going to deploy this internally, we don't care." If this is just for your enterprise, fine, but if you're going to be selling an API service like OpenRouter around it, you gotta cut us in. So there is definitely that. And Anthropic in their S-1 – again, every S-1 reads like a doomsday prophecy. And this S-1 of the things that they raise: open models are a threat on multiple levels, one of them being that a lot of their customers are startups sensitive to economic downturn. So those customers will likely be the first to jump ship to cheaper alternatives that are maybe not as good, but they can afford if the economy runs into any issues.

I wonder if that'll happen or not, right?

Was it Elon Musk who was tweeting about the end of the neoclouds recently? With financing getting tighter, a lot of the neoclouds living on borrowed money are going to find it harder to sustain their loans and are not going to survive this. So there will be a shakeout at some point. Does it hit the big companies? I don't know. All the cloud providers look pretty happy because they get business regardless. Even if Google's AI models are not first in people's minds, they're still serving all of this stuff.

We've said that on multiple episodes, and in multiple articles we've written, right? Basically, if the AI industry does implode, Google's going to be fine, Amazon's going to be fine, Microsoft's going to be fine; these guys have other businesses. Anthropic and OpenAI, not so much. That's all they do. And in many cases they're renting compute space from these other providers. So they might take a bit of a hit there, but by and large, they're going to be okay. They've got compute, they'll turn it around, they'll find other people to use it. Which is interesting, from your article, Tobias, you kind of summarize that the entire pitch this IPO makes is that bigger is better, right? But as we were just talking about, there are a lot of reasons to say that's probably not the case. It makes me wonder if they're still living in the token-maxxing era, whereas I just wrote a story this week about AWS telling its engineers to back off, stop using so many tokens, be more judicious, use AI well, don't just use it. And Microsoft said this months ago in August – they were saying tokenmaxxing doesn't factor into how they want to do business. So you've got two very big consumers of AI basically saying, "Y'all need to slow it down and be more purposeful." So, bigger isn't necessarily...

Anthropic's business is predicated on the idea that more compute means more revenue. However, the disconnect is: Can revenue scale fast enough? Is there enough user base? Is there enough token demand to support the scale they need to cash the checks they've already written? And it really looks like a house of cards. They warn about this in the S-1 – they have to – that if their revenue can't keep up with their compute commitments, they could default. And that default could turn into a cascade where if they can't pay one bill, they can't get enough compute to generate revenue necessary to pay the next bill, and it all falls apart.

If it happens to Anthropic, the other AI frontier labs are not far behind, because that's going to be a symptom of a larger problem. And that's that people are basically saying what a lot of non-AI companies or companies that do AI along with other things, like AWS, are saying: We don't need these massive frontier models for the vast majority of business purposes. They're not necessary.

Right. A lot of the enterprise AI products you see now are about trying to figure out ways to reduce that cost, too.You have some sort of gateway or harness system that looks at your jobs and routes them to an appropriately cheap model so that most of the time you're not using top-tier intelligence; maybe you're using a decision model, a regular classifier, or something like Gemma to do language translation. You don't always have to use that expensive model, and that price pressure is going to hit them, too.

To Tom's point, Cadence Systems, which does a lot of electronic design automation and circuit board layout, just rolled out a new product line called Maestro that's built around Nvidia's Nemotron open-weights models. The idea is that they had been using proprietary APIs to power their agents that assist engineers with PCB layout and chip design, but those agents generate a ton of data that could be used to train and fine-tune open weight models. So their latest pitch is, "Hey, we know our customers like this, but it's getting expensive to continue using these proprietary models from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google. So we're going to give you a way to take an inexpensive model, use the proprietary model to generate training data that we can use to fine-tune this open model, and then you can decide how much of the work you want done on the expensive proprietary models versus the cheap open models. You can deploy those models on-prem, in our cloud, or on your preferred cloud. Just use our agent platform and pay the subscription fee."

I can't imagine most businesses are going to fork over all this money to proprietary model providers when they don't need those resources. It really makes me wonder how much of this IPO is forecasting the bursting of the bubble. I feel sometimes like we talk about the AI bubble bursting like doomsday prophecies: "It's happening now!" But there have been more signs recently. Chinese AI stocks have been hammered recently. There have been recent earnings reports from American companies that have not looked  Yeah.

Google was hammered; they lost like $500 billion in stock value based on the fact that their search was underperforming

That's that one I wasn't able to think of, that minor little blip, right?

AI overviews not monetizing as well. So there's a lot, yeah.

I would agree that Anthropic's survival depends fairly heavily on pushing the frontier forward. In order to do that, it needs a disproportionate amount of compute that it may not be able to afford on a continuing basis, especially if Microsoft, Google, and all of these cloud CSPs that provide compute for them and are among their biggest customers decide, "We don't really need cloud for this. We've reached a point where our own open-weights models or small proprietary models are good enough for drafting emails or generating code bases for our customers."

So they're going to start buying fewer tokens from Anthropic or OpenAI when they eventually IPO. They're likely to go through very similar challenges because they're also getting most of their compute from companies like Oracle and Microsoft at this point.

Which was one of the questions I wanted to ask as we wrapped up: Do you think OpenAI is going to be in any better position once their IPO comes out? Because neither of them owns a lot of their compute, and OpenAI's attempts to build its own compute seem to have fizzled out a bit. Could they be in a better position or is it going to be more of the same?

I don't know with OpenAI whether they're going to be able to overcome the same risks that Anthropic has. It does feel like Anthropic is sidestepping a lot of hard questions by pushing forward with their IPO now.

With Anthropic going public this year, if OpenAI goes public next year, I don't think they can avoid the scrutiny, because the world is going to have woken up to the risk factors associated with these giant model houses. And I think they're going to face a much harder time with this, even before they get there.

OpenAI has the distribution of ChatGPT, which is demonstrating itself to be a useful tool that people like to use. But that's not where their monetization gold mine is going to be, unless they become the Google of AI search, and Google is already trying to get to that space, too. So I don't know how they're going to make it into the enterprise business and get the margins they need to pay back all the money they've taken.

OpenAI also has a different business model than Anthropic, and to a pretty hilarious degree, if you recall the advertisements during the Super Bowl about injecting advertisements into GPT....

The point being that OpenAI's revenue streams may be sufficiently different to insulate them from this. They have been trying to position themselves as an AI advertising company as another revenue stream, which Anthropic has flatly rejected. So it's possible that OpenAI's business model is sufficiently different by next year.

12 months is a long time in this industry. If Altman takes them public this time next year, the conversation might be very different. Having said that, Wall Street's eyes are going to be open to a lot of the risk factors in a way that Anthropic is sort of sidestepping right now by being the first really big model house to go public.

Which is honestly kind of surprising to see OpenAI press the brakes while Anthropic presses the gas. I'm assuming they saw an opportunity to get out the gate first and avoid answering the hard questions. Because OpenAI basically said, "Hey, we're going to pause our IPO while we assess these risks," given they've been in the doghouse regarding AI behaving badly this year, giving Anthropic that opportunity to scoot past and not have to deal with these things.

I think the other tell with Anthropic is actually that two-to-one compute ratio, because that's the first time that's ever happened. And it will be very telling if in their first or second public quarter that just disappears. So the timing might be related to the fact that they can now claim their cash flows are on a positive trajectory towards being cash flow positive and moving towards profitability. OpenAI delaying their IPO, I suspect, is largely because they need to get to a similar point. Otherwise, people are going to look at this and go, "This has no possibility of ever being profitable." At least with Anthropic's S-1, halfway through 2026, it looks like they could be profitable. Whether that's true in in their first public quarter is another matter until

To close us out here, I think this statement from your article, Tobias: "The only way to justify this kind of spend and risk is if you believe the upside is enormous, like the biggest economic transformation in the history of humankind enormous." And that raises my final question for you both: Is it going to be worth it? And what's the chance that Anthropic is going to flame out spectacularly in the next year or two?

Tom, I'll let you take the first crack at that one.

Yeah. I mean, I don't know how spectacular it will be. I think it's gotten to the point where it's sort of too big to fail, but I could certainly see some desperation moves where one of these big AI companies strikes a deal with Apple for distribution, because they really need the kind of money that Google was paying Apple for, or sorry, that Google is paying Apple for for distribution. And I can see something like that happening because they really need revenue. I don't really see it blowing up because it's everybody. So they're going to figure out a way to do the least harm if things go downhill. And that may mean parting out part of their businesses. Who knows?

I would tend to agree with Tom. I think about what happened with the dot-com boom as an indicator. The situation is quite a bit different because the AI industry has wormed its way so deep that it's not the surface-level situation we saw with the dot-com boom. There was a ton of fiber laid during the dot-com boom that didn't get utilized until much more recently, but it did get utilized. So I think AI is probably bigger than the internet and going to go down in the history books as the next industrial revolution, in much the same way the internet felt like that.

After the dot-com boom, it was big, but it wasn't as big as people prescribed the value to. It took another 10 years for it to actually become the thing everybody wanted it to become. It eventually rose to that valuation, but it took much longer than the market could sustain. And I think we're probably in for that.

So in other words, don't buy during the IPO. Don't buy high and hope to sell higher, because you might have 10 years to wait before you get back to that IPO valuation or above. Who knows? Maybe it'll go faster. No matter what happens, there's a good chance we're going to be right here to talk about it because this sure can fill a lot of podcasts and articles. Digital ink is going to be spilled on this topic for years to come. We hope you'll join us to hear all about it on the Kettle. Thanks for listening. ®

If there’s one theme that defined last week, it’s choice. The frontier models keep arriving, and the interesting question is no longer just “how smart is it?” but “which model fits this step, at this cost, at this latency?” That’s exactly what landed on Amazon Bedrock over the past few days: GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna from OpenAI, giving you two new points on the intelligence-versus-efficiency curve, and Claude Opus 5.5 from Anthropic, the first of the Claude 5.5 family.

GPT-6 Sol is built for the demanding, recurring work of development and operations, while GPT-6 Luna makes focused, repeatable tasks practical at high volume, and both ship at significantly lower pricing than their GPT-5.6 predecessors. Claude Opus 5.5, meanwhile, does more with fewer tokens than Opus 5 and is tuned for agentic coding and long-running tasks. #10135. Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services

LiteRT in Google Play services is Android's on-device inference runtime for custom models, handling more than a trillion inferences a day across billions of devices. Today, it gets its biggest upgrade yet: GPU inference that runs about 1.4x faster than the legacy GPU delegate, powered by ML Drift and available through the new CompiledModel API, LiteRT’s modern successor to the legacy Interpreter API.

Until now, taking advantage of this faster GPU stack required bundling LiteRT in your app. In our testing, apps that switched to LiteRT in Google Play services are about 8 MB smaller, making them faster to download and lighter on users' devices, because the runtime, including the GPU accelerator, ships once with Play services rather than inside every app. More than 100K Android apps bundle their own copy of LiteRT or TensorFlow Lite today, so the savings add up quickly as apps switch.

If your Android app runs custom ML models on CPU or GPU, we encourage you to switch to LiteRT in Google Play services. You can see it in action in the Google AI Edge Gallery app, where the Scrapbook feature's image segmentation runs on LiteRT in Google Play services.

Developers that adopt LiteRT in Google Play Services enjoy immediate benefits:

LiteRT is the evolution of TensorFlow Lite. It keeps the same .tflite model format you rely on and adds the CompiledModel API, which makes acceleration across fragmented hardware reliable:

Whether you're starting fresh or switching from bundled LiteRT, using LiteRT in Google Play services takes a few lines of code:

If you're already using the legacy Interpreter API in Google Play services, your Interpreter code keeps working on CPU when you switch to play-services-litert. To run on the GPU, move to the CompiledModel API.

Let your coding agent do the work. In Agent Mode, the new LiteRT skill for Android Studio automates the move to LiteRT in Google Play services and the CompiledModel API. Ask it to “migrate my TFLite code to CompiledModel,” or type @litert-runtime, and it switches your app to play-services-litert, rewrites your Interpreter calls, and sets up GPU acceleration with CPU fallback. It can also scaffold a new LiteRT app. Treat it as a strong first pass: review the diff, build, and compare outputs on a real device. Get the skill on GitHub.

Upgrading from legacy APIs? The legacy GPU delegate and custom delegate APIs are deprecated in favor of CompiledModel GPU acceleration and the Compiler Plugin and Dispatch APIs, and NNAPI will be removed starting in 2027. Older SDKs now receive critical security fixes only. Apps you've already shipped keep working, but plan your move to the CompiledModel API now: code that uses deprecated APIs won't compile against the latest SDK, and staying on an older SDK can cause conflicts as your other dependencies move forward. See the release notes for details.

Looking ahead, LiteRT in Google Play services is our foundation for running your own task-specific models on Android, with CPU and GPU acceleration.

#10131. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL now supports direct querying of Apache Iceberg and Parquet data in your data lake

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing a new capability for Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL that you can use to directly query operational data together with data stored in your data lake in Apache Iceberg and Apache Parquet formats, using your existing PostgreSQL applications and tools. By eliminating the need to extract, transform, and load (ETL) structured data from data lakes into your operational database, you can reduce operational complexity and simplify application development. You can also use Aurora PostgreSQL to query data from data lakes managed in Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC)-compatible catalogs, giving you access to data across a breadth of analytics systems without moving or duplicating it. Whether you’re powering real-time dashboards, enriching transactions with historical context, or building AI agents that reason over both live and archived data, you can now do it all through a single, familiar interface.

Previously, if your application needed to combine recent transactional data in Aurora with historical records stored in Amazon S3, a common approach was to build reverse ETL pipelines that duplicated data, increased infrastructure costs, and required ongoing engineering effort to keep everything synchronized. This challenge only grows as you increasingly embed AI agents into your applications, where it is impractical to predict and pre-replicate every dataset an agent might need.

DuckLabs, the team that maintains the DuckDB project, recently joined Amazon, and this capability is an example of how the efficiency of DuckDB is being integrated into our services. DuckDB is now embedded directly within Aurora PostgreSQL, so you can query live operational data (including uncommitted writes) alongside your data lake in a single query. Query processing stays within Aurora, with no additional network hops and no ETL pipelines that duplicate data. You can query Apache Iceberg tables managed through the AWS Glue Data Catalog, as well as Parquet and Iceberg data stored in Amazon S3 and S3 Tables. You do all of this using familiar PostgreSQL syntax and your existing applications and tools.

We’re excited to bring the speed and simplicity of DuckDB directly into Aurora PostgreSQL, so you and your agents can query and combine operational and Iceberg data using the familiar PostgreSQL applications, tools, and endpoints already in use. By building this capability around DuckDB, future improvements to the open source engine can continue to bring performance and functionality gains to Aurora and other AWS services.

What is newThis capability is supported on two Aurora PostgreSQL major versions: 17 (starting with 17.11) and 18 (starting with 18.6). To use it, you create an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster, attach an IAM role with the AuroraAnalytics feature, and enable the aurora_analytics extension. The IAM role is what gives Aurora access to your data in Amazon S3 and the AWS Glue Data Catalog. You then create foreign tables that point to your Iceberg or Parquet data in the data lake, and query them using familiar PostgreSQL syntax. You can complete this setup through the Amazon RDS console, or with any PostgreSQL client such as psql. The process is well documented in the Aurora PostgreSQL documentation.

You can query data across external IRC-compatible catalogs through AWS Glue Data Catalog federation. You register the external catalog once with Glue, and then create foreign tables for the tables you want to query, the same way you would for any Glue-native table. A single query can then join data stored in Aurora with Iceberg tables registered across multiple catalogs, so applications get a unified view without moving data or replacing your existing catalog investments.

Aurora also applies optimizations such as predicate pushdown and column pruning so that only the relevant data is read. This keeps queries efficient even as the underlying data grows. Frequently accessed data is also cached in your Aurora instance, so subsequent queries against the same data return faster. You can inspect this behavior per query using aurora_analytics_stat_statements(), which reports metrics such as rows scanned, bytes read from Amazon S3, and cache hits.

To see how direct querying works, I connected to my Aurora PostgreSQL database using psql and created the extension:

For my walkthrough, I set up a simple financial scenario. I have a recent_transactions table in Aurora with the last 7 days of customer transactions, and a Parquet file in Amazon S3 containing 5 years of historical transaction data. To make Aurora aware of the historical data, I created a foreign table pointing at the Parquet file in S3:

Notice the empty parentheses in the CREATE FOREIGN TABLE statement. Aurora automatically reads the schema from the Parquet file metadata, so you do not need to define columns manually. For workloads with many tables, you can skip creating them one at a time: a single IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA statement bulk-creates foreign tables for every Iceberg or Parquet table in an AWS Glue Data Catalog database, inferring schemas automatically.

With both tables in place, I ran a single query that combines the recent operational data in Aurora with the historical data in S3:

The result shows both recent and historical transactions in a single result set. The 7 most recent rows come from Aurora, and the rest come directly from the Parquet file in S3. DuckDB handles the analytical scan of the Parquet data under the hood, while Aurora handles the operational data. That single query would have previously required a pipeline to move the historical data into the database first.

If a query pattern needs single-digit-millisecond latency, you can materialize data from the data lake into a native Aurora PostgreSQL table using familiar commands such as CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, INSERT INTO ... SELECT, or MERGE INTO. The materialized table lives in Aurora and is queried like any other PostgreSQL table, giving you a low-latency path for hot data without operating a separate ingestion pipeline. The read queries can run on any Aurora PostgreSQL instance in your cluster, whether the writer or a read replica, so you can offload analytical scans from your operational workload. The materialization commands write data into Aurora, so they run on the writer instance.

Get started today Direct querying of Apache Iceberg and Parquet data from Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL is available today in all commercial AWS Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, at no additional charge. You pay only for the incremental Aurora compute the queries consume and Amazon S3 request costs for reading data lake files.

To learn more, visit the Amazon Aurora features page, read the Aurora PostgreSQL documentation, or try it in the Amazon RDS console. We welcome your feedback through AWS re:Post or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Esra Kayabali is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, specializing in analytics, including data warehousing, data lakes, big data analytics, batch and real-time data streaming, and data integration. She has more than ten years of software development and solution architecture experience. She is passionate about collaborative learning, knowledge sharing, and guiding community in their cloud technologies journey.

#10129. Frozen part II: Hackers remotely defrost produce in Euro supermarkets ... again

Let it go (bad): Dozens of stores report mass food wastage as managers start their week in puddles

The cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers in Europe continue, as a slew of grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden report widespread food wastage as a result of miscreants raising the temperatures to highs of 50ºC (122°F).

In Belgium, around 40 Delhaize stores were affected after the attackers reportedly switched fridges and freezers into defrost mode overnight, between Sunday and Monday, resulting in stock issues.

Diego Louwers, a Proxy Delhaize store manager in Overijse, near Brussels, told RTL Info that the consequences of the cyberattacks were "catastrophic," forcing the store to throw out the entirety of its fresh and frozen products.

"We can't have anything worse in our line of work," he said. "We have to throw away all of our merchandise, and it's both heartbreaking and very complicated operationally."

A Delhaize spokesperson said it took steps to ensure stores remain stocked, although fresh and frozen products are "temporarily somewhat limited."

"On Monday, 2 November, we identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen of our stores," they said.

"We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational and ensure that our customers can continue to do their shopping as usual.

"In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centres are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores.

"We are, of course, continuing to ensure that our products are stored and presented under optimal conditions, so that we can provide our customers with the quality and freshness they have come to expect from us."

Around 15 Carrefour stores are also reportedly affected, as are sites operated by Intermarché, Spar, and Shop & Go stores located at Q8 service stations.

Belgium’s De Laet & Van Haver chain of butcher shops reported temperature rises in its appliances too, but followed up with a statement on Monday saying there was no impact on its produce, and all stores remain open.

Simultaneously, similar issues have affected Swedish grocery chain ICA, which confirmed attacks on a "small number of stores."

"We can confirm that we have been informed of an incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network," a company spokesperson said.

"The incident impacted the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation."

ICA did not respond to questions about the scale of food wastage nor when normal operations are expected to continue.

One store, ICA Nära in Böda on Öland, said via social media that it is open today but has no fresh or frozen produce to sell.

"Unfortunately, we are one of the stores whose refrigerators and freezers have been hacked," it said. "We are open as usual, but unfortunately we have no refrigerators and freezers to sell.

"We have no status on when the refrigerators and freezers are expected to be up and running again."

The store manager, Mats Olsson, told SVT that he arrived to work on Monday morning and was greeted by a puddle of water and freezers set to 55 degrees C – a tale echoed by other managers across the country.

Coop stores are affected by similar attacks too, with six locations in central Sweden experiencing fridge-freezer issues, according to a company spokesperson.

Likewise, at least 13 SuperValue stores in Ireland are also affected, with fresh and frozen food being thrown out, according to parent company Musgrave speaking to RTE.

The news comes less than a month after various grocery chains in France resorted to discarding bucketfuls of produce after their appliances were remotely defrosted by cybercrooks.

Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others were hit with cyberattacks in mid-October, and hundreds of stores across the chains were reportedly impacted.

At least some of the affected stores were running outdated firmware on their Danfoss refrigeration controllers, and shortly after the attacks were confirmed, CERT-FR published an alert pertaining to numerous Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controller compromises.

Other retailers, such as Coopérative U, confirmed they were not Danfoss customers.

It remains unclear if the latest attacks across Europe used the same methods as those used for the disruption in France last month.

None of the companies that spoke to The Register on Monday responded to questions about who was behind the intrusions. ®

#10128. Amazon S3 Vectors now supports metadata pre-filtering for higher recall on filtered searches

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing metadata pre-filtering for Amazon S3 Vectors, which delivers higher recall on filtered queries by evaluating your metadata filter before the similarity search. You can filter on attributes such as tenant, category, status, or time, and pre-filtering adds prefix matching with $startsWith for paths, URLs, and hierarchical keys. Each vector carries up to 2 KB of filterable metadata, and a single query supports up to 100 filter constraints. There is no additional cost, no re-ingestion, and no change to your queries.

Most applications never search a whole index. They search the part of it that belongs to a particular user, account, or category, and they express that scope as a metadata filter. Semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic applications all need the same thing from a filtered query: a similarity search that covers the vectors matching the filter, and returns the closest of them. With pre-filtering, a filtered query returns more of the relevant matches your index contains, giving you higher recall on filtered searches.

Common use cases Pre-filtering applies wherever results have to be both relevant and correctly scoped:

How pre-filtering works Each vector in an S3 Vectors index can carry application-defined metadata, and a query can filter on those fields.

Every vector index has an index mode. On an index whose index mode is ENHANCED, S3 Vectors resolves your filter first, then searches only the vectors that match. On an index whose index mode is CLASSIC, S3 Vectors performs the vector search and filter evaluation in tandem, validating each candidate vector against your filter as it searches. Existing indexes use CLASSIC until you update them.

Consider a support knowledge base of 8 million tickets, where an agent searches one customer’s history for a recurring error. If that customer accounts for 400 of those tickets, resolving customer_id first means the similarity search runs across all 400 of them, so the agent sees that customer’s prior occurrences. Before the index was updated, the same query drew its candidates from the full 8 million, and the result set contained fewer of that customer’s matching tickets.

On highly selective filters, pre-filtering returns up to 5x more of the matching vectors than the same query returned before on CLASSIC indexes.

Getting started Before you start, make sure your IAM policy grants permissions for the new actions.

You can get started in three steps. The walkthrough below builds a small product-catalog index and runs a selective filter against it, the same pattern you would use for a multi-tenant RAG store or a document search scoped to one client.

The dimension must match the output size of your embedding model, and distance-metric should match how that model was trained (cosine is common for text embeddings). Second, write vectors with the PutVectors API, attaching up to 2 KB of filterable metadata to each vector:

Each vector carries the attributes your application filters on. In this example, tenant_id scopes results to a single customer, category narrows by document type, created_date records when the document was created, and active is a boolean flag. By default every metadata field is filterable, so you can query on any of them without declaring a schema up front.

Third, run a filtered similarity query with the QueryVectors API. The filter uses a compact JSON syntax where a bare key-value pair is an equality match, and operators such as $and, $or, and $gt combine or refine conditions. Pass --return-metadata so the query returns each vector’s metadata:

The expected result is a single vector, doc-001, the only one matching all three filter conditions (tenant_id, category, and active):

S3 Vectors first narrows the search space to vectors matching all three filter conditions, then returns the 50 most similar vectors from that subset. Because the filter is applied before the search, those results are drawn from across all the vectors that match it.

Prefix matching with $startsWith Pre-filtering adds a prefix match operator for filtering on paths, URLs, and hierarchical keys. A document store that encodes case and folder structure into a document ID can scope a search to a subtree in one condition:

$startsWith joins the existing operators: equality, numeric range, set membership, existence checks, and boolean logic with $and and $or.

Turning on pre-filtering for existing indexes Call UpdateIndexMode on an existing index to turn on pre-filtering:

Pre-filtering takes effect in place. Your existing vectors are not re-ingested, your queries do not change, and the new filter operators are available immediately.

Here is the difference on the same index and the same query. Before the update, a query scoped to one tenant returns two of the ten results requested:

After the update, the same query returns a full result set drawn from across that tenant’s documents:

Rolling out across your indexes Once you have validated pre-filtering on an index, set the default index mode on the vector bucket so that new indexes use ENHANCED without a follow-up call:

To bring the rest of your existing indexes across, list them and check the index mode on each one, then call UpdateIndexMode on the ones still using CLASSIC:

Now available Metadata pre-filtering is available at no additional cost in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions. You pay standard S3 Vectors pricing for storage, PUT requests, and queries. For full pricing details, visit the Amazon S3 pricing page. For regional availability, visit Amazon S3 Vectors Regions and quotas.

Whether you’re scoping a RAG application to one tenant, scoping an agent’s searches to one user’s documents, or narrowing a catalog search to a licensing window, pre-filtering lets you apply those filters without trading away recall. To learn more and get started, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation. Send feedback to AWS re:Post for S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#10126. Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents

Agent-User Interactions are now evolving from text exchanges to rich UIs. Until recently, most conversations looked like this:

User: "Find me a holiday package to Bali in March." Agent: (six packages in prose, each with dates, hotel, flights, price) User: "The five-night one with breakfast." Agent: "Here's the link. You can book it on the operator's site."

Agents could plan the trip, but everything came back as walls of text. They had no standard way to render a selectable list of packages, a map of the destinations, or a date picker to carry you through the rest of the booking, inside the conversation itself.

Generative UI is the layer that lets agents build interfaces at runtime, shaped by what each request needs - giving users a rich, interactive experience. Implementing that takes two pieces: a way to describe the UI and an agentic stack that connects your agent to your application and renders that UI.

Generative UI covers a spectrum of approaches, from using predefined higher order components, to enabling your AI agent to have the flexibility to decide how to build the UI.

At the controlled end, you build each component ahead of time, and the agent picks which one to render and with what data. It's brand-safe but it does not allow for deep customization and personalization based on the user’s intent. At the open end, the agent returns a raw UI program written in HTML, Javascript and/or Dart that renders inside a sandboxed iframe. That covers anything you did not plan for, at the cost of a surface that drifts from your design system and executes code a model wrote.

A2UI works through the entire spectrum. It participates in controlled generation with decision models like Typesafe’s Jev and also open-ended code generation that may output A2UI JSON messages. The declarative mode, where agents assemble pre-declared components and functions, is the most popular. A2UI is the framework-agnostic standard for declaring UI intent, so local or remote agents can generate your UI from your existing component catalog using a common language.

Frontend developers can now ship the building blocks once, and the agent composes them for each request.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

The Basic Catalog ships 18 general-purpose primitives across layout, display, input, and containers. The agent can compose entirely different interfaces from the same 18 primitives, depending on what the request needs.

The Basic Catalog is deliberately sparse, so most production apps define their own custom catalog. A custom component can be anything your frontend already renders, including a live map the agent fills with coordinates while your renderer draws the route.

CopilotKit is built on AG-UI (Agent-User Interaction Protocol), which supports A2UI payload and provides Agent SDKs across many agentic backends.

Your agent emits A2UI operations. AG-UI carries them to the client as typed events. When the user takes any action, the values are sent back along the same stream.

A2UI works with any AG-UI compatible agent. Frameworks like Google ADK, LangChain, Mastra and Strands are all AG-UI compatible, so the setup is identical whichever one your agent runs on.

Setup comes down to two things: connecting your agent to CopilotKit, and defining which components the agent is allowed to use.

Using Google ADK as the example, the ag_ui_adk package wraps any ADK agent and serves it as an AG-UI endpoint on FastAPI:

On the app side, you register that endpoint with the CopilotKit runtime at /api/copilotkit. It's a few lines of standard setup, covered in the Google ADK quickstart, and it needs nothing A2UI-specific.

A2UI itself turns on from the client, where your components already are. Define what the agent is allowed to draw, map each definition to a renderer, and pass the catalog to the CopilotKit provider.

The description goes into the agent's prompt, so the model knows when to reach for FlightCard instead of a generic card. The Zod schema validates the props it sends back.

The A2UI configuration can be set up ahead of time on the server, or it can be created dynamically, shipped from the client to the server with the request. The ADK code above used dynamic configuration which is why it used generate_a2ui without defining it. The docs cover both approaches.

That’s the CopilotKit path. You can also consume the event stream directly with @ag-ui/client and hand the A2UI operations to any compliant renderer: @a2ui/react, or the Flutter, Lit, or Angular equivalent.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Most agent-generated UI is one-shot. The agent draws something, you read it, and it goes stale the moment anything changes.

A2UI surfaces are bi-directional and the components are reactive, which makes multi-step flows possible. Any action the user takes on the interface (picking dates, choosing a flight, entering passenger details) travels back along the same stream, and the agent re-emits the surface from there using those values.

Here is a high-level architecture example of an end-to-end booking flow, with an AG-UI agent on Cloud Run streaming A2UI surfaces to a CopilotKit frontend.

Two things make the round trip work: inputs bound to a data path, and a button carrying an action that names which paths to send back.

Validation runs on the client, so a bad email shows an error inline without a model call. Nothing reaches the agent until the button fires.

Then the client sends the bound values, and the agent re-emits against the same surfaceId. That is how the whole flow lives on one surface: flight search, results, passenger details, and confirmation.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Every AG-UI integration inherets these benefits, so you don't have to build them yourself:

Create a complete A2UI + CopilotKit application. This creates a starter A2UI application with Copilotkit Agent integration.

The CopilotKit Dojo has runnable A2UI demos: fixed server-side schema, dynamic schema against a custom catalog, and an error-recovery example where an invalid first render heals into a valid one.

Explore how to build Generative UI Agents with CopilotKit, or dive into A2UI documentation to learn how to integrate A2UI with any framework of your choice.

#10125. Microsoft's Canada timezone troubles leave admins fixing calendars, pretending they're in Bogota

Canadian regions stop turning back the clocks, Microsoft wishes it could

Microsoft has discovered once again that few things strike fear into the heart of a software engineer quite like a government deciding to fiddle with the clocks.

Parts of Canada stopped observing seasonal clock changes on November 1, leaving affected areas of British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba permanently on UTC-07:00, UTC-06:00 and UTC-05:00 respectively. Unfortunately, Microsoft's sprawling software empire hasn't entirely caught up.

The company has confirmed problems across a chunk of its software estate, leaving some customers facing incorrect times, broken schedules and a collection of workarounds while Redmond catches up.

Outlook users have been left with the most homework. Switching to the new Canadian time zones won't automatically update existing calendar entries, meaning that meetings scheduled after November 1 are potentially an hour out of whack.

Microsoft advises users to change their Outlook calendar time zone, then update upcoming events and meetings to use it. For meetings involving other people, only the organizer can make the change.

Recurring meetings come with an additional treat: changing the time zone resets any previously moved occurrences, which then have to be recreated. Anyone with a calendar full of recurring meetings may wish to put the kettle on first.

Microsoft is working on an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet to remediate non-recurring meetings, but according to its guidance, that's not due until later this week. A fix for recurring meetings remains "in development," with an ETA yet to be confirmed.

Things get stranger with Power Automate and Fabric, where Microsoft's temporary fix involves pretending you're somewhere else entirely. Depending on the product and province, that could mean Saskatchewan, Arizona or, for Manitobans, Bogota. Because apparently time zones weren't confusing enough already.

SharePoint On-Prem customers, meanwhile, have to wait until November 10 for the correct time zones to arrive, while Power Pages users could see server-formatted dates appear an hour out until a service fix lands. Microsoft's current milestone for that is December 12.

Admins dealing with the fallout aren't exactly delighted. One sysadmin on Reddit said Microsoft's guidance had been "terrible" and claimed to have written roughly 900 lines of PowerShell to change users' Outlook settings and manually adjust calendar events. Others described switching systems to Saskatchewan time while waiting for Microsoft's new zones to settle in.

Microsoft published its guidance on October 26, less than a week before the change took effect, and was still adding affected products and workarounds four days later. Meanwhile, admins were urged to test calendars, recurring meetings, and schedules before the November 1 switch, leaving little time to find out what might break.

If any of this sounds familiar, it's because time has caused trouble for Microsoft before. In 2022, Chile delayed its switch to daylight saving time by a week. Microsoft responded by warning that Windows clocks could be wrong, scheduled tasks could run at unexpected times, and timestamps on files, transactions, and logs could end up an hour out.

Four years later, governments are still messing with time and software is still apparently objecting. ®

#10124. Amazon S3 Tables now support all Apache Iceberg V3 data types

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Amazon S3 Tables now support all data types in the Apache Iceberg V3 specification. You can create V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables to take advantage of V3 features like deletion vectors, row lineage, and new data types such as variant, nanosecond timestamps, unknown, geometry, and geography.

Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for managing large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data in open Parquet files in data lakes on object storage like Amazon S3. Amazon S3 Tables offer storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with fully managed features like automatic compaction, maintenance, replication, and Intelligent-Tiering.

Teams running analytics on Apache Iceberg V2 tables often hit the same limits as their data grows. A compliance request to delete 50,000 user records from a 2-billion-row table leaves behind positional delete files that slow queries until compaction runs. Semi-structured events land as JSON strings that every query has to parse. Geospatial coordinates and nanosecond-precision timestamps get encoded as strings or integers. Each workaround adds storage cost, query latency, and pipeline code. With V3, Iceberg solves these challenges by offering native support for semi-structured and geospatial data, faster row-level operations, and built-in row lineage for data governance.

Starting today, Amazon S3 Tables support all V3 data types, including variant, nanosecond timestamps, geometry, geography, and unknown, along with deletion vectors and row lineage. You can create new V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables in place, and S3 Tables continue to run compaction and maintenance for you.

Apache Iceberg V3 V3 is the latest version of the Iceberg specification. Among its many improvements, V3 introduces capabilities that address the most common pain points in V2. This includes:

Deletion vectors replace V2’s positional delete files with a compact binary format. That 50,000-row compliance delete now writes a single deletion vector file instead of thousands of small deletes, significantly reducing compaction time and delete file overhead.

Row lineage adds _row_id and _last_updated_sequence_number to each record automatically. Your downstream pipelines can query these fields to find changed rows without scanning the full table.

New data types let you store semi-structured, geospatial, and nanosecond-precision data natively instead of encoding it as strings or integers:

Variant data type stores semi-structured data in columnar format. During writes, the engine shreds variant data into hidden columns and collects statistics. At query time, those statistics enable file pruning that significantly reduces I/O compared to parsing JSON strings.

The following sections walk through how to use these V3 capabilities in practice, with examples that show how to create tables, work with the new data types, and manage data at scale.

Getting started A retail analytics team tracks user behavior across web and mobile apps. Each event has a different structure: page views include URLs and duration, purchases include items and amounts, and searches include query terms and result counts. With V3’s variant type, you store all event shapes in one table without predefined schemas:

Insert events with different payload shapes without worrying about schema evolution:

Now query the variant column directly, without PARSE_JSON at read time. With Amazon EMR Spark, use variant_get:

To enable deletion vectors for write operations, configure merge-on-read mode:

Now when you run a compliance delete, V3 writes a small deletion vector instead of rewriting data files:

S3 Tables compaction handles these deletion vector files automatically on the next maintenance cycle.

Upgrading from V2 AWS provides backwards compatibility for both versions to minimize disruption during migration to V3. Existing V2 readers continue to work on upgraded tables until you’re ready to fully adopt V3 features. For more details, see the S3 Tables Iceberg V3 documentation. Upgrade an existing table atomically without rewriting data:

On the next compaction cycle, S3 Tables remove old V2 delete files. New modifications use deletion vectors automatically. Row lineage fields initialize on the first data modification after the upgrade.

This is a one-way operation. The Apache Iceberg specification does not support downgrading from V3 to V2. Verify that all engines accessing the table support V3 before upgrading.

Using row lineage for incremental pipelines After your table has V3 data, use row lineage to build efficient incremental pipelines:

This returns only rows modified after sequence number 42. Your downstream jobs can checkpoint this value and process only new changes on each run, instead of scanning the full table.

Compatibility across AWS analytics services AWS offers the broadest native Apache Iceberg support of any major cloud provider, with Iceberg-compatible services at every layer of the data stack: ingestion, storage, catalog, and analytics. You can store and automatically optimize V3 tables in Amazon S3 Tables, write data with Amazon EMR Spark, integrate and manage data with AWS Glue, and run analytics with Amazon Redshift. To learn more about AWS analytics support for V3, see the Apache Iceberg on AWS prescriptive guidance.

Both S3 Tables and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) API, enabling interoperability across engines regardless of the catalog endpoint.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables support for all Apache Iceberg V3 data types is now available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables are supported. Apache Iceberg V3 support is available at no additional charge; standard S3 Tables pricing applies.

To get started, visit the Amazon S3 Tables documentation or create a table bucket from the Amazon S3 console. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. Send feedback to AWS re:Post or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#10121. UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The United Arab Emirates says it's creating a foundation of security and safety as it transforms its public service footprint.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) plans to move half of its government operations, services, and sectors to autonomous AI agents over the next two years, prompting a conversation around how it intends to secure and monitor those AI agents.

To that end, the UAE has implemented a "control tower agent," conducts audits using agents and humans, and considers monitoring and establishing trust as critical to its efforts, Omar Sultan Al Olama, minister of state for artificial intelligence, told attendees on Oct. 14 at the World Economic Forum's (WEF) Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai. Security and trust are critical to achieving the nation's goal of autonomous government systems that improve quality of life and to not risk harm to citizens, he said.

"There is an oversight that ensures that we understand what agents are doing, how they're taking certain actions — there's a continuous audit that is being done," Al Olama told attendees. "There's an audit that's done by agents, and there's an audit that's done by humans to ensure that this doesn't go haywire in any way, shape, or form."

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

In April, the UAE Cabinet unveiled a framework to transition 50% of the federal government's sectors, services, and operations to agentic AI within two years. The effort aims to redesign government policies and processes to embrace AI capabilities, creating "smart systems" that take proactive actions to reduce operational costs, provide more efficient services to citizens, and make government more efficient, according to public notes from the meeting.

The UAE's plans for agentic AI should not be surprising. While global AI diffusion — a measure of the number of adults who used a generative AI product in a specific period — hit 19% in the second quarter of 2026, the United Arab Emirates has taken the lead globally with more than 73% of the population using AI during the quarter, according to Microsoft's "Global AI Diffusion: Q2 2026 Trends and Insights" report.

Yet at the same time, the risk landscape is changing, often because of AI use. The UAE has already faced significant increases in attacks over the past two years, many powered by AI agents, as political tensions and military conflicts continue to build in the region.

The government's Agentic AI Project will roll out in several phases across ministries and federal entities, it said. On Oct. 9, the Ministerial Council for Artificial Intelligence and Development reviewed the first phase of the project, focused on "building government capabilities, surveying and assessing government services, operations and tasks, and setting priorities," according to a statement announcing the review. The second phase will establish a national technical ecosystem for agentic AI, under the name "FedAI," that will enable government agencies to develop and operate agentic services and conduct internal competitions, such as hackathons, to develop applications.

Related:Australian Gov't Weighs Mandatory AI Incident Reporting

The UAE leads other nations with 73% of its population using generative AI at least once in the quarter. Source: Microsoft

The coming phase includes training for government employees in agentic AI development and generative AI technology to provide a foundation for the future, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahya, one of the UAE's two vice presidents and deputy prime minister, said in the statement.

"We are building a government system that is smarter, more flexible, and more proactive; a system that leverages agentic AI to develop services, operations, and tasks, and to shape policies and decisions," he said. "This should be achieved in a secure and reliable digital infrastructure, in a way that strengthens the readiness of the UAE Government for the future and reinforces its leadership in developing government work models."

Security and trust are critical for operations conducted by agentic AI systems, and that means monitoring and auditing agentic activity, says Evin McMullen, co-founder and CEO of AmanTrue, an Abu Dhabi-based startup creating a governance control layer for agentic AI.

Related:EU Cyber Resilience Act to Enforce New Reporting Requirements

"Any institution, certainly a government that's adopting AI agents at scale, [and] especially related to internal operations or citizen services, should be able to show who acted in the event of an agent action," she says. "Which agent, who authorized it — which human being and associated institution — and what the limits or definition of the task was."

Governance is a key problem facing deployments of AI agents. Because of their often transitory nature, their ability to obscure on whose behalf they are acting, and their occasional penchant for going rogue, agents and their actions need to be tracked closely. However, 29% of security teams have discovered unknown AI agents running in production that were never registered, and nine in 10 organizations had a security incident in the past year attributable to agentic AI, according to an Oct. 20 report released by cloud-computing and AI-infrastructure platform ServiceNow.

As more organizations adopt agentic services, governance becomes more important, especially when multiple organizations work through agents on the same data and services, says AmanTrue's McMullen.

"When many services intend to act through the coordination of agents, an institution has to be able to show which agents specifically accessed a given data record on whose authority, within what defined limits, with what output," she says.

Gaining trust in autonomous systems will require that the AI agents are closely monitored, tracked, and controlled, the UAE's Al Olama said at the World Economic Forum event.

"The government's only currency is trust," he said, adding that "if the government makes one wrong decision, you lose a lot of that currency. ... The same would be true with AI. Once we have one breakthrough event, where AI exits the sandbox and goes and harms people, I think it's going to take a long time for us to regain that trust."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. #10120. Announcing AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered intelligence to optimize your cloud environment (preview)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing the public preview of AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered service that analyzes your AWS environment to deliver targeted, contextual recommendations for improving your applications’ cost, security, performance, and resilience. The AWS Well-Architected Agent analyzes your infrastructure, understands unique business goals, and delivers contextual recommendations with ready-to-implement fixes. It delivers context-aware optimization without relying on manual audits or generic checklists.

The agent evaluates your environment as an experienced cloud architect would. It automatically correlates utilization metrics, resource configurations, and application topology, and analyzes against Well-Architected best practices across 65+ AWS services. It generates recommendations aligned to your declared business goals, delivers implementation packages with every finding, and surfaces cross-pillar trade-offs making it simpler to remediate the findings.

Here are the three main features of this service:

AWS Well-Architected Agent in action To get started, create an agent profile to define the scope of what Well-Architected Agent can access and provide recommendations on, complete the IAM role setup to access resources, conduct architecture review, and remediate recommendations.

Create an agent profile In the AWS Well-Architected console, choose Get started with Well-Architected Agent. You can define an agent profile that specifies which AWS accounts and applications to monitor, which optimization pillars to focus on, and the permissions required.

You can choose AWS accounts or AWS Regions to monitor and optimization pillars that matter most to your business. You can also set goals for each pillar: cost optimization, performance, resilience, and security.

To give access to the agent for your AWS environment, provision customer-managed IAM roles the agent uses to read resource configurations, utilization metrics, and application topology. To learn more, visit the IAM prerequisite for AWS Well-Architected Agent.

When you choose Get Started, the agent creates your agent profile. Resource and application recommendations will be generated within 24 hours after profile creation.

You can conduct an architecture review on pre-deployment workloads by uploading an IaC project in Terraform, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) to be analyzed. Choose Conduct architecture review in the dashboard, upload a.zip file containing IaC project or repository file, and select which Well-Architected lens to use for reviewing your infrastructure.

You can define your applications to add context which will enhance the relevancy and further contextualize recommendations. Choose Add application context in the dashboard, add your applications with AWS accounts, AWS Regions, AWS services, tags if you want to narrow the scope to specific resources, and the details of applications.

Review prioritized recommendations and start remediating Now you can see generated prioritized recommendations generated by the agent across your resources and applications, selected pillars, ranked against your declared goals, with automation-ready remediation included.

When you choose the specific recommendation, you can see the details, insights into why the agent are suggesting the recommendation, impacts and trade-off, and recommended fixes across affected AWS resources.

Choose Start remediation to address recommended fixes. You can choose the console, updated IaC template, CLI commands to remediate by the resolution type. It provides detailed step-by-step instructions and you can roll out this instruction and verify the result.

When you choose Using updated IaC template, the agent provides the code changes needed to update your existing IaC templates such as the CDK function shown above which you can copy directly into your codebase.

You can also configure API access to integrate recommendations directly into your existing development and operations workflows. To interact with the agent programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the AWS Well-Architected Agent documentation.

Things to know Here are some things that you should know about the Well-Architected Agent.

You can still use existing AWS Well-Architected Tool to manually evaluate your cloud architecture with user-defined lenses that measure your workload using your own best practices.

Join the preview Access to the AWS Well-Architected Agent and its recommendations is available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). You can onboard workloads from any AWS commercial Region. AWS Well-Architected Agent is delivered by AWS Support and available to AWS customers with an AWS Support plan.

Give it a try today in the AWS Well-Architected console and send feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.

#10118. Nuclear threats and street brawls: Russia, Ukraine report attacks on their emergency alert apps

Within minutes of a ceasefire lifting in Kherson, Ukraine’s citizens were pummelled with threatening notifications

Cyberattacks on both Russia’s and Ukraine’s emergency alert apps resulted in fake messages about missile and nuclear strikes broadcast to the public.

Officials from both countries confirmed the attacks, which occurred at similar times, on Sunday evening.

According to public statements and messages sent via social media, Ukraine’s alert app was hit first, with the country’s Air Force quick to dispel nuclear fears.

"The Air Alert app has likely been compromised," it said via Telegram at around 2100 UTC. "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel!"

At around 0030 UTC on Monday, Russia's Ministry of Emergency Situations confirmed the country’s app had also been abused, with fake messages sent to citizens' devices.

"Attention! The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public," it said, also via Telegram. "Work is currently underway to patch the vulnerability and restore normal operation."

The ministry issued an update around 90 minutes later, saying the app was once again functioning normally, and pointing out that an attack on the app was not the same as a compromise of the state’s national alert system.

"Citizens are alerted through primary channels: regional and municipal alert systems (sirens, loudspeakers), communication networks (SMS messaging), and television and radio broadcasts. The mobile app is merely an additional, supporting information service," it stated.

Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Affairs also issued a public announcement reminding citizens about how to receive emergency warnings while its “Alarm!” app was down. These include enabling iOS and Android emergency alerts, state-controlled sirens, and other official sources, such as the official social media accounts of Ukraine's government.

According to the messages sent to devices after the compromise of Ukraine's alert app, the fake warnings pertained to various threats, such as street fights in Kyiv, chemical attacks, and radiation hazards.

Alerts about the threat of nuclear fallout from official government warning systems would normally lead to panic, however, one of the earliest messages sent to citizens was written in Russian and referenced the "Oreshnik" missile, which was an immediate signal that the message may not be genuine.

Equivalent alerts sent to Russian citizens also warned of impending nuclear strikes "at all regions of Russia," referencing "P1-Sun," the name of a Ukrainian attack drone.

Oleksander Merezhko, who chairs the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee and noted the suspicious Russian-language alert, told the BBC the attack was almost certainly part of Russia's cyber war.

"It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that," he said. "It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities."

Russia has not explicitly blamed Ukraine for the attack on its app, and official sources say the app is running as normal.

Ukraine's announcement of the alert app cyberattack came almost simultaneously with the official conclusion of a six-day ceasefire in Kherson.

Russia agreed to the rare temporary suspension of conflict to allow hundreds of Ukrainians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Olehsky.

Russia did not agree to a proposed extension of the ceasefire, which officially ended at around 2100 UTC – around the same time Ukrainians began receiving fake warning messages. ®
