#10072. From the Hugging Face Hub to robot hardware with Strands Agents and LeRobot

A walkthrough of the LeRobot integration in Strands Robots - one agent loop, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot, with sim-to-real datasets in the same on-disk format and policies you swap with a string.

You have a robot, a folder of demonstration data on the Hugging Face Hub, and a new task you want it to learn. Today that takes five separate tools: one to record new demonstrations, another to train, a third to test in simulation, custom code to deploy on hardware, and yet another to coordinate when you have more than one robot. The pieces work on their own. They don't talk to each other.

Strands Robots is an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools that you compose into a single Strands agent. The integration is deliberately thin: LeRobot's own scripts handle hardware recording and calibration, and the Strands AgentTools come in for the parts an agent actually orchestrates. The simulation tool records LeRobotDatasets in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware. LerobotLocal serves policy inference behind one interface for GR00T, ACT, SmolVLA, and MolmoAct2 checkpoints. A peer mesh fans the agent out to remote robots. The dataset format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it; the agent loop is the glue.

This post walks you through five steps inside a single agent: build the agent over the LeRobot AgentTools, record a demonstration as a LeRobotDataset in simulation, run a policy on the same robot, deploy the same agent code to a physical SO-101 with one keyword argument change, and broadcast commands across a fleet over the Zenoh mesh. At the end, you can clone the working sample application from GitHub and run it on your laptop in simulation. No hardware, no GPU, no Hugging Face credentials needed for the default path. The runnable companion to this post lives at examples/lerobot/hub_to_hardware.py and hub_to_hardware.ipynb. The notebook is sim-only and Mock-policy by default.

The Strands Robots SDK exposes the LeRobot stack as AgentTools that you compose into one Strands agent. The example agent in this post does four things: record new demonstrations in simulation, push the result to the Hub as a LeRobotDataset, run a policy in simulation against that same format, and deploy the same agent code to a physical robot with one keyword argument change. When you have more than one robot, the agent can coordinate the whole fleet through a built-in peer mesh. For hardware recording and calibration, LeRobot's own CLIs (lerobot-record, lerobot-calibrate) handle the bring-up; the agent picks up from there.

Figure 1. Robot("so100") defaults to a MuJoCo-backed simulation; mode="real" returns a hardware robot driven by LeRobot. Both modes share the same DatasetRecorder and the same policy providers, so a dataset captured in sim and a dataset captured on hardware use the same on-disk LeRobotDataset format.

Two design choices make this work. First, Robot("so100") returns a simulation by default (no hardware, no risk), and mode="real" returns a hardware-backed robot driven by LeRobot. The agent code is identical across both modes. Second, the DatasetRecorder that writes a LeRobotDataset is shared between the simulation path and LeRobot's own hardware recording, so a dataset captured in MuJoCo and one captured from a physical SO-101 are in the same format.

The whole workflow in five lines of Python:

What follows is what's actually happening inside that call, step by step.

That's it. The example in this post runs end-to-end on a laptop with these three.

Install Strands Robots and get the example files:

Export your Hugging Face token if you want the agent to push datasets or pull policies from the Hub. This is optional for the default simulation path in this post; the example runs end-to-end with the Mock policy and writes the dataset to your local cache without needing Hub access.

The runnable example lives at examples/lerobot/hub_to_hardware.py (Python script) and hub_to_hardware.ipynb (notebook), in the strands-labs/robots repository alongside the MuJoCo examples. The notebook is the recommended starting point: open it in JupyterLab and run cells top-to-bottom in simulation mode without any hardware connected.

The simulation tool records LeRobotDatasets in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware. No hardware required. The Simulation tool's start_recording action writes through the same DatasetRecorder class: same parquet schema for joint states and actions, same per-camera MP4 layout. The agent prompt is almost identical:

Figure 2. The recording scene in MuJoCo simulation: the SO-100 arm reaching toward a red cube on the ground plane, captured to a LeRobotDataset. No hardware, no GPU, no Hugging Face credentials needed for this default path.

The Mock policy is intentional: it generates placeholder joint actions so the workflow runs end-to-end without a trained checkpoint. The robot moves through random motions rather than completing the grasp, and the recording is structurally complete (valid joint states, valid camera frames, a well-formed LeRobotDataset episode), but the demonstration itself isn't useful as training data. Step 3 below swaps in a GR00T checkpoint through LerobotLocal for real grasping behavior. To see actual cube-picking in this step, run --policy lerobot_local --checkpoint allenai/MolmoAct2-SO100_101 (a MolmoAct2 checkpoint, auto-detected from its config.json and routed through the LerobotLocal path); the prompt, dataset format, and agent code stay the same.

The proof is what happens next. LeRobot's own dataset loader reads the sim-recorded data with no Strands-specific code path:

This features dict is identical in shape to any LeRobot dataset on the Hub: same column names, same parquet+MP4 layout, same loader path. Training scripts that consume hardware-recorded data consume the sim-recorded data without modification. Datasets pushed from sim sit alongside hardware recordings in the same Hub repository if you want them to.

A single episode from a recorded LeRobotDataset, played back from the per-camera MP4 the recorder wrote, the same on-disk video a training script reads.

To record demonstrations on a physical SO-101 instead of simulation, use LeRobot's record CLI directly. The Strands integration doesn't wrap that command as an AgentTool because LeRobot already does the job cleanly:

The dataset that lands on the Hub from this command is in the same format as the simulation recording. To fine-tune a policy on it, run LeRobot's training CLI (lerobot-train); training itself is out of scope for this post and follows the standard LeRobot workflow. From Step 3 onward, the agent picks up either the original or a fine-tuned checkpoint interchangeably. For full SO-101 hardware setup, calibration walkthroughs, and troubleshooting, see the README in the example folder.

With the dataset on the Hub, the next step is to run a policy. The example uses the Robot() factory in its default sim mode and runs a GR00T checkpoint through the LerobotLocal provider, in the same process:

Under the hood, the agent runs a run_policy action on the simulated robot with policy_provider="lerobot_local". The provider downloads the checkpoint from the Hub and loads it through LeRobot's GR00T policy in the same process. The simulation steps with the policy's action chunks, and a render of the result is available via Simulation.render. To run inference on a separate GPU host instead, start strands_robots.inference.server.PolicyServer there and use policy_provider="remote".

Figure 3. With a trained policy (a GR00T or MolmoAct2 checkpoint), the agent drives the SO-100 to grasp the red cube in simulation, the behavior the Mock policy stands in for.

The same provider loads any LeRobot checkpoint. A model ID under the lerobot/ organization routes to it by name:

LerobotLocalPolicy supports ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, and π0.5, anything LeRobot's own policy registry can resolve from a config.json. Real-Time Chunking turns on automatically for flow-matching policies that ship an rtc_config (π0, SmolVLA).

NVIDIA's recently released Cosmos 3 is also available as a policy provider behind the same interface, so the agent code stays the same whichever provider you point it at.

Note: LerobotLocalPolicy loads Hugging Face models with trust_remote_code=True. Set STRANDS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE=1 to opt in, and only load checkpoints from organizations you trust.

This is the same code as Step 3, with one keyword argument changed. The Robot factory returns a hardware-backed robot driven by LeRobot's make_robot_from_config:

The same agent prompt now runs against a physical arm. The hardware path uses LeRobot's robot abstraction for joint commands and camera reads, and the same GR00T checkpoint, loaded in-process, generates the action chunks.

Before this runs against your SO-101, calibration for both follower and leader has to be in place. Run LeRobot's calibration command (lerobot-calibrate) once per device; the files land under ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/calibration/ and any Strands code path that touches the hardware reads them from there. If a calibration is missing, the agent surfaces the error from the LeRobot driver layer.

Up to now we've driven one robot at a time. The mesh is how Strands Robots handles more than one. Picture a leader arm on your desk teleoperating a follower arm in another room, or five SO-101s running the same warehouse task in parallel, or a humanoid coordinating with a mobile base. All of those are mesh patterns. The mesh is built on Zenoh, an open source peer-to-peer protocol, and you don't manage IP addresses, write discovery code, or pick a broker; new robots show up on the mesh the moment they come up, and the agent can talk to all of them at once.

A Robot() or Simulation() joins a Zenoh peer mesh when you pass mesh=True, or set STRANDS_MESH=true; the mesh is off by default. The robot_mesh tool gives the agent a vocabulary for fleet operations such as discovery, structured commands, broadcasts, and emergency stop:

By default, every physically-actuating mesh action pauses for a human approval interrupt before it runs: the fleet-wide broadcast and emergency_stop, plus the single-peer tell, send, and stop. You can tune this set with the STRANDS_MESH_HITL_ACTIONS environment variable (set it to all, none, or a comma-separated subset). The first time you run this example, you'll see a robot_mesh-broadcast-approval prompt in your terminal; type y (or yes / approve) to authorize the broadcast. The approval is delivered out-of-band of the LLM's tool arguments, so a prompt-injection attempt that tries to slip an approval flag into the command body cannot bypass the gate.

The transport scales without touching agent code. The built-in Zenoh mesh is the automatic fallback: on the LAN, Zenoh peers find each other with no broker (gossip by default; set STRANDS_MESH_MULTICAST=true for multicast scouting), and adding the [mesh-iot] extra routes traffic through AWS IoT Core (MQTT5 with mTLS) for cloud fleets, with a BridgeTransport that fans LAN and cloud behind one API (select it with STRANDS_MESH_BACKEND=bridge).

For production fleets, Device Connect, a device-aware networking layer developed in collaboration with Arm, handles discovery, presence, structured RPC, event routing, and safety. The same robot_mesh tool dispatches through Device Connect when it is available and falls back to the built-in Zenoh mesh otherwise, so the agent code in this post is unchanged either way. See the Device Connect documentation for setup and current availability.

The full sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in the examples/lerobot/ folder. It packages all five steps into a single CLI script (hub_to_hardware.py) and a notebook (hub_to_hardware.ipynb). The CLI defaults run end-to-end in simulation with the Mock policy. No GPU, no Docker, no Hugging Face credentials needed.

The recorded dataset lands at ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/local/strands-cube-pick/. To push to the Hugging Face Hub instead of keeping it local, pass --hf-user after exporting HF_TOKEN with write scope. For real grasping behavior in Step 3, pass --policy lerobot_local --checkpoint nvidia/GR00T-N1.7-3B, or another Hub checkpoint. This needs a GPU and STRANDS_TRUST_REMOTE_CODE=1.

The notebook (examples/lerobot/hub_to_hardware.ipynb) walks through the same workflow cell by cell, with narration between each step. Open it in JupyterLab and run top-to-bottom in simulation mode.

The code snippets shown in this setup represent a “hello world” example of setting up Strands Robots with HuggingFace. For more serious, production-ready use cases there are some important considerations users should be aware of:

Supplying untrusted data into agents can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. Given the actuation of these robots in physical space, this is an important risk to track. To mitigate this behavior, developers should be careful to feed the robots only data that comes from a trusted source. If not all input data can be trusted, developers should restrict the tools available to the agent to prevent the robots from making safety-critical actions.

The STRANDS_MESH_LOCAL_DEV=1 setting shared in the code snippets in this blog initializes the robot mesh without authentication or access controls. This means that any device on the same network can provide commands to the robot fleet. This is acceptable for trusted development environments, but is not suitable for untrusted networks or production environments. For these use cases, STRANDS_MESH_AUTH_MODE=mtls is required.

The robot_mesh tool's physically-actuating actions affect peers on the network: broadcast and emergency_stop reach every peer, while tell, send, and stop reach a single targeted peer. To prevent an agent from issuing these commands autonomously (or under prompt injection), all five are gated behind a human-in-the-loop interrupt by default. When the agent invokes a gated action, the Strands runtime pauses the agent loop and asks the operator to approve out-of-band of the LLM's tool arguments. You can adjust the gated set with the STRANDS_MESH_HITL_ACTIONS environment variable (all, none, or a comma-separated subset). Per-action rate limits, command validation, and an audit trail run alongside the interrupt. Outside an agent loop (a bare script or unit test), the gated actions fail closed.

The preceding workflow opens serial ports on hardware and writes a local dataset cache. To return your environment to a clean state:

The integration's central design choice is that Strands Robots doesn't reimplement what LeRobot already provides. Hardware abstraction, calibration, and the dataset format stay upstream. Strands adds the AgentTool surface that makes them composable from natural language.

Two consequences follow. For users, every dataset on the Hub is an asset an agent can extend, fine-tune from, and deploy against with no conversion step. For developers, simulation data and hardware data share a single file format, so training scripts written for one consume the other unchanged. The line between sim and real becomes a deployment detail, not an architectural divide.

Figure 4. The Strands Robots catalog spans arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, and hands, all in the same MuJoCo simulation and behind the same Robot() factory. The SO-100 in this post is one of many supported embodiments.

The full Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policy providers, the mesh, and Device Connect in depth. For larger workloads, Strands Robots also ships heavier simulation backends, Isaac Sim and Newton. Both backends plug into the same Robot abstraction shown in this post, so the agent code stays the same as you scale up.

Contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this workflow, open an issue with what worked and what didn't. The SDK improves fastest when developer feedback lands directly on the surface that needs it.

Cagatay Cali is a Research Engineer at AWS focused on Agentic AI and robotics. He designs interfaces that connect AI agents to physical robots, enabling developers to control robotic systems through natural language and making agents and robotics development accessible to builders at any skill level.

Sundar Raghavan is a Sr Solutions Architect at AWS on the Agentic AI Foundations team. He leads the developer experience for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, owning the SDK and CLI, and drives the framework and ecosystem integrations strategy. He focuses on how developers build, deploy, and scale production AI agents on AWS. He is currently extending that focus into physical AI, collaborating on Strands Robots to bring the same agent developer experience to robotics.

Fantastic to see! The single-kwarg flip from MuJoCo sim to mode="real" (same agent code, same LeRobotDataset format end to end) is exactly the friction-removal that gets robotics agents into real labs. Work like this lifts all the ships: the easier and more open we make agent-to-hardware control, the faster the whole industry moves. The Device Connect team at Arm is excited to collaborate!

#10071. Microsoft Links Storm-0940 to ConnectWise Supply Chain Attack

The China-linked actor used an AI-enabled penetration-testing tool to automate and accelerate its attack on more than 2,200 tenants.

A China-linked threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940 used an agentic AI penetration-testing framework to accelerate a supply chain attack involving ConnectWise Cloud Backup.

The attackers used compromised application credentials associated with the service to attempt to access the Microsoft 365 environments of more than 2,250 downstream customer tenants. In multiple instances, the attackers obtained privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure in less than three hours after initial targeting, Microsoft said in an analysis published this week.

The activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and scaling their operations exponentially, Microsoft researchers wrote. "While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," they said.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

ConnectWise provides software and IT management technology that managed service providers use to deliver a broad range of services to their customers, including backup and recovery for Microsoft 365 data. Delivering these services requires the company to have authorized application access to customer Microsoft 365 environments to back up and restore data.

On Oct. 16, ConnectWise disclosed unauthorized access to application identities associated with its Cloud Backup product. The company subsequently published additional details and containment guidance but has not publicly explained how the attackers initially gained control of the application identities.

Microsoft described the incident as part of a broader Storm-0940 campaign that began as early as September and targeted hundreds of organizations worldwide across several industries including manufacturing, aerospace, chemicals, energy, defense, and financial services. The threat actor has been using an AI penetration-testing framework called ARTEX to automate and accelerate its operations.

"In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access," Microsoft said.

In the ConnectWise incident, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate reconnaissance and scanning, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse. The threat actor used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants, generating as many as 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute. That pace left defenders with little time to detect and respond to the activity, Microsoft noted.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

"Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations," the company said.

ConnectWise suspended its Cloud Backup service and also took its SaaS Security and Cloud Management services offline following the incident. In an Oct. 22 update, the company noted it was continuing work on restoring disrupted services and urged customers to keep affected ConnectWise application connections offline until further notice.

"Investigation and monitoring continue alongside restoration. Existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication of compromise," the company said. ConnectWise called on customers to review their individual Microsoft 365 environments using the company's technical investigation and remediation guide and related information.

Microsoft meanwhile highlighted its own mitigation and protection guidance, which included recommendations like reviewing every Microsoft 365 tenant that might have been tied to ConnectWise and to preserve logs and other forensic evidence before making any changes.

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Ross Filipek, CISO at Corsica Technologies, says that before reconnecting with ConnectWise, affected organizations should have a clear understanding of what might have happened inside their environment. He pointed to Microsoft's discovery of application credential changes that could give attackers a way back in to compromised environments. Organizations are going to need to investigate whether their Microsoft 365 environments are safe before they reconnect, he says.

"Keep affected connections disabled in line with vendor guidance. Investigate unauthorized changes that could leave another way in. Preserve evidence without delaying containment," Filipek tells Dark Reading. "There's also an immediate business question: Are backups still running? Assign someone on each side to check coverage during the interruption. A restored connection needs verification that backup jobs are completing and recovery works."

Going forward, organizations need to have a recovery plan that takes into account the potential of their losing access to a service that they normally would depend on for recovery, Filipek adds. Incident responders should know which applications connect to the organization's Microsoft 365 tenant and how to quickly sever those connections when necessary, and exercise that scenario with their service provider.

"Establish who checks backup coverage during containment and who decides whether the business can tolerate the interruption. Leaving those responsibilities implied is how both sides end up assuming the other has checked," he says.

Jon Baker, vice president of threat-informed defense at AttackIQ, wants affected organizations to preserve sign-in and audit records and to investigate application sign-ins, Microsoft Graph activity, new credentials, privilege changes, and unusual data access. "Remove confirmed unauthorized access and verify vendor and tenant remediation separately," he advises. "After containment, controlled validation can test whether comparable application behavior can still reach sensitive resources or establish another foothold."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

Learn how to move an agent session from the GitHub Copilot app into VS Code without losing the conversation, code changes, or working context.

The agent has finished the bulk of your change. Now you want to inspect one implementation detail, adjust a few lines by hand, and run the project locally before you ship it.

But the work is sitting in the GitHub Copilot app… and your editor is where you review diffs, debug code, and make final adjustments. Do you have to choose between staying in the session and starting over in Visual Studio Code?

You don’t. You can open the Copilot app session directly in VS Code and continue with its conversation, code changes, and working context intact. That means Copilot can handle the repetitive or time-consuming work, then hand control back to you for closer review, hands-on editing, and local testing.

This tutorial assumes you are already comfortable navigating VS Code, running commands in its integrated terminal, and working with Git branches and pull requests.

Open the session you want to continue. Before handing it off, take a moment to review the task and the work Copilot completed.

A session contains more than a collection of modified files. It also records the task, the plan, and the conversation that produced those changes. That context is important when you want to understand why Copilot chose a particular implementation or ask it to revise part of the work.

You do not need to summarize that history or copy it into a new chat before moving to VS Code.

From the session, select Open in VS Code. If the app presents more than one supported editor or VS Code installation, choose the one you want to use.

VS Code opens the project using the worktree associated with the session. It also displays the existing session in the Copilot sidebar.

That gives you three connected pieces of the original work:

You are continuing the existing session, not reconstructing it in a new editor window.

Before editing, inspect the diff in VS Code. Open the Source Control view to see the changed files, then select a file to review its changes line by line.

Review the implementation as you would any other proposed change. In particular, check that:

The preserved conversation can help explain how Copilot arrived at the implementation. If something is unclear, continue prompting Copilot in the sidebar. For example:

You can also ask Copilot to make another change. Because the session and worktree remain connected, you do not have to describe the task from the beginning.

Once you understand the proposed changes, edit any file directly in VS Code.

This is useful for adjustments that are faster or easier to make by hand, such as:

You are editing the session’s existing worktree, so your manual changes build directly on the agent’s work. You do not need to copy files between directories or manually re-create the branch.

Use the VS Code integrated terminal to run the project’s normal validation workflow. The exact commands depend on the repository, but some web app examples may include:

Treat agent-generated changes the same way you would treat code written by a person: run the relevant tests, inspect failures, and verify the behavior yourself.

If the development server prints a localhost URL, open it to test the change in a browser. When supported by your VS Code setup, you can open the URL in VS Code’s integrated browser and inspect the result without leaving the editor.

For a user-interface change, verify both the requested behavior and nearby states. For example, check the modified component at different viewport sizes and confirm that loading, empty, and error states still work.

At any point, you can choose the interaction that best fits the next step:

For example, after making a manual UI adjustment, you might ask Copilot:

Add a test for the updated label and run the relevant test file. Do not modify unrelated components.

Because you are still in the original session, Copilot retains the context needed to interpret “the updated label.”

When the implementation is ready, review the final diff one more time. Then commit and push the changes using the Source Control view or the integrated terminal:

Use your repository’s normal branch, commit, review, and approval practices. Because VS Code opened the worktree and branch associated with the session, pushing the branch updates the pull request already tracking that work.

There is no need to copy the finished files into another checkout or reconnect the work to the pull request manually.

Opening a Copilot app session in VS Code gives you a clean division of labor without splitting the work itself. Copilot can take on a larger or repetitive implementation, while you can move into the editor for detailed review, targeted changes, local testing, and final polish.

The session, diff, and worktree move with you. Start by directing the work in the Copilot app, switch to VS Code whenever you want hands-on control, and push the finished result through the same pull request workflow.

Ready to try it? Download the GitHub Copilot app, start a session, and open it in VS Code when you are ready to continue coding.

#10069. Is it agentic enough? Benchmarking open models on your own tooling

Benchmarking transformers revisions across different metrics

This is a human-made, agent-focused blogpost.

Coding agents increasingly work with our software instead of us: describe a task, and the agent picks the library, writes the calls, runs them, and debugs its own mistakes. When the library gets in the way, it will happily bypass it and rewrite the logic from scratch. This introduces a new concept in library development: the code should not only be correct and fast, but should be designed so that an agent can drive it effectively. A clunky API or stale docs annoy us developers, but it now also sends the agent down a longer, more expensive path.

Most benchmarks just look at the final answer. We wanted the whole process instead: not just whether the agent got it right, but how much work it took to get there, and how that shifts across models, library revisions, and tasks. We measured exactly that, using transformers as our case study.

Here, we will introduce a tool specific benchmark focusing on how the answer was found, and provide a simple implementation of one such harness, running entirely on open models driven by the pi coding agent, with the full sweep of models × revisions × tasks fanned out across Hugging Face Jobs so every run sees identical hardware.

But, how do you optimize software for agents?

We're strong believers in the following two software principles:

This remains the same within the realm of agentic-optimized tooling, and, for once, the two are directly tied to each other.

You want your tool to exist for an agent: it needs to be discoverable. The API needs to be clear and the docs need to be extensive. They need to be structured in a way that the agent has rapid access to the useful files and examples. If you want your tool to work for an agent, then you should test it for agentic-use.

We'll use transformers as an example throughout this blogpost: agents using it to solve ML tasks (classifying text, captioning images, transcribing audio), not contributing code to it; though the harness was designed to work with any tool that can be operated from the command line.

Our intuition on transformers was that usage could be dramatically simplified with a few changes: a CLI, a Skill, and self-contained, task-specific examples. This is the same recipe recently applied to the hf CLI, redesigned to be agent-optimized, where agents used 1.3–1.8× (and up to 6×) fewer tokens. We wanted to know whether that kind of win generalizes, and whether it could be useful for transformers as well.

Intuition is a powerful tool, but we wanted more evidence before we opened PRs that add several thousand lines of code to such a widely used codebase as transformers. We set out to measure what success looks like.

Two agents can both produce the correct label for a sentiment-classification task, but one:

Both reach POSITIVE (0.9999), and here are the two paths an agent actually took on this exact task:

Both methods reach the same result. But they have very different profiles in cost, latency, token usage, and failures.

If your evaluation only checks the final string, you're blind to these as well as whether a change you shipped to the library (a CLI improvement, better error messages, a Skill) actually helped agents.

Our goal with this harness is to evaluate how much work an agent has to do to perform a given task, and whether changes to the library improve performance.

A few words on how we'll evaluate agents here.

We run every task under three variants (or "tiers"); three different ways an agent can come at transformers:

These aren't nested: skill doesn't contain clone (it ships curated docs, not the source tree), and neither strictly contains the other, each gives the agent a different kind of help. As we'll see, a model can sometimes do better on clone than on skill.

Not all models driving agents are equal, and their difference changes what you should look at when running them.

At one end, you have the largest, most capable open models. On reasonably common tasks, these should get the right answer, eventually. For them, task completion saturates near 100% and stops telling you much about your tool; a more relevant benchmark is the effort it took the agent to get there: how many turns, tokens and seconds it took, and whether they walked a clean path or used deprecated APIs.

Local models vary widely in size, and so do their abilities. Metrics such as "match %" are more relevant than for their larger counterparts, as you can see how model sizes/capabilities affect results on your specific tool.

This harness not only provides guidance to library maintainers on how to improve a repository for agent interactions, it also helps assess how different agents and models perform on the tasks users care about.

The harness scores every run on several axes, so that you can ask what actually matters for each class of model:

All of it lands in a report you can directly examine:

The live report: Overview, Coverage, and Results, all client-side.

And because it captures the native agent trace of every run, numbers are just the beginning: you can read exactly what the agent did, command by command. The traces are shareable through the Hub's agent-traces viewer:

A run rendered in the Hub's agent-traces viewer: MiniMax-M2.7 on the answer-question task. Open this trace on the Hub ↗

Before the results, a quick recap of the setup. Each run varies four things: the model driving the agent, the transformers revision it runs against, the task, and the tier (bare / clone / skill). As discussed, we look at different metrics for the two different model categories.

Since a large open model will usually get to the correct result, what you're really measuring is the effort it took to do so. Did it take ten turns or one? Did it follow an API path you deprecated because it trusted obsolete documentation? Did it hit an error you hadn't foreseen?

The natural experiment is to fix one strong model and vary the tool's revisions: the successive git versions of transformers we test against, from released tags like v5.8.0 and v5.9.0 to the specific commit that introduces the CLI and Skill. We want to watch whether the load it puts on the agent goes up or down. We used the harness on transformers to check whether adding a dedicated CLI and Skill actually lightened the agents' work.

For the three large models we used in our tests, the average time spent on all tasks indicates that the Skill commit results in less time spent working on the tasks:

Median time per revision, by tier: the skill commit (green dot) is the fastest.

On the other hand, in the experiments in which we cloned the repository, we can see a significant increase in token consumption due to the commit that introduced the CLI and examples, as we'll see in a moment.

Median new tokens per revision, by tier: the clone variant jumps once the CLI lands in the repo.

Reading the clone-variant traces explains why. The commit adds a command, but it also ships the CLI's implementation and a set of cli/agentic/*.py usage examples into the repository directly.

On the clone variant the agent has a full transformers checkout in front of it, and roughly a third of the runs go read the new surface (the /cli/ tree and the example scripts) to learn the interface before calling it. This raises the median input from ~4k to ~6.4k tokens.

The two charts are then two sides of one tradeoff: the commit buys the large models less time (they reach for the CLI instead of debugging Python) at the cost of more tokens (they read the code that taught them the CLI). A tradeoff worth knowing about before merging PRs.

One caveat works in the CLI's favor, though, which isn't benchmarked yet: the cost of reading it is amortized with successive runs. Our setup is built for one-off experiments. Each run is a fresh agent that rediscovers the CLI from scratch, so it pays the discovery cost every time. In real usage an agent learns the interface once and then solves task after task within the same session, amortizing that cost across many requests. The token bump we measure here is closer to a worst case than to what a user would see day to day.

Open models give us fine-grained control over the variables that matter most here: size, configuration, quantization, provider, training, and anything that would differ from one model to the next. They're also where a good tool surface matters most: a small model asked to "use transformers to do X" on a bare environment can guess an API that changed some releases ago, may do unnecessary tool calls, and can get the wrong answer.

So here the experiment is the opposite of the above: hold the revision and sweep the model. This helps see which models actually take care of the task, not just by token count and time, but down to which ones can't reliably handle the tool calls. Our intuition is that the smaller the model, the harder both tool use and the task get; we ran the harness across a range of model sizes to test exactly that:

Match % across models, by tier: the skill tier lifts the larger models but drops the smaller ones.

which also seems to be correlated with the number of tokens ingested

Median new tokens across models, by tier.

A note on fair comparison: naively averaging across tasks is misleading when coverage is uneven (a model that only finished the quick tasks looks fast). The report has a "shared tasks only" toggle (across models and/or revisions) so you compare like-for-like, and a Coverage heatmap so you can see exactly which task × revision × model cells actually ran.

Two things come together here: how to look past whether the agent succeeded to what it did and how it did it; as well as the first results we pulled out of the harness.

Match %, tokens, and time tell you the cost of a run but don't tell you much about what happened under the hood.

This is why we've introduced the concept of markers. A marker is a named pattern the profile (the small per-tool plugin that teaches the harness how to build and drive a given library) matches against a run.

It is a one-line label for a behavior you care about, checked against the shell commands the agent ran, the code it wrote, the files it read, or its final answer. A run can fire several markers or none; the report shows how often each one fired, per model and per revision.

For transformers we declare a handful but we'll only look at the two most relevant ones:

These are what we watch to see whether a change actually shifted the agent's behavior. Interestingly here, the larger the model, the more it leverages the new context instead of using its memory; therefore leveraging the newly introduced CLI.

CLI adoption by tier across models: only the skill tier reaches for it, and more so as models grow.

CLI adoption is new: the CLI lands in a single commit, isn't in any model's training data, and is only lightly documented. The effect is clear: it's the Skill variant, the one that ships the CLI's documentation, that actually reaches for it, at 55.3%.

Comparing the commit across model sizes, the CLI + Skill helps the bigger models: on the skill tier, Kimi and the other large agents reach for the CLI and finish in fewer turns. (On clone they spend more input tokens first, reading the new CLI code, as we saw above, so the win shows up in time and turns, not raw tokens.)

Kimi-K2.6, GLM-5.1, and MiniMax-M2.7 across revisions

But in some smaller-model settings, it appears to hurt performance. One plausible explanation is that small models lean on memorized API patterns, reproducing pipeline(...) snippets they've seen in their training data. The new concepts are then a larger surface for them to get wrong. You can watch this directly on the harness: lower match %, more retries, the cli marker barely firing. It is particularly striking on the Qwen3-4B model: the Skill barely changes its match rate yet its cost distribution is significantly affected.

Almost all of that comes from the clone tier. The checkout now contains the CLI's implementation and cli/agentic/*.py examples, and the 4B agent reads them in bulk: its median new tokens jump from ~2.4k to ~23k, with time and output skyrocketing as well, for no gain in accuracy.

Qwen3-4B across revisions. The CLI + Skill commit fans the cost distribution wide open, on the clone tier the agent reads the newly-shipped CLI source in bulk (~10× the new tokens), for no gain in match %. (repeat tokens stays flat: this setup uses no prompt caching.)

Sometimes, though, the Skill breaks correctness outright. Reading the traces shows how, for example for Qwen3-14B: adding the Skill drops its overall match rate from 67% (bare) to 43%, and on the simplest tasks the collapse is very visible: classify-sentiment goes from 100% on the clone variant to 0% with the Skill.

Qwen3-14B on classify-sentiment, by tier: clone (blue) holds at 100% across revisions, but the Skill variant (green) collapses to 0% at the CLI + Skill revision.

Looking at the traces, the model mistakes the CLI for a tool it can call directly (as in an agentic-harness tool, like web-search). The Skill is not an executable tool: it's documentation loaded into the agent's context, and the transformers CLI is only ever meant to be run from the shell (via bash); so this will not work.

Qwen3-14B reads the Skill and, in 39 of its 56 Skill runs, either emits a transformers(command="classify", ...) tool call (a tool that was never registered) or, finding nothing like it among its read/bash/edit/write tools, concludes it can't run a model and gives up. Either way, rather than fall back to the one-line pipeline(...) that scored 100% on the clone checkout, it declares the task impossible.

Qwen3-14B on classify-sentiment (Skill variant): it reasons that read/bash/edit/write can't run a model, and gives up.

This is exactly what we built the harness to catch: the same change that speeds the large models ends up breaking the small ones, which seemed a bit counterintuitive to us at first and something we'd likely have shipped as-is. The takeaway for maintainers: agent-facing APIs should be evaluated across model sizes, because a new affordance can reduce work for strong models while adding ambiguity for smaller ones. It also hints at a fix: rather than hand-write a Skill and check it after the fact, you could generate and validate one against the weaker models up front.

This is exactly what Upskill does: it turns a strong model's solution into a Skill only when it measurably helps the smaller ones.

The harness is one CLI, agent-eval. Install it, run a suite, fan it out across models × revisions on HF Jobs, and publish the report as a Hugging Face Space.

Trusted local use only. The harness runs a coding agent with bypassed permissions and executes code from whatever revision you point it at, and traces can contain prompts, output, and local paths. See SECURITY.md before pointing it at code you didn't write or sharing results.

The full, kept-current setup and usage instructions live in the README.

Checking the final answer tells you whether an agent can use your library. It doesn't tell you what it costs: the turns, tokens, errors, and the path it took to get there. This harness measures that, across the revisions and models you pick.

On transformers, it caught something we'd have shipped on faith: the CLI + Skill helps the largest open models and hurts the smallest ones. Worth knowing before merging!

It's profile-based, and designed to be adaptable: point it at your own library, define a few tasks and their expected answers, get the same report. Code and tasks are in the repo, traces are on the Hub. Let us know if you use it for your project!

This harness stands entirely on pi, Mario Zechner's coding-agent CLI: it drives every open-model run, and only needs an HF_TOKEN to serve a model, which is what made the open-model sweep practical at all.

Thanks to the model builders and inference providers behind the models we swept. Across the board they performed well above what the bare baseline would suggest.

#10068. Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware

Your industrial IoT gateway isn't exposed to the internet, right? RIGHT?!

Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot.

Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating.

Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.”

One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said.

Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer.

The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote.

While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted.

Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher.

One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote.

The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote.

“If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post.

While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

Three Java Champions share how they use GitHub Copilot to solve problems, accelerate development, and keep humans responsible for the results.

AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships.

To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software.

How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently?

I’ve been using it to analyze, design, and implement various features in both Hypersistence Utils and Hypersistence Optimizer.

For example, I’ve been wanting for a long time to develop a web application that provides Optimizer event history so we can see how performance improvement efforts are materializing in application performance. Before AI, I kept postponing this task because it would have taken me weeks to develop. But using Copilot is like having a new team member, so I used it to create an app that will ship in the next version of Hypersistence Optimizer. Instead of weeks, this task took just two days to implement.

What’s your typical usage? Are you using GitHub Copilot as an IDE plugin or the GitHub Copilot app?

I use GitHub Copilot in IntelliJ IDEA because it’s convenient to run while reviewing source code or during a debug session.

It’s very useful as a code assistant, and it helps me speed up both investigations and building prototypes for features that need validation.

I still review the plans and the code that is generated by AI since their goal is to improve my productivity, not replace me entirely. While AI provides the right answer in many situations, there are still times when the response is not satisfactory and requires my intervention.

Can you share some tips and best practices? For example, which skills are you using?

I created my own skills so that whatever text Copilot generates looks like something I wrote by hand.

This skill captures my voice from 65 of my published articles, so a draft comes back sounding like my blog instead of like a language model. This is really useful when generating documentation for this project, since it lets the LLM learn from 12 years of blogging and provide examples that follow the same principles, such as expressiveness, testability, and simplicity.

Throughout my career as a software engineer, I’ve learned that we spend far more time on code maintenance than on creating it. Therefore, because maintenance and stability are critical for existing products, I developed skills that help AI mimic existing code practices in accordance with the principle of least astonishment.

One tip is to change the model type based on the type of operation. For thorough thinking, I use Opus with the 1 million context window and Extra High or Max reasoning. However, for simpler tasks, such as generating reports, release notes, or verifying documentation, I use lighter models that consume fewer tokens.

Your work involves coaching teams. What is your approach?

A lot of my work happens while the normal business still has to keep running. You cannot stop everything for six months to “transform.” We usually start by solving immediate problems together, understand where the team currently stands, define where we want to go and how we will know that we are improving, and then move there step by step.

Depending on the situation, that can mean Software Craft practices such as TDD, refactoring, continuous delivery and XP; architecture and modularisation with Spring Boot, Spring Modulith; Spring Security; optimising Java and Spring Boot applications for containers; or increasingly, agentic engineering.

The important part for me is that I work with the team. We make decisions together. I don’t want a team to become dependent on me. Ideally, after some time they no longer need me except perhaps as a sparring partner.

And maybe that explains why I find this new generation of AI tools so interesting: I like working with people, learning, experimenting, and solving problems. AI gives us another very powerful tool for doing exactly that.

Can you share a good story about how GitHub Copilot has helped you recently?

There are actually three very different examples that changed how I think about working with GitHub Copilot.

One was a migration of around 900 teaching slides across 15 presentations from Reveal.js to Marp. These were not simple slides. Many contain code, animations, and even interactive examples where I can change JavaScript live while teaching. More importantly, the presentations had already been battle-tested with students. The flow worked. Losing one small piece could break the story I use in the classroom.

Doing that migration manually would probably have taken me a week or more—and realistically, I might simply have avoided doing it because it was such tedious work.

With Copilot, I approached it differently. We first analysed the existing material, defined the target, created a migration plan, established constraints, provided examples, and defined what had to remain intact. Then we worked from the big structural changes down into the details.

The really important part was verification.

We generated screenshots of the Reveal.js and Marp versions and compared them visually and algorithmically. We built a small application where I could run both slide decks next to each other to verify animations manually. We even compared the generated PDFs.

That meant the agent did not just say, “Migration complete.” We had evidence.

The entire migration took me roughly eight to ten hours. I still owned the content, the teaching intent, and every meaningful change. Copilot could fix a typo automatically, but if content, versions, dates or meaning changed, that was something we discussed.

For me, that experience reinforced an important principle: delegate execution, not responsibility. I own the result.

A second example came from building a terminal UI application with Tamboui. It initially worked perfectly in Linux under WSL, and I had completely forgotten that somebody might run it directly in Windows CMD or PowerShell.

They discovered that the Enter key was simply ignored in some forms. That is another principle I strongly believe in: ship software early, because you learn from how people actually use it.

We used Copilot to turn that feedback into reproducible UI tests. On Linux, Copilot was navigating the application with tmux. Through working with it, I learned about psmux and could execute similar flows in PowerShell. We reproduced the problem, created a local fix, traced the real problem into Tamboui, and I submitted the upstream fix, which was merged.

During this work, the test descriptions themselves became too large for the available context. So I asked Copilot to help me redesign the way the tests were represented. Instead of verbose tables containing identifiers, names and repeated descriptions, it proposed a much more compact arrow notation: step → step → input, with additional information only where it was critical.

That surprised me. We were not just using AI to execute information; we were working together on how information should be represented for execution. It did not have to be maximally human-friendly. It had to preserve the semantics while being efficient for the agent.

The third example is completely different again.

Someone close to me needed to practise mathematics, and I thought: why don’t we build a small learning app?

It covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and division with remainder for grades one through four. But I did not want to build another simple quiz application. Together with Copilot, I researched learning approaches such as spaced repetition, immediate feedback, adaptive difficulty, motivation, cooperative learning and gamification without dark patterns.

Interestingly, during that research Copilot challenged one of my original assumptions. I initially wanted the application to be generic for children everywhere. The research led us toward looking at the actual school curriculum instead. I realised that the order in which topics are introduced, the operations and number ranges differ enough that making it “universal” immediately was unnecessary.

So we focused on Switzerland first and aligned the progression accordingly. Because Switzerland is multilingual, the application is available in German, French, Italian and English.

It also has cooperative and competitive two-player modes, and when someone gets an answer wrong, the application explains one way to solve it and brings similar questions back through spaced repetition.

I deliberately chose an architecture without a backend. There is no reason for me to collect children’s personal data on a server, so the data stays on the device and the application can simply be hosted on GitHub Pages.

What started as a small experiment is now being used and shared among friends. It accidentally became a little product.

That experience showed me another side of Copilot: don’t only use it to implement your solution. Use it as a sparring partner to expand and challenge the solution space before you start building.

I actually don’t use the classic Copilot autocomplete experience anymore.

My work has moved almost completely toward agentic workflows.

I use VS Code when I need a tight visual feedback loop—when I want to look closely at documents, code, presentations or intermediate results and adapt the process as I go.

For larger execution-oriented tasks, I often work with the coding agent from the terminal. There I am more comfortable delegating a piece of work, letting it execute, and then inspecting the complete result. The interface I choose depends mostly on the feedback loop I need.

I also had a fascinating experience using the coding-agent workflow through GitHub while travelling to JavaLand. I had started exploring an idea for a Maven plugin that optimises which Spring Boot auto-configurations are loaded. During roughly a four-hour journey, I was steering the agent from my phone: giving it a task, reviewing what it had done, thinking about the next step, and sending the next instruction.

By the time I arrived, I had a working Maven plugin, a CI pipeline, performance tests against a sample application, and reports that could demonstrate whether the optimisation actually worked.

That was the first time I had worked that way, and I was amazed that it actually worked. I wasn’t trying to write Java on my phone. I was reviewing, deciding and steering while the agent executed.

I also use MCP servers when they give me useful capabilities or context. For example, I have used Context7 for documentation, integrations with my Logseq knowledge base, and I have experimented with an MCP integration for Adobe Premiere Pro.

But I don’t use MCP just because I can. If a good CLI exists, I often prefer the CLI because it feels more direct and faster to me.

The agent is also not a “junior developer” in my mental model. I think of it much more as a sparring partner. But just like anyone joining a project, it first needs to be brought up to speed.

Can you share some tips and best practices?

The biggest thing I would recommend is: stop one-shot prompting.

For anything non-trivial, I want to understand the problem before execution starts. Quite often I explicitly ask the agent to interview me first. The purpose of that interview is to uncover assumptions and expectations that are still implicit.

A good agent can execute the wrong idea incredibly quickly. That does not make the detour cheaper.

I experienced this myself while working on my Spring Boot auto-configuration optimiser. Initially I wanted to support both Spring Boot 3.5 and 4.x. There were architectural differences, so we implemented both approaches. Later I realised I no longer needed the 3.5 path and removing it was painful.

The lesson was simple: detours are expensive. Get the requirements right before you accelerate.

Once the intent is clear, I want a plan. When I review that plan, four things matter especially to me: are assumptions visible, are verification gates defined, does the approach fit the architecture, and does it avoid unnecessary work?

The second principle is to define task-specific verification gates.

“Done” should not mean that the model says it is done.

For a refactoring, the gates might include passing tests, proving that all intended files were handled, updating documentation and leaving no TODOs behind. For the slide migration, the gates included screenshots, visual diffs, animations, PDF output and content completeness.

The gates depend on the task. The principle does not: the agent should be able to provide evidence that the work satisfies the definition of done.

I recently came across a skill called unlazy that follows a similar idea: create explicit gates, work through them deliberately, and prove that they have been completed rather than taking shortcuts.

The third principle is to turn your lessons into reusable skills.

I have started writing and maintaining my own Agent Skills. When I learn something from an execution—perhaps the agent misunderstood a convention, a useful check was missing, or I found a better way to approach a task—I update the skill.

The next time I perform that task, the lesson is already there.

One example is a skill I call maintainer-audit, inspired by work in the open agent skills community. I use it across my own repositories. It checks and, where appropriate, fixes the things I expect a maintained project to have: repository documentation, CI pipelines, Dependabot configuration, CodeQL, consistent cleanup and other project standards.

The goal is not to generate another audit report for me to read. It brings the repository back toward the baseline I want automatically. That makes my projects more consistent and easier to maintain.

I think of these skills as living engineering knowledge rather than static prompts.

The fourth principle is to put deterministic engineering tools around the probabilistic model.

I have my own quality harness that wraps tools such as Checkstyle, PMD and Spring Modulith architecture checks and produces a consolidated report that the agent can consume. I can run that from hooks and let the agent iterate:

change → execute checks → read findings → fix → execute again.

It continues until there are no findings left.

That does not mean I stop looking at the software. I still run the application, interact with it and decide whether it behaves and looks the way I expect. Sometimes I deliberately implement feature by feature because the feedback loop is much tighter.

I learned that asking for everything at once because “the AI can do it” is usually a bad idea. Large, generic specifications create large, generic implementations—and cleaning them up afterwards can be harder than building smaller increments correctly.

More broadly, I think we developers need to talk much more about how we use these tools. Share the experiments that worked. Share the ones that didn’t. Borrow ideas from each other and adapt them to your own context instead of looking for one universal AI development process.

That is also why I like the idea of AI as a sparring partner. On a Friday night, when I want to experiment with something and no human pair is available, I suddenly have somebody—or something—I can challenge an idea with, review an approach with, or use as a very sophisticated rubber duck.

But I still take those ideas back to real people. Human feedback, product understanding and real-world context remain essential.

How do you think AI is changing our profession?

I don’t think software engineering students should primarily aspire to become code-producing machines. They need to become strong problem solvers. They need to understand users and stakeholders, discover the real problem behind a requirement, challenge assumptions, understand products and markets, make architectural trade-offs, think critically, work in a structured way and transfer useful solutions from one context into another.

The model is extraordinarily good at generating possibilities and executing things. But as a human, I usually know much more of the actual context—including the things nobody ever documented.

So I want to remain in charge of shaping the solution and let the agent take over more of the execution.

In that sense, I think AI is putting the engineering back into software engineering.

I’ve been fascinated by computers since I got a Commodore 64 when I was 11. Took some side steps into video production and television work after school but turned back into coding as that video needed to be put on DVD and the very first websites… Yes, I’m that old ;-).

How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently?

It’s a perfect companion to evaluate pull requests and investigate bug reports.

One remarkable story is about the Pi4J library that lets you build Java applications to interact with electronic components on the Raspberry Pi. In February 2026, we released V4 which has a new plugin using the Foreign Function & Memory API. We tested it thoroughly before releasing, but still, shortly after the release someone reported that using 5 input buttons doesn’t work as expected. Pushing one of the first four configured buttons triggers a code execution as expected, while nothing happens with the fifth button.

This is the kind of report you don’t want to get. Nothing was visibly broken. No exception, no warning in the logs, the fifth button was simply silent. And it got worse: with the older gpiod plugin, the exact same hardware and the exact same application, worked fine. So the problem was in our new FFM code, which sits on top of the Linux kernel’s GPIO character device and talks to it through native calls. That is not the part of the codebase where you expect to find a quick answer.

So I assigned the issue to the Copilot coding agent and gave it two file paths as a starting point, the provider class and FFMDigitalInput. About half an hour later there was a pull request, with an explanation I really did not expect.

Each input runs an event watcher that blocks in a native poll() call, waiting for the kernel to report a change on its GPIO line. Those watchers ran in virtual threads. And a virtual thread that blocks inside a native call cannot be unmounted from its carrier thread. It stays pinned there for the whole duration of the call. A Raspberry Pi 4 has four cores, so the virtual thread scheduler has four carrier threads. Register four inputs, and all four carriers are parked in poll() forever. The fifth watcher is created, but is never scheduled. That is exactly the bug that was reported. Not “events are flaky”, but “the fifth one does nothing.”

What I liked most was not the diff, it was the conversation that followed in the review. I left a comment asking Copilot to explain this in more detail:

I thought the goal of virtual threads was exactly to step away from the platform thread limit? So how is this a problem that four virtual threads block the four threads on a four-core processor like the Raspberry Pi?

Check the pull request for the full conversation. Copilot was able to link the use of the Raspberry Pi which has four CPU cores with the reported problem. It was able to propose a simple fix for the problem, plus some extra improvements it found during its investigation.

Can you share some tips and best practices?

Louis Erbkamm built the first prototype in his free time. Now GitHub Copilot helps him maintain it alone.

We moved a copy of 99.99999% of GitHub’s repositories to Azure. Here’s how per-reference quorums will bring over the rest, and how object storage lets reads scale independently.

Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip.

In an earlier blog post, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture:

In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own.

The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly.

While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. Given our scale and how critical the service is to the community, we needed to sequence the work carefully: move the data first, then evolve the architecture once it arrived.

Git operations are a Tier 0 service: they’re a core function of GitHub, and nearly everything in GitHub depends on the repository data. That meant the data, services, and every dependency had to move first. The first copy of a repository landed in Azure’s Central US region in August 2025. Today, most repositories have two of their five replicas in Azure, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic. For most of that time, Azure absorbed our growth while our own data centers held steady.

During the migration, traffic follows the data. Most repositories have five replicas to balance durability, availability, and scale. To minimize read latency, Spokes uses preferential routing to direct traffic to a replica in the same region and availability zone as the request. As replicas move to Azure, the share of the traffic that can be served from Azure grows with each one, until the last replica arrives and the old region stops receiving requests entirely. Every repository goes through this process:

So, what about the remaining 0.00001% of repositories?

In our current architecture, a repository hosted in more than one region has a lower write throughput ceiling. Spokes’ quorum only needs a majority to commit a write, but it waits for every healthy replica to respond (up to a timeout) before moving on, so slow replicas delay every write rather than falling behind. In practice, that means the slowest healthy replica sets the latency of every write, and because each write holds a repository-wide lock until it commits, it also sets the throughput ceiling. Once a replica lives in the target Azure region, it’s about 1,000 miles from our data centers, making each network round trip around 25ms, and a write requires multiple round trips. A repository already near its throughput ceiling can’t absorb that on every serialized write; it would fall further behind with every push.

This is where our first principle, minimizing coordination, comes into play. Specifically for this case: don’t serialize what doesn’t need to be. Git’s consistency requirements apply to each reference individually. Once the server accepts an update to a reference, no client should see an older value afterward, only that value or a newer one. That holds whether the update is a fast-forward, a force push, or a delete. But in most cases, updates to different references don’t depend on each other and can be applied independently.

So, we’re changing the scope of the quorum from the whole repository to individual references.

Holding a repository-wide lock for the entire reference update, round trips included, turns the quorum into a single, unordered request queue with one write in flight at a time. Each write in that queue takes as long as the slowest healthy replica. As the write rate grows, so does the queue, and each write waits longer than the one before it.

With per-reference serialization, only writes that contend on a shared reference must wait for each other. In practice, most writes to a repository touch different references—for example, agents and developers pushing to their own branches—so they no longer wait on each other. Each write still experiences the cross-region latency but writes to different references can be in flight at the same time. That removes the single bottleneck on the repository. We can visualize how queueing and timeouts build up by comparing the two approaches side by side under similar load:

These changes raise a repository’s write throughput ceiling roughly in proportion to how many references are being written at once, and get the last remaining repositories into Azure. In internal testing with realistic traffic, writes to different references consistently saw 3–4x higher throughput at lower latency.

Most repositories are heavily read-skewed, with somewhere between 100 and 1,000 reads for every write. Today, reads and writes hit the same replicas, so they compete for the same resources and can’t be scaled independently.

Decoupling storage from compute changes that. Once repository data is durably stored in Azure Blob Storage and updated with each incoming write, we can begin to decouple read traffic from the write quorum, and independently scale the compute needed for each. For example, reads would benefit from far more in-memory cache than we give them today, but that memory is also needed for compaction. Once they’re separated, each gets its own configuration.

The first step is making object storage a member of the quorum, but a special one that we call a virtual replica. The compute that represents it is our first fully ephemeral node. It serves as a bridge to object storage, streaming incoming writes and serving no reads. Because it’s a member of the quorum, a write isn’t acknowledged until it’s durable in object storage.

That adds a little latency to each write, but just like the cross-region round trip, per-reference serialization keeps it from becoming a throughput bottleneck. The virtual write replica also coalesces transactions on disjoint references into a single set of network I/Os to object storage, so a busy repository pays for one round trip across many concurrent writes instead of one per write. For now, the virtual write replica also handles compaction, and read replicas inherit the compacted state.

With the virtual write replica in place, we can scale out as many virtual read replicas as a repository needs, on demand. Each read replica warms its cache from Azure Blob Storage and starts taking read traffic without joining the quorum, using object storage as the source of truth and reconciling its local state against it in the background.

This step unlocks significant read scale. In internal testing, our distributed load testing harness routinely found ceilings in the current architecture. Against virtual read replicas, the harness hit its own limits first. It also comes with a few challenges that are solved in subsequent steps:

How can we push write throughput further?

The GitHub of today was built on the Spokes quorum, and over the years Spokes has become much more than a quorum coordinator. It’s also an intelligent routing and load balancing layer, a unified API that internal clients use to access and transact repository data at well over 100 billion operations per day, and a collection of background systems we call “sweepers” that handle repository placement, repair, and rebalancing between storage nodes.

The vast majority of what lives under the Spokes service umbrella applies just as well to the new architecture as it does to the existing one. But we also recognize that the commit protocol that has taken GitHub to a billion repositories won’t take it to the next billion and beyond.

We’re not done yet. With these steps in place, the next limit is write throughput. Every write still waits on replicas that each hold a full copy of the repository, yet very little of a write actually needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, so they can be stored without anyone agreeing on them. What’s left is small, and the hard part is ordering it as fast as possible without moving the bottleneck somewhere else. Designing for that on a whiteboard is one thing. Doing it underneath a billion repositories that developers and agents are writing to around the clock is another. Getting there forced us to rethink the second-order effects too, like where durable reference state lives and how compaction and garbage collection scale.

Agent traffic isn’t slowing down, and each of these steps gives repositories more headroom as it lands, without waiting for the end state.

Coming next week: At GitHub Universe and in the final post in this series, we’ll take a tour through that end state, what it does for write throughput, the second-order problems we had to solve to get there, and why there’s still a (small) consensus group somewhere in the stack.

Thanks to Brian Celenza for their contributions to this post.
