Today, we laid out our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive, end-to-end software delivery system in the world.

Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters.

Today at GitHub Universe, we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it.

The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better.

This agentic software delivery system solves for three things:

GitHub is built for developers and their agents. We’re also making the underlying primitives available, so you can build your own bespoke solutions. You stay in control of the work, the tools, and the cost.

Today at Universe, we showed some of the latest products and features in action, starting with the GitHub Copilot app.

The GitHub Copilot app is designed from the ground up for agentic software delivery. It connects your agents and tools across projects, so you can direct the work without making every handoff. And it’s for more than producing code: you can write specs, present design discussions, or analyze telemetry in one agent-first surface.

Different tasks need different models. Developers shouldn’t have to manage every model choice to get the right result at the right price. Copilot Fusion evaluates what a task needs across reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use, then chooses how to execute across one or more models. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40% less time per task.

Available natively in the GitHub Copilot app starting today, Copilot projects let you run agent work across multiple repos in fully managed, parallel sessions. You have one place to track progress, make decisions, and direct what happens next. That means you can spend less time managing execution and more time deciding what’s worth building.

Your work shouldn’t restart when you switch devices or tools. Session continuity lets you start and follow the same cloud agent session across the GitHub app, VS Code, the CLI, and the web. Start from your phone at standup, steer it from VS Code at your desk, and check in on it from github.com at lunch. The agent keeps working in the cloud. Our multi-model harness that enables it is powerful, fast, and cost-efficient.

Copilot automations let you create AI-powered workflows within your repo. They run in the cloud, and you can kick them off manually or set them up to respond to an event or run on a schedule. That lets you coordinate agents to handle tasks such as issue triage and code review. And now, automations can learn from their outcomes and propose improvements for you to review and approve. That’s the learning engine in practice. Use the results of the completed work to make the next run better.

More code means more pull requests and more demand for review. Moving faster only helps if we can maintain the quality of what ships. Copilot code review surfaces meaningful, actionable bugs that developers need to catch. Today, we introduced Copilot code review Max, which posted the highest F1 score on ReviewBench for high-severity issues. Lite and Balanced keep everyday reviews fast; the new Max provides a deeper look when a change needs it.

Starting today, GitHub Enterprise customers can use all Copilot features without buying a separate subscription. That includes GitHub Copilot app, code review, automations, and more. You pay for the AI credits you use.

This is available through GitHub Sales today, with self-serve coming soon. Existing Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise customers can keep their current plans or move over when they’re ready. GitHub also remains open and extensible. Keep using the tools your team depends on, including Cloudflare, Datadog, Figma, and more.

All of this depends on a foundation that’s fast, reliable, and built to scale. Agents are changing the volume and shape of software development. Adding capacity matters, but capacity alone won’t get us there. We’ve also had to change the architecture.

We’re also migrating to a multi-region deployment in Azure, while continuing to serve incredible levels of traffic from developers around the world. We expect to complete the migration early next year. Those investments give us more room to grow. The next step is building the systems that handle the work.

We’ve scaled Git for years as activity on GitHub has grown. The agentic era calls for a different ceiling on throughput and reliability. Three principles guide our new Git architecture: simplify the primitives, decouple storage from compute, and minimize coordination.

Git’s just one example of the work we’re doing to scale the platform. We’ve done a lot of work across GitHub’s AI gateway, the harness, and much more.

Our jobs are changing, but developers are more important than ever. I think all the software we’ve written to date will amount to less than 1% of the software we’ll write in the next five years. The opportunity isn’t just to produce more code. It’s to solve problems we couldn’t solve before.

That’s why we’re connecting the full software delivery system, giving developers better ways to work with agents, and evolving the infrastructure for what comes next. And we’re doing it on GitHub, where we can build together.

Jay Parikh is a seasoned executive, board member, and advisor to some of the world’s fastest growing and most successful consumer, developer, and enterprise technology companies. As Executive Vice President of CoreAI at Microsoft, Parikh leads the organization building the end-to-end agentic system required to build, ship, and run AI agents in the Enterprise. His teams, including GitHub, also build the tools and platforms developers need to create the next generation of software.

Previously, Parikh was CEO of a cloud security startup and, before that, was Facebook’s global head of engineering and infrastructure. For more than a decade, he led the teams that built and operated the physical infrastructure and software that supported the company’s growth from 300 million people to more than 3 billion. His teams worked across the stack, from data centers, servers, and subsea cables to software, data, AI, and security systems. Through leadership roles in the Open Compute Project and Telecom Infra Project, he helped extend infrastructure innovation beyond a single company to benefit entire industries.

Earlier in his career, Parikh held leadership roles at Akamai and Ning. He brings a systems thinker’s perspective to a deeply human challenge: how to build teams that keep learning, moving, and delivering as the world changes around them.

#10055. Polyend releases the Tracker firmware source code

Today we’re publishing the firmware source code for the original Tracker, Tracker+ and Tracker Mini on GitHub. We’re also releasing Tracker Community Edition 1.0 with tons of new features and improvements. You can install it on any of the three instruments, modify the firmware yourself and share your own version. We’ve built in a recovery system to keep a faulty firmware build from bricking your Tracker. Explore the Tracker Community Edition repository on GitHub

“Here at Polyend, creativity is what we value most. We’ve seen it firsthand in the unofficial Tracker mods you’ve built, and we’re sharing the firmware source code to support that work. Maybe you want to build an entirely new instrument on the Tracker hardware. Or maybe there’s just one thing you wish your Tracker did differently. Either way, you can now try it on the unit you already own. I bet some of you already have ideas for the original Tracker that never crossed our minds.” Piotr Raczyński, CEO of Polyend

All three models also get wavetable envelopes and LFOs, faster project loading and saving, and tighter MIDI clock timing. You can design custom Tracker themes and fonts in your browser. See all the new features, improvements and fixes in the full changelog

You can already see from the numbe rof firmwares on Backstage that this might help prevent a deluge of firmwares on the site, and be a good way to organise.

But as mentioned, this is now a open platform, with a democratic process. So we are more than open to suggestions and implementation proposals.

So if it’s technically feasible and people want it, ain’t nothing stopping us

GitHub’s annual month-long game jam is back for its 14th year! This November, make a game inspired by the theme SHIFT. Change gears, swap perspectives, bend reality, or just press a certain key.

Game Off, GitHub’s annual month-long game jam, returns for its 14th year this November. Thousands of developers have joined us over the years to make everything from polished platformers to wonderfully weird experiments.

Whether you’re making your first game or your fiftieth, we’d love for you to join us.

Shift gears. Shift perspectives. Shift dimensions. Shift bits. Work the night shift. Or make a game where the only buttons are the Shift keys.

How you interpret the theme is entirely up to you.

You have until December 1, 2026, at 13:37 PST to build and submit a game inspired by SHIFT. Strong or loose inspirations apply!

Acronyms (that we definitely just made up)

Or invent your own. We love seeing where you take the theme.

Of course, you could also build a game about shifting tectonic plates, shape-shifting aliens, shifting alliances, shifting sands, or a particularly ambitious stick shift.

Don’t overthink it. Pick an interpretation that interests you and see where it takes you.

Pro tip: Start with one mechanic and one playable level. Get those working before adding the multiverse. Future you (and your bug tracker) will thank you.

Need another perspective? Try brainstorming with GitHub Copilot. Give it the theme, a few constraints, and see what it comes up with:

Work alone or form a team. Use whichever programming languages, game engines, frameworks, libraries, and tools make sense for your game.

Here’s the fun part: you decide who wins.

Once submissions close, it’s your turn to play and rate the games your fellow developers have created. Every vote helps determine which games take home the bragging rights.

Entries will be evaluated in the following categories:

Voting will end on January 1, 2027, at 13:37 PST. Winners will be announced on the GitHub Blog and GitHub social channels shortly thereafter.

Game Off is intentionally relaxed, but there are a few guidelines to help keep it fair and fun:

That’s it. Keep it creative, respectful, and fun… and make sure your final code is pushed before the deadline.

You don’t need to be an expert to participate. Many Game Off participants create their first game during the jam.

Some use established engines. Some build their own. Others make games for old consoles, unusual hardware, terminals, calculators, or platforms we assumed had been lost to time.

However you build your game, there’s no single correct way to play.

Here are a few engines and frameworks you might want to explore:

Looking for teammates or a place to share progress? The Game Off 2026 Community is a great place to ask questions, share progress, and look for teammates. There’s also a friendly community-run Discord server.

Game Off is the perfect opportunity to check it out. Version control pun fully intended.

Whether you spend November shifting pixels, shifting bits, shifting timelines, or shifting unfinished tasks into the final 24 hours, you’ll be part of a global community making games together.

So take a different perspective, change the rules, and see what happens when you press ⇧.

Good luck and have fun! Can’t wait to play, err, test all your games! <3

Senior Program Manager, GitHub Developer Relations. Open source hype man, AI whisperer, hackathon and game jam wrangler. I write && manage programs, support dev communities, and occasionally ship something.

#10053. Experimenting with the proposed Cross-Origin Storage API in Transformers.js

(This is a guest post by Developer Relations Engineer Thomas Steiner from the Chrome team at Google.)

Transformers.js provides Web developers with a simple way to use the power of transformers in their Web apps through task-specific pipelines. To run inference in the browser, developers create an instance of pipeline() and specify a task they want to use the pipeline for. As a concrete example, the following snippet shows how to set up an automatic speech recognition (ASR) pipeline.

You will notice in the source code that I specified Xenova/whisper-tiny.en as the model, which is a very decent choice for common English automatic speech recognition tasks. In fact, it's even the default model according to the Transformers.js default model resolution, as per the linked excerpt.

When you run this example in the browser, Transformers.js automatically takes care of downloading and caching the relevant model resources and Wasm files. The following screenshot shows the Chrome DevTools Cache storage section after visiting the app. When you reload the page, the resources are served from the Cache API, and the model returns results almost instantly.

However, Xenova/whisper-tiny.en being a popular model (and, as mentioned before, even being the ASR default model in Transformers.js), you can well imagine that more than just one app that you visit would use it. To simulate this situation, here's the same example app from before, but served from a different origin. When you visit this different origin app, rather than being usable almost instantly, the browser instead has to download and cache all the model resources again, even if they're byte-by-byte the same as before. Even in this toy example, this adds up to 177 MB of duplicate download and storage, as you can examine in the Storage section of the Chrome DevTools Application panel. You can imagine that this quickly adds up.

But it gets worse. Let's add a second pipeline to the toy example: sentiment analysis. Sentiment analysis by default uses the Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english model. By not specifying the model, Transformers.js' default model resolution automatically picks it for you.

Two entirely different AI models, but they depend on the same 4,733 kB ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm WebAssembly (Wasm) runtime file from the underlying ONNX Runtime library that Transformers.js is built on top of. Open the extended demo on a different origin, and you will notice in the Network tab how also the Wasm runtime gets downloaded and cached again.

So even if you run apps that don't share the same AI models, your browser still makes redundant requests for shared Wasm resources you already have, and on top of that also caches them again, which consumes space on your hard disk.

By default, AI model resources come from the Hugging Face Hub, and ultimately the Hugging Face CDN. The browser makes a request for a resource like https://huggingface.co/Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english/resolve/main/config.json which then gets redirected to the final CDN URL like https://huggingface.co/api/resolve-cache/models/Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english/0b6928efcb76139cae2c6881d49cda67fe119f42/config.json?%2FXenova%2Fdistilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english%2Fresolve%2Fmain%2Fconfig.json=&etag=%223c36342ef1f74de2797d667c68c6b7b988d0b87c%22 in this case.

The Wasm runtime resources are served from the jsDelivr CDN by default. For example, ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm comes from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416-b7804b056c/dist/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm at the time of this writing.

The concrete implementation may vary by browser, but in Chrome, cached resources are keyed using a Network Isolation Key in addition to the resource URL. The Network Isolation Key is composed of the top-level site and the current-frame site. Take the previous toy examples hosted on the origins https://googlechrome.github.io and https://rawcdn.rawgit.net. If they both use the Wasm runtime from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416-b7804b056c/dist/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm, their cache keys will look like in the following table.

So even if the resource URLs are exactly the same, since the Network Isolation Keys don't match, there's no cache hit, which means duplicate download and duplicate storage. This is the challenge that the Cross-Origin Storage proposal aims to tackle.

💡 Note: The Cross-Origin Storage API is an early-stage proposal that isn't final. While the proposed API is not yet natively implemented in any browser, you don't have to wait to experiment with it. Install the Cross-Origin Storage extension to inject the navigator.crossOriginStorage polyfill on all pages and test the complete flow.

The proposed Cross-Origin Storage (COS) API introduces a dedicated navigator.crossOriginStorage interface through which web apps can store and retrieve large files across origin boundaries, identified not by a URL, but by a cryptographic hash.

That last point about cryptographic hashes is key. Because COS identifies files by their hash rather than by their URL or origin, the same ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm Wasm runtime you downloaded while visiting https://googlechrome.github.io is recognized as identical to the one https://rawcdn.rawgit.net is about to request, no matter where either of the two origins fetched it from. See the following code snippet that illustrates the basic flow.

If the resource is in COS, you get back a FileSystemFileHandle from which you can read the blob directly via getFile() (the resulting File inherits from Blob). If the resource is not in COS, you fall back to the network, and write the resource into COS for the next app that needs it, which could be your app, or another unrelated app, potentially on a completely different origin.

The API is deliberately shaped after the File System Standard's FileSystemDirectoryHandle.getFileHandle() you likely are familiar with from the Origin Private File System (OPFS) API. The hash parameter plays the same role as the name parameter in OPFS: uniquely identifying a resource. The options.create flag works the same way: absent or false for read-only access, true when you intend to write.

Not every resource should be globally shared. COS gives developers precise control over visibility through the origins option when storing a file.

One important rule: visibility can be upgraded but never downgraded. If a file is already globally available, a later attempt to store it with a restricted origins list is silently ignored. This prevents a malicious actor from re-storing a public resource and narrowing its availability. The reverse is possible: a file initially stored with a restricted origins list can later be made more permissive. Any site, not just the original storer, can call getFileHandle() for the same hash (hashes are not a secret) with create: true and a broader origins value, and given the browser verifies the hash matches, the resource becomes available to the wider audience from that point on. Note that the upgrading site must still write the full file through the returned handle. This requirement exists to prevent sites from exploiting the upgrade path as a side-channel to detect whether a particular file was already stored in COS.

A subtle but important property of COS is that the browser verifies the hash when you write a file. If the data you write doesn't match the declared hash, the write fails with an error. This makes integrity checking automatic: an app reading a file from COS can be confident it's getting exactly the bytes it expected. The same guarantee it would have had if it had computed the hash itself after a network download.

This turns out to be doubly useful in the Transformers.js scenario. Today, after downloading model weights, most apps have no practical way to verify that the CDN served the right bytes. With COS, every file in the store is implicitly verified on write, no matter where it came from, the official Hugging Face CDN or a random site's self-hosted mirror.

Of course a cross-origin shared cache raises the same question as the partitioned HTTP cache in reverse: if any site can probe for the presence of a file by hash, couldn't an attacker learn something about the user's browsing history by checking whether, say, a game engine Wasm module is cached?

COS addresses this through two complementary mechanisms:

Crucially, this means an error is not a definitive answer. It might mean "not stored", or it might mean "stored, but the browser isn't telling you". Apps should always handle it the same way: fall back to the network.

Going back to the toy examples from before: the ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm runtime weighs in at 4,733 kB and is shared by every Transformers.js-powered app regardless of which AI model it uses. With COS, the first app to load it downloads it once and stores it under its SHA-256 hash with origins: '*'. Every subsequent app, whether on https://googlechrome.github.io, on https://rawcdn.rawgit.net, or any other origin, finds it in COS immediately. The 177 MB of duplicate Whisper model weights? Same story: Xenova/whisper-tiny.en gets downloaded once, recognized by hash the second time around, and served from COS in milliseconds. And of course, the same also happens for Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english.

Transformers.js itself is already piloting the COS API at the library level. Pull request #1549 introduced an experimental COS cache backend behind an opt-in flag. Enabling it takes a single line before you set up your pipeline:

Note the experimental_ prefix on the flag. It's intentional and signals that the underlying browser API has not yet been standardized and may change without a major version bump. With that flag set, Transformers.js resolves the SHA-256 hash for each Xet-tracked model file (the large ONNX weight files) by fetching the raw Xet pointer (example raw pointer file) and extracting its oid sha256: field. It then uses that hash as the key for navigator.crossOriginStorage. If the model is already in COS (because another site stored it there first), it's served instantly without a network round-trip. If not, it falls back to a regular download and stores the result in COS for the next caller. With the toy example, the advantage in practice is that Xenova/whisper-tiny.en and Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english (and of course ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm) only ever need to cross the ether once, regardless of how many different origins ask for them.

The toy example works just fine with Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, but of course you possibly wouldn't say no if the user already has any of the other Whisper variants in their COS cache. For example, the user might already have Xenova/whisper-large-v3, which, as the name suggests, is a lot larger than the tiny variant. Transformers.js's Model Registry makes being flexible about your models possible. If you know your app's needs can be addressed by, for example, any of Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, whisper-medium.en, or Xenova/whisper-large-v3, you can check the registry for the associated files for each model, probe for their existence in the COS cache (which may partially or completely contain the model resources you need), and then take a decision what model to choose eventually. The ModelRegistry.is_pipeline_cached() API directly integrates with COS (and of course the Cache API), so this operation is really ergonomic.

The COS API is not yet natively implemented in any browser, but you don't have to wait to experiment with it. Install the Cross-Origin Storage extension to inject the navigator.crossOriginStorage polyfill on all pages and test the complete flow. Check out the source code of the extension and follow the usage instructions to get started.

With the extension installed, try the full end-to-end experience right now: open the first toy example with COS enabled, let it load Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, then open the toy example with COS enabled from the second origin. Instead of the 177 MB re-download you saw before, the model is served from COS in milliseconds. When you open the extension's popup window, you can see COS in action. If you View by Resource, you can see the resource with the SHA-256 hash 950978b1dbcbf250335358c1236053ba19a7f7849b33dc777f4421b72b7626fa shared across https://googlechrome.github.io and https://rawcdn.rawgit.net. It may not be obvious, but as you can verify by comparing the SHA-256 hash on Hugging Face, you're looking at https://huggingface.co/Xenova/whisper-tiny.en/blob/main/onnx/decoder_model_merged.onnx. For now, the extension is mostly aimed at power users like you. Once implemented in the browser, there will be a friendlier integration in the browser's Settings page. The screenshot below shows the extension's popup window with the View by Resource tab active, where you can see the shared resource with its hash and the two origins that have it in their COS cache.

If you're building your own Transformers.js app, the call to action is simple: add env.experimental_useCrossOriginStorage = true before your first pipeline() call, install the extension, and watch the duplicate downloads disappear from your Network tab. Every site that opts in makes the experience faster and cheaper for every other site's users. Opting in is completely risk-free: if the COS API isn't supported because the user doesn't have the COS extension installed, the code just falls back to the default path (the Cache API).

Transformers.js is not alone in experimenting with COS. WebLLM (opt-in, see documentation) and wllama (automatic, see PR) are likewise excited about this proposed API.

On the Chrome team, we're considering implementing the COS API natively in the browser. As an early stage proposal, we welcome feedback on the API, and the shape of the proposal itself. The Cross-Origin Storage repository is the place to file issues, express support, or open PRs.

#10052. State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Relatively small data breaches in India can turn quite serious, thanks to a sophisticated underground market for trading PII.

An anonymous hacker has leaked a small batch of sensitive customer records from the State Bank of India (SBI), with potentially serious consequences for the thousands impacted.

SBI has been posting a lot about cybersecurity on social media lately. In August it introduced a new CGI mascot named "Captain Y." Captain Y from SBI is "your Cyber Protector," he says in his promo video, "with awareness as his superpower." SBI's best plug for cybersecurity awareness came on Wednesday, though, when it publicly disclosed that it had suffered a breach of customer data.

In a notice to India's National Stock Exchange, the organization's compliance and company secretary acknowledged that 3,897 customer records had been leaked online. They did not specify whether those records belonged to 3,897 individual customers. In a public notice to customers, the state-run bank emphasized that the incident really only impacted "a very, very small number of customers."

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

For a bank that serves north of 500 million people, a few thousand records does indeed qualify as very, very small. Cyber experts note, though, that for those affected, the consequences could be significant thanks to India's sophisticated underground economy for buying and selling personally identifying information (PII).

Last week, a new account with the name "Siriusim" published a post to the mainstream data breach website BreachForums. They had new user data from SBI, they claimed, including personal user information, new account and loan applications, and more. The data included a table with 375,000 rows, and 2,722 PDF files. Importantly, neither figure necessarily indicated the total number of individuals impacted.

As part of the post, Siriusim featured a few documents with handwritten personal information. Mumbai's Free Press Journal verified that PII from the breach samples was valid, belonging to real Indian citizens. One individual, for example, lost their mobile number and know your customer (KYC) documentation in the breach, and the WhatsApp photograph associated with their number matched the passport photo included in the KYC file.

SBI acknowledged that leaked data included names, genders, mobile numbers, email addresses, home addresses, dates of birth, bank profile IDs, metadata associated with loans, and "other files." Follow-on reporting out of Mumbai suggested that this extra data included Central KYC numbers — a single identifier for financial accounts in India — and video KYC verification data, and the kinds of files one might have to submit in the process of creating a new bank account, or filing for a loan. For instance, one published document included an individual's employment and income declaration, with details about their current employer, work experience, and salary.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

Exactly what precipitated the leak, and why it affected only 0.0008% of the bank's customers, remains unclear. In its formal declaration, SBI emphasized that "the bank's core business functions continue to operate normally without disruptions." Altogether, these clues might point to a breach of some peripheral digital service or data-handling system, rather than the core bank system.

In fact, SBI's last major customer data leak followed just such a script. In 2019, it exposed customer account data through a single server at a Mumbai data center, which was missing password protection. The server supported its "SBI Quick" system, used to text and call customers about basic account information. That one machine put millions of customers at risk, perhaps highlighting just how minor this new leak really is.

"If the data is genuine, the main risk is not direct account theft but credible-sounding phishing, vishing, and identity or loan fraud, since attackers who know someone’s details can impersonate the bank convincingly," explains independent security researcher Sushant Bhardwaj.

Related:Warlock Ransomware Hits Large Spanish, Portuguese Orgs

Email addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth carry fairly obvious risk in the hands of bad actors, and less common kinds of PII can add color to otherwise generic identity attacks. For instance, "KYC details are hard to change, so they can support identity fraud, such as applying for credit in someone else’s name or answering account-verification questions," Bhardwaj notes. And with regard to loan metadata, "a caller who can quote real loan details can pose as the bank or a recovery agent and pressure a borrower into paying a 'fee' or sharing a one-time password (OTP)."

Brian Hussey, senior vice president for Cyderes' Howler Cell, goes deeper. Last month, his team reported on an Indian data broker selling personal records for only about 5 rupees (6 cents or so) per lookup, through a Telegram bot and business application programming interface (API) platform. Using these simple lookups, cybercriminals targeting Indian citizens can obtain vast stores of PII belonging to regular citizens in an instant. And data breaches like SBI's, Hussey notes, can feed into this underground economy. "A breach dump goes stale the day it's posted. A live lookup service is always current, because it is asking the authoritative source in real time. India’s underground data market has both, and they work together," he explains.

"India built one of the most connected identity systems in the world, and an entire industry exists to query it," he warns. "That connectivity is what makes a leak in one place so impactful and useful somewhere else."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#10051. Open models can do 90% of agentic work at a twentieth of the cost of a frontier LLM: Gartner

Models are commodities, harnesses are the valuable part

For-profit model-makers, many of which are spending billions on AI infrastructure, will be chasing revenue from just ten percent of steps involved in agentic AI workflows, according to analyst firm Gartner.

“Nine in 10 agent workflow steps are routine, and open-weight models handle them at parity for a quarter of the price of the cheapest closed model,” the firm’s senior director Mark Petty and group vice president Raymond Paquet wrote last week in new document titled “Open-Weight Models Will Run 90% of Enterprise Agentic Workflow Steps.”

“Typical operational workflows involve hundreds of routine executions, such as classification, tool calling, passing, validating and reconciling data,” the pair observe, before suggesting open-weight models “can handle hundreds of these routine steps for every one that needs frontier reasoning.”

“Against the cheapest closed model at the same score, the open model costs a quarter as much. Against a frontier model run on every step, it costs as little as a twentieth,” the pair add.

Those are the best-case numbers, because the analysts admit “Current open models can be more verbose and retry more often, so the saving per task against a frontier model is closer to five or six times.”

That’s still a lovely saving, but the analysts rate it as the welcome by-product of moving to open models rather than an end in itself.

“Years of workflow history are a large part of what an acquirer pays for in a SaaS company and every routine step sent to a frontier API moves a slice of it outside your perimeter,” the pair wrote. “Open-weights preserve your control. The cost saving is a bonus.”

The two analysts therefore offer the following strategic planning assumption: “By 2030, 90% of enterprise operational agent workflow steps will execute on open-weight models.”

They argue that enterprises will mostly adopt domain-specific open-weight models, because they do well “in scenarios where a small number of highly stable steps run millions of times a month.”

Most models, however, are already commodities. Harnesses, the tools that run agents and manage agents, are the source of value in AI products, because one of their roles is to route work to the most appropriate model for a job, without users noticing any impact. A good harness saves money, imposes strong guardrails, and manages agent fleets. Less powerful harnesses leave users with more to do.

The paper suggests frontier models will continue to have a role as the engine of research and development and are effectively capital expense. Open-weight models become an operational expense after frontier models do the heavy lifting. ®

Louis Erbkamm built the first prototype in his free time. Now GitHub Copilot helps him maintain it alone.

Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it.

I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet.

Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors.

Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school.

That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow.

Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with.

The project didn’t have a name yet, so it borrowed the town’s unique moniker.

When Arnis added elevation, its worlds stopped being flat, and geospatial specialists from all over showed up with ideas on how best to integrate it. They started discussions on their own, and Louis says that’s exactly what he needed.

Bigger calls happen in the open too: before porting Arnis from Python to Rust, Louis opened discussions on GitHub to hear different perspectives. Contributors have since translated Arnis into about 20 languages and built major features of their own.

The best thing that has happened to me is essentially this big community on GitHub to see actually people from all kinds of different fields coming together to work on something that I started as a side project.

Some features start on a walk. Louis noticed how many trash bins there were in his city, and there were none in his generated worlds.

Minecraft has no dedicated bins, so he took the question to the community, and together they found a block that fit. Placing one follows the same path as everything else: for the area a user selects, Arnis queries OpenStreetMap for every mapped element, then looks up each element’s coordinates and type.

If an element isn’t mapped, Arnis can’t place it. For structures too detailed for the map to describe, like the Statue of Liberty in New York, or Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, Arnis converts 3D models into Minecraft blocks.

As the sole maintainer, Louis reviews every pull request himself, and they stack up. He usually spends evenings or weekends working on Arnis, which means the community has to wait for him to be done with work for the day.

He uses GitHub Copilot to get an overview of open issues and bugs from the latest release, see how many people are running into them, trace where a bug came from in the codebase, and create a fix. Since he brought AI into the project, he says, code reviews and documentation have both increased.

I could delegate those annoying and boring tasks to Copilot, while I could still have a look at those really cool topics that are related to the development of it.

Big features arrive as big pull requests.

Louis opens a large pull request in the GitHub Copilot app for a first overview and a performance review, with Copilot running in the background looking for small changes that would cut memory usage or generation time.

It takes just one wrong calculation in street lights, for example, to make the generation time of an entire city much slower.

He also keeps a mental list of the areas of the codebase that need extra care whenever someone changes them, and he has written the same warnings out by hand over and over.

I’m starting a few sub agents with the GitHub Copilot app to have a look specifically at those cases, and to come up with corner cases to test to make sure that we do not introduce any regressions into new releases.

He likes that the terminal, his files, the code changes and the pull request all sit in one app next to the chat.

Louis’s favorite use of Arnis is in schools, where teachers have generated their city or a neighborhood park.

Some turn it into a contest: every student starts from the same generated area, improves a nearby park or playground using Arnis and Minecraft, and the class looks at the results together.

Recent releases have gone beyond the bounds of Earth, adding the Moon and Mars. Louis wants Arnis to stay easy to use while getting closer to reality, with more detail in less time, and he would like to see it in more schools.

Download Arnis from github.com/louis-e/arnis, pick a place on the map, choose where to spawn, and click Start Generation: within a few minutes, the world is ready to open in Minecraft. Louis suggests a place you know, like your hometown or somewhere memorable you’ve been, such as the Grand Canyon or Niagara Falls. Then look for what’s missing.

So maybe you see a bench that was not generated even though it is there.

Map it on OpenStreetMap, or tell Louis if it’s a bug and he will fix it.

#10049. Shipping huggingface_hub every week with AI, open tools, and a human in the loop

huggingface_hub is the Python client at the base of the Hugging Face ecosystem. transformers, datasets, diffusers, sentence-transformers and dozens of other libraries depend on it to talk to the Hub. Every week we don't ship a new release is a week of fixes and features stuck on main.

For a long time we released every 4 to 6 weeks. We now release every week from a single GitHub Actions workflow. We built it using open-source tools and open-weights models and kept a human in the loop at the one place where judgment matters. Nothing in this post requires a vendor contract, a closed model, or infrastructure you can't run yourself. That was a design goal from the start since we wanted a workflow other maintainers could pick up and adapt.

By the end of this post, you'll have everything you need to build your own.

The old process was partly automated, mostly manual.

Writing good notes for a new version was the heavy part, aggregating tens of PRs on different topics. Nothing technically hard but a few hours of focused attention. Add the announcements on top and a minor release was easily a half-day of work spread over several days.

So we decided to streamline the whole thing. Looking at that list, the work splits in two.

Some steps are purely mechanical and can be automated: bumping the version, committing, tagging, pushing, opening downstream test branches, opening the post-release PR. Nobody needs to think about those. They just have to happen in the right order, every time, which is what a CI workflow is good at.

The rest is different. Writing release notes, deciding what to highlight, phrasing an announcement for a human audience: that's brain work. It's the kind of judgment that kept the release manual for years. This is where AI comes in, turning a blank page into a solid first draft in seconds. It's also where we have to be careful because a draft that looks confident and is subtly wrong is worse than no draft at all.

When we decided to fix this, we set one constraint up front: every moving part had to be something any maintainer could run themselves. No closed model behind an API we couldn't swap, no proprietary release platform, no secret sauce.

The second principle: the model drafts, a human decides. Language models are good at turning thirty terse PR titles into readable release notes. They are not good at being trusted blindly. So the workflow is human-supervised: the model does the first pass, a deterministic script checks its work, and a human reviews and edits before anything ships (more on that below).

The full workflow is a single file, .github/workflows/release.yml, triggered by hand from the Actions UI. It takes exactly one input:

From there, the jobs run roughly in this order:

The remaining manual steps are reviewing and publishing the draft release notes, and reviewing and posting an internal Slack message. Those two steps are where we want a human in the loop.

Here's the failure mode everyone worries about with AI-generated release notes: the model quietly drops a PR or invents one that isn't in this release. A changelog that's almost right is worse than no changelog because nobody re-checks it.

We don't trust the generated release notes to be complete on the first try, we verify it deterministically. Before the model runs, a Python script retrieves all PRs that belong to the release and stores them as ground truth.

Then model drafts the notes from them. Once done, we check its output against the initial list of PRs:

If anything is missing or extra, we don't fail and we don't ship a wrong file. We hand the discrepancy back to the agent and ask it to fix exactly those PRs:

This is the pattern that makes the whole thing trustworthy: a non-deterministic model wrapped in deterministic guardrails. The model is great at writing prose and unreliable at being exhaustive. So we let it write and let code enforce the consistency.

Completeness is one half. Accuracy is the other. A model summarizing a PR from its title alone will cheerfully invent a code example that doesn't match the real API.

To prevent that, when we fetch PR metadata we also pull the actual documentation diffs from each PR: the unified diff of any .md file under docs/ that the PR touched.

That diff goes into the model's context so when it writes "here's the new CLI command," it's quoting the example the PR author actually wrote in the docs. That's the same logic as before: give the model real source material and a narrow job.

The prompts themselves live as Skills: small Markdown files (SKILL.md plus reference templates) checked into the repo. The release-notes skill spells out how to pick highlights, how to structure sections, when to add a doc link, etc. It reads like onboarding instructions, which is exactly the right mental model.

After the RC is published, the draft GitHub release sits there with the AI's first pass in it. This is where the human comes in:

The reviewer's time goes into polishing, turning a half-day of writing into a fifteen-minute editing session.

We also keep a paper trail to improve over time. We archive two files side by side to a Hugging Face Bucket: the raw AI draft, uploaded at RC time before anyone touches it, and the human-edited version, uploaded when the final release is cut.

Collecting both every week gives us a growing dataset of "what the model wrote" versus "what we wished it wrote". Dataset that we can then reuse to update the agent's skill.

Revamping the release process was a good opportunity to tighten security, especially against supply-chain attacks.

No PyPI token. Publishing uses Trusted Publishing: PyPI verifies a short-lived OIDC token minted by GitHub for this exact workflow, and issues PEP 740 attestations / Sigstore provenance for every artifact. There's no long-lived secret to leak or rotate.

The agent runtime is pinned and verified. We don't curl | bash the latest OpenCode and hope. We pin a version and check its SHA256 before running it:

Open tooling doesn't mean careless tooling.

Almost nothing. A full release (notes plus the Slack announcement, across 20-40 PRs and a few rounds of prompting) costs about $0.25 on Inference Providers. With open weights billed pay-as-you-go, the only real question each week is "is there something worth shipping?", and there always is.

The cadence went from one release every 4 to 6 weeks to once a week. The secondary effects were the interesting ones:

This is the part we cared about most. The workflow is shaped around huggingface_hub but the structure is generic.

To adapt it: fork the workflow file and scripts, point it at your package, rewrite the skill Markdown for your project's voice, set two repo variables (the model ID and your OpenCode version), set up Trusted Publishing on PyPI, and delete the downstream-testing job if you don't have downstreams. The trust-but-verify loop is the part worth reusing as-is. It's what makes a generated artifact safe to ship.

The parts of a release that used to need a half-day of focused human work (writing notes, drafting announcements, coordinating downstream checks) are the parts a model is good at drafting. Everything else is mechanical and fits in a YAML file. The trick was never just "let the AI do it". It's to let the model draft, let deterministic code verify, and let a human decide. It's built entirely from open tools and open weights so the cost rounds to zero and anyone can run it.

The full workflow file is public. If you maintain a Python library, fork it, adapt it, and let us know how it goes!

#10048. AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Microsoft's Project Perception adds Guardian Agents to monitor and contain anomalous AI agents, but experts warn that policing unpredictable agents with other agents may compound — not contain — the risk.

Microsoft wants security teams to treat artificial intelligence (AI) agents like they treat employees with privileged access: insiders who can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

Earlier this week, the software giant introduced new capabilities to Project Perception, enabling it to discover agents running within an organization, assign an identity and permissions to each agent, and continuously score each organization's risk. When an anomalous agent is discovered in the organization's environment — a problem that Microsoft describes as the "agentic insider" — Project Perception can now cut off the agent's access.

The first release of Project Perception, made available in public preview through Microsoft Defender in August, was designed to defend against AI-driven attacks. Focused on Microsoft's security operations center threat and investigation scenarios, it coordinates red agents to scan for attacker paths, blue agents to identify the greatest risks, and green agents to mitigate threats. Project Perception's initial use was vulnerability management, through MDASH, Microsoft's AI code scanner, which is still in preview. MDASH uses several AI models, including MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, the company's first cybersecurity-specialized model.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"We're expanding Perception so that we can go secure the AI insider," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, in a brief video accompanying the announcement.

To do that, Microsoft is adding what it calls Guardian Agents, which monitor the AI-based agents running across an organization and can contain them when they stray into unexpected behavior.

Today, many agents run with the permissions of the user who launched them or by invoking the user's credentials. Microsoft's approach separates the two, Microsoft said in a blog post detailing the new capabilities.

Nadim Abdo, corporate vice president for identity and network access, tells Dark Reading that the system gives every agent a distinct identity separate from the user's "and will ensure that the agent starts with no permissions at all, and only up-scopes to the permissions it needs to complete the task the user is asking it to do,"

Specifically, Microsoft said the new release can detect 35 more types of agents running locally on devices, bringing the total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. It also includes:

Extensions to Microsoft Entra Agent ID that can assign an identity to an agent that was never built to work with Entra.

Dynamic Agent Risk, a continuously updated score built from Entra, Defender, Intune, Purview, Sentinel, and signals from Global Secure Access, Microsoft’s security service edge (SSE) solution that unifies network access and identity protection.

Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, which can block writes while keeping reads, restrict network paths, revoke access, or stop an agent's runtime as risk rises.

Microsoft Execution Container (MXC), a sandbox that keeps credentials and security controls outside the agent's reach.

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

With Project Perception, Abdo describes an expense-approval agent that reads a malicious instruction hidden in an expense report.

"If someone got a prompt that convinced it to start to try to do wire transfers, we can actually watch it accessing a wire transfer system and say, 'Wait a second, that has nothing to do with the intent,' and that raises its risk," he says.

Microsoft says it can act on rising risk immediately, interrupting an agent's live session, network connection, or runtime without disrupting the user's own work, though those are vendor-stated capabilities in preview.

Project Perception has an expanded agent registry that now shows up across the Microsoft 365 admin center, Defender, Entra, Intune, Purview, and a new Perception Agent Insights view. And Dynamic Agent Risk replaces previously siloed risk scores.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

The controls themselves sit outside the agents they watch.

"The first thing [an attacker will] do is they'll manipulate the security controls," Abdo says, so the credentials and monitoring tools run outside the container.

Perception and Agent 365, Microsoft's control plane for governing that was introduced last year and made generally available since May, "need to be battle tested," acknowledged Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a fireside chat with Gallot during a CISO conference last week at Microsoft's Redmond, Wash., headquarters. He also admitted that Microsoft's own detection must improve.

"If I look at the state of the art of behavioral monitoring of, let's say, Defender, it has to go way up," he said.

Gallot framed the risk in terms of how models behave.

"Those models have proven to be unpredictable," she said. "They'll do anything they can to get from point A to point B, and what they do may not be what you intend them to do."

Much of what Microsoft describes echoes what other vendors announced in recent weeks. Okta's Agent Gateway separates an agent's permissions from those of the user directing it, and Okta plans a kill switch that would reject tokens already issued to a deactivated agent. Teleport, backed by Cisco, ties privileges to tasks so they disappear when the work ends. CrowdStrike announced an Agentic Identity Provider and Falcon Guardian, which discovers agents and controls that may run on Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints.

Abdo argues that each vendor sees only part of the picture.

"If you're primarily an identity vendor or primarily a network vendor or primarily an endpoint vendor, that lens gives you some visibility to what agents are doing, but you need to have the other components as well," he says.

Microsoft's advantage, he adds, is that Entra, Defender, and Intune are already widely deployed and integrated, so customers aren't "having to string these things together from multiple vendors."

Microsoft says it will also take in signals from third-party security products. Partners can already publish agent risk events into Agent 365 through public APIs, Abdo says, though he could not yet name which partner integrations are public.

Forrester principal security and risk management analyst Andras Cser is skeptical.

"Most of Microsoft's integration with third-party players, especially in security, has not been first rate so far," Cser says. Because Microsoft has most of the products it needs in its own ecosystem, he adds, it is "interested in pushing its own products."

The question is whether that approach fits environments where agents run across AWS, Google Cloud, Salesforce, and ServiceNow. Last month, Okta announced the formation of the Blueprint Alliance with AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors.

Microsoft is not among the named members. Asked whether it would participate, Abdo said Entra has "always been built on open standards" and that "we're always exploring those things."

Okta, which formed the alliance, argues that no single vendor sees enough.

"No one company can secure agents alone," said CEO and co-founder Todd McKinnon in his keynote at Oktane, the company’s annual conference, last month.

Reacting to this week’s Project Perception launch, Harish Peri, Okta's senior vice president and general manager of AI security, says, "Microsoft's Guardian Agents feature will only be as good as the broader ecosystem it plugs into. If you want to catch intent drift in real time, you need signals pulling from your entire stack, not just one vendor's cloud."

Nevertheless, Peri echoes Nadella's framing. Because agents must be allowed to behave unpredictably to be useful, "we can't secure agents by trying to control how their models think," Peri says. "We need to control their authority."

The answer, Peri says, is "deeper interoperability and cross-vendor signal sharing built on open standards."

Cser interprets the Blueprint Alliance as "more of a partnership kind of map" than a true standard. Cser believes vendor-specific efforts like this alliance are "a marketing ploy" that tend to fade within a year or two. Enterprises need open standards any vendor can implement, he says.

Consequently, that leaves CISOs with an imperfect choice in what Cser calls "still a very fluid market." The current choices, he says, are either a Microsoft-centric approach built mainly on Microsoft products or a multivendor approach with "many vendors, many price lists," where integration "is almost always a suspicious kind of promise."

Some security vendors agree that treating agents as insiders extends the long-standing zero-trust and least-privilege principles rather than replacing them.

Denis Calderone, CTO of Suzu Labs, says the most malicious behavior may never look like an agent straying from its task.

"Dynamic permissions scope what an agent can touch, but the worst outcomes happen inside the authorized envelope," he says.

Calderone points to July's OpenAI incident as evidence that agents can work against the systems watching them. More than 1,000 agents in a cyber evaluation coordinated to game the system grading them, some by faking tool calls, before roughly 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face, according to METR.

Further, Calderone has concerns about Guardian Agents, noting that they are agents themselves.

"Securing agents with agents means the Guardian Agents themselves are overprivileged actors that can be manipulated or compromised," he says.

Cser shares Calderone's concerns about Guardian Agents. An unpredictable agent watched by another unpredictable agent creates "non-deterministic nature squared," Cser says. "Most organizations today are very careful about bringing guardian agents into the mix."

Following Perception's July launch, Forrester principal analyst Allie Mellen urged organizations to enforce "least privilege and least agency," limiting not just what agents can access but what they can do on their own. Microsoft meets the first test but not yet the second, Cser says.

"It is least privilege, but I wouldn't go as far as describing it as least agency," he says, adding that some specialist vendors are further along.

While Perception itself is in public preview, the new Guardian Agent capabilities are in use only inside Microsoft and with "a small set of select customers." They will be expanding to more external customers this week and to broader preview rings over the next few months. Microsoft plans to say more at its annual Ignite conference next month.

Project Perception builds on the controls in Microsoft 365 E7, the $99-per-user-per-month suite that includes E5, Agent 365, and Entra Suite, which supply the signals and enforcement points that Perception relies on. Microsoft hasn't disclosed whether the new capabilities are included in E7, but Project Perception is priced based on consumption.

Cser expects the release to push customers toward E7.

"I would almost be sure that this is another kind of making people buy stuff in more expensive packages that they don't currently need but may need in future," he says.

By his estimate, E7 comes to about $1,200 per user per year at list price, or roughly $600 after typical volume discounts of 40% to 50%, which "can be prohibitively expensive for a lot of organizations."

Meanwhile, Calderone says organizations don't have to wait. He recommends inventorying every agent, including those running on developer machines. Each should be assigned its own identity and credentials set to expire, and each should require human approval for consequential actions.

"That work is free today," he says, "and it's the foundation every one of these Microsoft controls assumes you already have."

Jai Vijayan contributed reporting to this article.

#10047. Forget retraining - AI can now tweak another AI's weights

'Weight-Space Programming' fiddles with nerd knobs to boost benchmark scores

The outputs of AI models are the result of a complex interplay between neurons, weights, training, and inference, and are therefore difficult to follow.

But in some ways they're starting to look more like open books. Recent work by Anthropic safety fellow Joshua Fonseca Rivera has revealed how certain neurons in a neural network can be associated with a specific persona.

Now, computer scientists from MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) have found that frontier AI models like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra can rewrite the weights of another model directly, as opposed to indirectly through training, and alter their behavior.

"We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights," said Rikiya Takehi, a PhD student at MIT CSAIL, in a social media post. "Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly."

To demonstrate that, Takehi and colleagues Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to make it better at math.

Astra changed only 0.016 percent of the model's weights, reducing its reasoning loops and improving its math performance by as much as sixfold on the MATH-500 benchmark, while boosting its instruction-following score on the IFEval benchmark roughly threefold.

There was no training using gradient descent; Astra just revised the numerical values that constitute Qwen's weights.

"All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops," the researchers wrote in a blog post. "It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

"Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights."

Astra's ability to program weights extends to being able to write a neural network from scratch, zero-shot. The researchers told Astra: "write, from scratch, the weights of a policy network that plays [Breakout] as well as possible." And it did so.

Takehi suggests this technique shows promise for improving models without the consequences of catastrophic forgetting, which can occur when a model is revised to include new knowledge.

More generally, the authors expect Weight-Space Programming will open the door to new ways to understand models and optimize them, and to implement recursive self-improvement. The technique may also prove useful for reducing model sycophancy and improving interpretability and alignment.

The next step, the authors say, involves building a benchmark and a harness for carrying out Weight-Space Programming on LLMs. "We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline," they say. ®

#10046. Introducing the FFASR Leaderboard: Benchmarking ASR in the Real World

🚀 First open far-field ASR benchmark: community-driven evaluation across 14 simulated rooms, validated against real-world measurements: https://huggingface.co/spaces/treble-technologies/ffasr

📉 The gap is real and it is large: across all submitted models, far-field WER at low SNR is consistently several times higher than near-field WER on the same speech content

🔬 Methodology you can trust: hybrid wave-based simulation, sim-to-real validation, moving-source splits in beta, held-out audio, and standardized evaluation hardware across all submissions

⚡ Accuracy and speed together: the Pareto front plots average WER against RTFx so you can evaluate the tradeoff that is right for your deployment

👀 More is coming: multi-talker scenarios, microphone array support, and echo cancellation are on the roadmap

The gap between benchmark performance and real-world deployment is one of the more persistent frustrations in ASR development. Models that score well on standard evaluations often behave differently once real room acoustics are involved: reverberation, background noise, microphone distance. The complex interactions between these factors affect performance in ways that clean-speech benchmarks do not capture. The FFASR Leaderboard is our attempt to quantify that gap.

Treble Technologies and Hugging Face are launching the Far-Field ASR (FFASR) Leaderboard, the first open, community-driven benchmark designed to evaluate ASR models under realistic far-field acoustic conditions. It is live now, and we are inviting the community to submit models, explore the results, and help shape what comes next.

Voice interfaces have expanded well beyond the headset and the smartphone. AI voice agents, conference room transcription, in-car assistants, humanoid robots, smart glasses, and hands-free tools are all seeing rapid adoption. What they have in common is that they operate in acoustically complex environments: reverberation, background noise, overlapping sounds, and a microphone that may be anywhere from one to several meters from the speaker.

The dominant ASR evaluation paradigm has not caught up with this reality. Clean, close-microphone benchmarks remain the standard, and while they are useful for measuring core recognition quality, they do not predict far-field performance. A model that performs well on LibriSpeech or other near-field sets may degrade substantially once real room acoustics enter the picture. While there have been several research efforts around far-field and noisy speech evaluation — including CHiME, URGENT, and NOIZEUS — the community has not had a standardized, open way to measure that degradation consistently across models in a continuously updated leaderboard format. That is what FFASR is built for.

A major challenge of far-field evaluation is the availability of data. Collecting far-field recordings across a representative range of room types, microphone distances, and noise conditions at scale is prohibitively expensive with physical measurements alone. Simulation makes it possible to cover that space systematically and to extend coverage over time without a corresponding increase in measurement cost.

Another goal of FFASR is to encourage the development of models that are explicitly robust to these conditions. Leaderboards have historically been effective at directing research effort. By making far-field performance visible and comparable, we hope to raise the priority of real-world acoustic robustness across the field.

The FFASR Leaderboard evaluates models across nine conditions. The four that determine the primary ranking score are (as of 22 June 2026):

To give a sense of what these conditions actually sound like, the samples below let you hear the same speech utterance as dry anechoic audio, then convolved with a room impulse response, and finally with noise added at each SNR tier. The difference between the dry recording and the low-SNR far-field condition is a reasonable proxy for the scale of the problem the leaderboard is measuring.

Two additional columns, Lab Measured and Lab Simulated, serve as a sim-to-real validation track. The leaderboard also includes moving-source splits, currently in beta, which evaluate models against audio where the speaker is in motion rather than stationary. This condition reflects use cases such as humanoid robots, in-car speech, and mobile voice assistants where the acoustic geometry between speaker and microphone changes continuously.

The acoustic data is generated with Treble's hybrid simulation engine, which combines a wave-based solver at low to mid frequencies with geometrical-acoustics modeling at higher frequencies. This approach captures physical phenomena that simpler simulation methods often miss: diffraction, scattering, interference, and modal behavior. The result is simulated data that closely matches measured acoustic conditions, which the Lab Measured and Lab Simulated columns confirm directly by running the same evaluation on both.

Fourteen fully furnished rooms are included in the benchmark, ranging from 20 to 470 m³ and covering bathrooms, living rooms with hallways, offices, classrooms, and restaurant spaces. Each acoustic scene contains one target speaker, recorded in an anechoic chamber to avoid reverberation artifacts from the recording environment, and up to three noise sources. Every scene includes both a transient noise source such as coughing and a continuous noise source such as HVAC, at three SNR levels. This coverage is designed to reflect the actual variety of spaces where deployed voice systems operate.

Alongside WER, the leaderboard reports RTFx (audio seconds per inference second) for every submission, evaluated on an NVIDIA L4 GPU under identical conditions. Accuracy and latency together are what matter in real deployments, and the Pareto front view in the Analysis tab makes that tradeoff explicit.

This benchmark is build on simulated acoustic spaces via Treble Technologies proprietaty simulation engine. An example of the output from the enginge can be found in the Treble10 dataset released last year, which established the simulation pipeline and made far-field RIRs available for training and research. FFASR extends that foundation into a standardized evaluation framework with a held-out test set, consistent normalization, and automated scoring.

With the leaderboard live, a consistent pattern is emerging across all submitted models: the gap between near-field and far-field performance is large, and it grows significantly as SNR decreases. Near-field WER values, on clean dry speech, look comparable to what the same models achieve on established benchmarks. Far-field WER at low SNR tells a different story, often several times higher. The benchmark makes this degradation visible and comparable in a way that was previously difficult to do outside proprietary evaluation pipelines.

The Pareto front of average WER against RTFx is also revealing. There is a genuine spectrum of approaches represented in the current submissions: models that prioritize speed at the cost of some accuracy, models that push accuracy at the cost of throughput, and a smaller number that achieve a competitive position on both axes. Visualizing these tradeoffs against far-field accuracy rather than clean-speech accuracy produces a materially different picture of where the real differences between systems lie. The Analysis tab is worth exploring beyond the main ranking table.

One observation worth highlighting for developers: the leaderboard reports both near-field (dry) and far-field WER side by side. This separation is intentional and useful. It makes it possible to distinguish between a model that is genuinely accurate and one that is accurate but brittle to acoustic conditions, which matters for deciding whether to invest in far-field fine-tuning, speech enhancement preprocessing, or a different architecture altogether.

Open the Submit tab on the FFASR Leaderboard, paste a Hugging Face model ID, and evaluation runs server-side against the held-out dataset. The pipeline supports Whisper variants, IBM Granite Speech, Cohere Transcribe, Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT CTC heads, SpeechBrain ASR, and most other ASR architectures on the Hub without any custom configuration.

For teams using more complex inference stacks, including systems that combine speech enhancement with ASR, a custom evaluator option allows you to define your own evaluate() function. Custom evaluators run on Hub Jobs after moderator review, and the submission notes field is a good place to document any preprocessing steps so results are interpretable by others.

The held-out evaluation set uses 2,000 anechoic speech samples across 14 rooms at three SNR tiers, approximately 8 hours of audio per condition, with Whisper-style text normalization applied consistently. The audio is not exposed to submitters, to avoid test-set contamination.

The conditions we are actively exploring for future tracks include multi-talker scenarios, where more than one speaker is active simultaneously, microphone array evaluation, covering beamforming and spatial filtering approaches, and echo cancellation, relevant for any device that plays audio while also listening.

What we build next will depend on where the community tells us the gaps are largest. If you work on a deployment environment or a use case that is not well represented in the current benchmark, we want to hear from you. The FFASR Leaderboard is designed to grow, and the direction it grows should reflect real needs.

Submit your model, explore the Analysis tab, post your ideas and suggestions on the FFASR forum, and help us build a benchmark that is actually useful for the problems the field is working on.

Far-Field ASR — clean / noisy / reverberant benchmark

Btw one related idea I've had sitting on the back of my mind: there's a class of synthetic audio scenarios that don't really occur naturally but are both tricky and relevant to real deployments.

Most ASR models lately seem geared toward clean meeting transcription. But if you run a Granola style setup that pulls every audio stream on your machine and mixes them together, things get messy fast. The system audio from the meeting, your physical hardware mic, and sometimes your own voice echoing back through the meeting can all be mixed/delayed/noisy in the same track the model sees. (I use VibeVoice for this myself since I figured it would be more robust; it's held up okay, but I haven't done a real comparison)

Mixed multi-stream audio like that feels like a natural fit for the kind of robustness/"real world scenario" this benchmark is measuring, even though it's a synthetic condition rather than a recorded room

#10045. Final_FINAL_v7.docx is not a version control strategy

EVENT: Join The Register for dinner in London on 24 November and hear, off the record, how your peers are fixing it.

The Register and LucidLink are hosting a dinner for senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair. The subject is one most of them will know from their own shop, where the same file lives in several places at once and nobody is quite sure which copy is current.

Most organisations have a folder that proves it. There's a file called final, another called final2, and then the one people are actually using, which somebody emailed to a contractor last Thursday.

It's mildly funny until two people spend a week editing different copies and one of them loses the argument. Meanwhile the storage bill picks up another copy of everything, and each team that builds its own way round the problem gives IT another place it can't see into.

Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers at the table, and nobody is there to give a presentation. Because the evening is held under the Chatham House Rule, people tend to say what really happened, like the team that quietly built its own sync service because the approved one was too slow, or the leaver who could still open a file share months after going.

From there the conversation widens out to unstructured data that won't stop growing, the duplicate storage piling up, the security risk of access scattered across all those copies, and how to modernise without binning the storage and governance the business has already paid for.

Drinks start at 6.30pm, then it's dinner around one table until 9pm. Places are limited.
