#10001. Common Beliefs About DNSSEC Put to the Test: An Invitation to Fact-Check Your Assumptions

This article—the second in a series of four, examining the complex legacy, technical evolution, and future prospects of DNSSEC—sets out to fact-check common beliefs on DNSSEC, point to future-proof data collections on DNSSEC matters and provides an up-to-date perspective on what DNSSEC is like today. It was widely circulated for comments and has been endorsed by over 60 people across the Internet industry (see list1).

In the first article from our series on DNSSEC, long-standing DNS luminary Roy Arends and Barbara Jantzen (communicator at the DNSSEC-focused non-profit organization deSEC) have engaged in a dialogue, recounting how DNSSEC adoption has been substantially hindered by the protocol’s bad image—an image that cannot be accounted for by factual failures alone, demonstrating the impact of narratives on the perception of technical devices.

Image-wise, two narrative items have indeed been particularly influential: First, the IANIX list of DNSSEC-related outages since 2009, and second, “Against DNSSEC” (with its follow-up FAQ), a DNSSEC-critical blog post written by Thomas H. Ptáček in 2015. Both helped harden the perception that DNSSEC is more trouble than it is worth, and references to them still surface in forum threads on DNS matters, even as the protocol, tooling, and operational practices have evolved. It therefore seems timely to check how fit they still are to help assess DNSSEC’s usefulness today.

In every field of knowledge, if we want to assess phenomena, we need thorough documentation to establish and collect facts, to witness evolutions, to develop hypotheses as to underlying causalities and try them. And although absolute numbers can provide a fair amount of insight, relative numbers are more helpful in assessing significance—especially when data is collected multi-dimensionally, allowing analysts to grasp inter-dependencies and derive a hint at potential causes. Because ideally, when dealing with broken things, we need to know not only how broken they are, but also how they broke.

A list can be a starting point for documentary work, though. The IANIX list, however, despite its objective looks, is more of a discourse than a documentation (as highlighted2 in our first article). In addition, it lacks transparency about its collection and curation methodology, making it difficult for readers to assess the list’s reliability and significance. As the IANIX site further does not disclose its operator’s name or contact, information on its modus operandi cannot be obtained.

Looking back, the IANIX list can be credited for having drawn the DNS community’s attention on DNSSEC-related outages and, in doing so, having acted as a strong driver for improving the protocol. However, with its bulk of information lying far in the past, and entries becoming scarce since 2020 (without any possibility to know if that is due to a recent decrease in reportable events or simply to less active maintenance), the IANIX list does not make a meaningful contribution today.

To broadly assess the actual outage impact of DNSSEC, we need state-of-the-art alternatives. What should these look like?

Such longitudinal studies, consequently, could prove insightful in putting DNSSEC-induced resolution failures into perspective to other failure modes, in particular network issues or HTTPS misconfigurations that impact availability.

Good starting points in that direction are the DNSSEC and DANE Deployment Statistics page, which also has statistics on misconfiguration rates per TLD; a timeline of measured TLD validation statuses, provided by deSEC (the author’s non-profit employer) and based on prior work by Jaap Akkerhuis; the comprehensive dataset (2010-2025) used in a recent study by John Kristoff et al. (expected to be published later this month, at which time it will be linked here) which explores DNSSEC-induced outages and provides unweighed as well as downtime- and impact-weighed analysis (results cited at the end of this article); new measurements by deSEC contrasting percent-level error rates of both DNSSEC and HTTPS amongst the top 1M most popular domains. Another useful metric would be a public record (as recently started by Quad9) of how frequently resolvers use so-called Negative Trust Anchors (NTAs) to temporarily turn off DNSSEC validation when working around human errors, with the long-term trend being of particular interest.

The blog post “Against DNSSEC” was published by Thomas H. Ptáček in 2015, and got widely relayed. Its harsh critique of DNSSEC fell on fertile ground as numerous DNSSEC-related outages were happening and were given visibility by the IANIX list. This helped turn the blog post’s set of negative claims into potent beliefs that persist to this day and obscure actual implementation reality.

At the time of its publication, some of the blog’s criticisms reflected genuine limitations and operational experience, others were disputed even then. A decade of protocol, tooling, and operational evolution makes it useful to revisit how well they describe DNSSEC today, for the sake of a fresh assessment of implementation options.

To be fair, this is not the first effort to matter-of-factly assess the claims voiced in “Against DNSSEC”, but one of several such publications, spanning from 2015 to the present3—which incidentally corroborates the blog’s perceived influence.

These level-headed accounts, although they have not spread through the tech community as easily as earlier criticism did, still reflect (and contribute to) a gradual shift both in tone and in content, observable for instance in Hacker News forum threads where sweeping allegations on DNSSEC now get challenged instead of being swiftly echoed. However, even today in 2026, with automation standards having brought a substantial improvement to the protocol (RFCs 7344, 9615, 9859, 10026), common beliefs die hard—mostly among those less directly involved in technical matters, but with the power to weigh on decisions.

So, what are the common beliefs around DNSSEC? And how much truth is there in them today, in 2026? Because, obviously, common beliefs can also be true, half-true or formerly true.

The first set of claims brought forward by “Against DNSSEC” dismisses the DNSSEC protocol as fundamentally flawed, for being structurally incompatible with its objective (preventing the manipulation of DNS answers). Verbatim: “DNSSEC is Unnecessary”, “DNSSEC is a Government-Controlled PKI”, “DNSSEC is Incomplete”.

The main argument used in “Against DNSSEC” to dismiss DNSSEC as unnecessary is that “with TLS properly configured, DNSSEC adds nothing”, and that the security of TLS certificates is mainly bounded by an attacker’s ability to hijack a domain validation email sent to a domain owner (and thus, bounded by the security of email).

The first part of this argument ignores real-world attacks that DNSSEC would have prevented while TLS could not, as for example the nameserver routing hijack of MyEtherWallet.com in 2018, enabling the theft of $160,000 within two hours.

The second part overlooks that a significant part of data fetched from the DNS are not about finding an IP address for establishing a TLS-secured connection (like HTTPS web site connections), but about providing other information—such as TXT records (used for a myriad of purposes), or NS and (upcoming) DELEG records (both used for declaring a domain’s responsible nameserver). Without DNSSEC, these are prone to various kinds of attacks, which can enable impersonation of the domain owner, traffic interception, or a hijack of the entire domain. Most notably, without a DNSSEC-based indicator, the MX records used to find a domain’s mail server cannot enforce that the subsequent email delivery happens through an encrypted connection (unlike in the web, where the “https://” URL prefix indicates the encryption request).

In addition, while “Against DNSSEC” acknowledges that insecure email can be a problem during certificate issuance, it fails to recognize that DNS lookups are involved in any certificate issuance process, regardless of whether validation happens trough email, or one of the other (and more common) validation methods which involve publishing a validation string under the domain.

Actually, today, you can use CAA records to restrict methods for domain control validation during certificate issuance and simply ban the insecure email method for your domain. As a byproduct, DNSSEC not only secures certificate issuance by hardening domain control validation, but also provides an indicator to secure email, by linking the email server’s TLS key to the domain directly within the DNS. This technology, called DANE, has already been rolled out by large players such as Microsoft, and secures about 4.6M email domains today.

Which means that actually both email and certificate issuance security are bounded by the security of the DNS, and that’s why it is material to up the authenticity level at this crucial layer of technology.

All in all, DNSSEC provides a much needed capability that TLS/HTTPS alone does not: It delivers signed, verifiable proof of origin for anything a registrant publishes, independently of any single application or delivery method. As such, it is a key enabling technology that lays a highly effective trust foundation on which applications such as DANE or CAA/TLS can rely to protect Internet users.

Is DNSSEC a government-controlled PKI?—YES and NO

DNSSEC is the PKI for the Internet’s unique global namespace. It is a globally consistent, well-governed, and well-managed namespace that applications can rely on for identifying servers, devices, and other named resources.

Just like in the certificate PKI world (where trusting a certificate typically requires trusting a chain of Certificate Authorities (CAs) tying back to a “root CA”), DNSSEC’s security guarantees rely on intermediaries, namely the TLD registries (and potentially other sub-registries, if the domain has multiple dots). These registries, as all organizations (CAs included), are indeed subject to some degree of government control, in particular of the jurisdiction in which they are based. That fact, however, is unrelated to DNSSEC: the same security model applies to DNS without DNSSEC. DNSSEC itself does not increase or decrease the risk of legal action. That said, if this is a source of concern to you as a domain owner, you are free to choose which TLD you want to use, according to whom you trust and what is your control preference—without relying on CAs or third parties you don’t have a prior relationship with.4

As far as the root zone keys are concerned, government control has been significantly reduced by what is known as the “IANA transition” in 2016, when IANA functions were shifted away from direct control by US-government’s telecommunications agency NTIA to ICANN’s multi-stakeholder governance. As a result, DNSSEC’s root governance and operation are grounded in a transparent multi-stakeholder model, its implementation is highly distributed, and many operational practices (such as key ceremonies and DNSSEC practice statements) are intentionally transparent and publicly observable.

“Incomplete”, in the blog’s elaboration, refers to DNSSEC not covering the so-called “last mile”, because validation often happens on a DNS resolver trusted by the client5, instead of happening on the client itself. While true, making this choice is a trust decision, not a design limitation of DNSSEC. In fact, Apple has been supporting client-side validation since 2022, and Section 5.3 of NIST’s “Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide” does recognize such deployment realities. Explicit requests for client-side validation features, if directed at software vendors that currently lack support, could create momentum for others to introduce client-side validation as well.

Meanwhile, it is worth noting that most Internet traffic is protected with authentication and encryption certificates (first and foremost: HTTPS web traffic). For certificate issuance, Section 4.2.2.2 of the certification rules requires Certificate Authorities (CAs) to perform DNSSEC validation when making DNS queries, including the DNS queries made to verify that the requestor is actually under control of the desired certificate domain name. This legitimacy check is vulnerable to DNS attacks, but DNSSEC, if in place, prevents the check from being hijacked.

This means DNSSEC makes sure that an illegitimate requestor cannot actually obtain a certificate based on a DNS attack. Barring non-DNS attacks (such as a compromise at the registrar or the CA itself), only the legitimate certificate will be in circulation. Browsers in turn will only communicate with servers that have this certificate configured. In other words: DNSSEC’s security guarantees transfer to the domain’s HTTPS certificate, ensuring that a browser does not communicate with a rogue actor: Even if a browser or other end-user application does not itself perform DNSSEC validation, the fact that CAs do perform it effectively protects the client’s last mile HTTPS traffic.

Besides, many important DNSSEC use cases do not have a “last mile” and thus don’t suffer from this problem: Both DANE-secured email and DNSSEC validation during certificate issuance does not involve end user devices, but only server-to-server communication where the validating resolver typically is directly under control of the participants (CAs and email providers). In these use cases, server-to-server not only equals end-to-end, but is at least equally important.

Finally, the word “incomplete” raises the expectation that technologies may reach completion. Like just every other protocol (including TLS, whose incremental versioning is met with equanimity), DNSSEC is incomplete insofar as it is a living standard.

Operational practices and standards continue to improve, including:

Regarding the “last mile” issue specifically, there are experimental efforts to facilitate end-to-end validation on the client without paying the latency price from additional DNSSEC-related lookups, by replacing them with pre-fetched DNSSEC chain data included in the TLS handshake (RFC 9102).

Three further claims revolve around the idea of DNSSEC being technically defective. Verbatim: “DNSSEC is Cryptographically Weak”, “DNSSEC is Unsafe”, “DNSSEC is Architecturally Unsound”.

DNSSEC is often dismissed as cryptographically deficient because it doesn’t encrypt DNS responses. That criticism misses the point: DNSSEC is not designed to protect the confidentiality of DNS responses, but their integrity—by cryptographically signing them6.

For that purpose, DNSSEC adopts well-tested cryptography and continues to move with operational reality, including broad migration to and use of the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, dubbed ECDSA (algorithm 13) and well-matched to DNSSEC’s resource constraints. The same algorithm globally leads and is generally recommended for the signatures that constitute HTTPS certificates.

Moreover, work on post-quantum cryptography for DNSSEC is underway in the research and standards community. The PQC DNSSEC agenda includes efforts to assess and mitigate the resource impact of newly standardized and proposed PQC signature algorithms—which generally have much larger signature and/or key sizes than ECDSA.

In short, DNSSEC’s cryptographic strength has successfully evolved to meet modern cryptographic demands, and is poised to continue evolving to support the post-quantum future.

The argument made by “Against DNSSEC” to bring home this point is that security decisions are best made according to each application’s needs, and that DNSSEC is not an application-layer protocol. While this objection seems valid for a range of things (take captchas, for instance: some applications may be fine with bots, others may not), it does indeed seem fair for a domain owner to assert that they want their domain’s DNS information to come along with verifiable signatures, in order to prevent clients from connecting when validation has failed. It is true that this is not always done end-to-end (although that’s not a design limitation, see the “last-mile” problem above)—but the objection that network-level security mechanisms are architecturally unsound by definition is overreaching. The same argument could be made against Wi-Fi encryption, BGP route validation, or IP packet checksums (which are all network-level), but these security mechanisms are generally accepted.

One of the most hard-dying assumptions about DNSSEC is its costliness—which is likely to dissuade non-technical people in charge of budgets from engaging in deployment. According to “Against DNSSEC”, both the adoption and the deployment of the protocol are resource-intensive. Verbatim: “DNSSEC is Expensive to Adopt”, “DNSSEC is Expensive to Deploy”.

Is DNSSEC expensive to adopt and to deploy?—YES and NO

For end users, DNSSEC is essentially free to adopt, with the added benefit of protection against attack-related losses (see the MyEtherWallet.com case above). In practice, all cost is carried by the resolver operator and the signing DNS operator. Measurements have shown that resolver-side memory and compute cost is small in practice. On the signing side, cost depends on how much specific expertise the signing operator needs to build8, and how many domains are being operated. Compared to signatures involved in HTTPS connections, DNSSEC signatures are computed much less frequently, so the cost of signing itself is not significant in light of the overall cost of operating an online service.

Overall, for well-run mid-size to large-scale operations, DNSSEC signing and validation during ongoing operations does not fundamentally change the financial equation.

Adapting software is certainly costly, but that task has largely been completed, and nameserver software today includes mature DNSSEC implementations by default. Also, while replacing old components in order to adopt more modern (automatic) solutions can be complex, the cost of new deployment and long-term operations has decreased significantly, with many DNS providers (such as Cloudflare, Squarespace, one.com, deSEC) and resolver operators (such as Cloudflare, Google, Quad9, DNS4EU) now routinely operating DNSSEC with full automation. Some work remains to be done with respect to the automation of DNSSEC configuration updates at the registry side, but progress is happening there as well.

“Against DNSSEC” also argues that network software is not equipped to handle DNSSEC failures smoothly (such as distinguishing expired signatures from an actual attack), and that “mak[ing] DNSSEC workable” would involve a lot of expensive code rewriting. That concern is diminishing, as browsers recently have made an effort to increase visibility into the origin of connection errors by implementing more detailed DNS error feedback based on RFC 89149. Such developments indeed come with some cost, but that cost—unlike suggested—does not preclude large-scale deployment, as demonstrated by > 90% validation deployment in countries like New Zealand, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Ghana.

The common beliefs that have emerged from “Against DNSSEC”, however extensive and influential, are dwarfed by a much more impactful claim: DNSSEC’s alleged threat to availability—exposed and broadcast by the IANIX list, as laid out above. But, historical records aside, how true is that today? Or, in other words, does DNSSEC have high availability in practice?

Yes, it does. The above-mentioned study by John Kristoff et al. (expected to be published later this month, at which time it will be linked here) has developed a measurement-based methodology and impact-weighted evaluation to quantify DNSSEC-induced outages. Its results show not only that the global DNSSEC deployment has had availability of over 99.99% in 15 of 16 years measured, but also confirms a sharp decline of incidents over the last five years. Accordingly, the occasional disruptive event (which still occurs, but has become exceptional) should not obscure the practical record of overall DNSSEC deployment.

As with any technology at Internet scale that requires interoperability amongst disparate implementations and operational environments, early DNSSEC adopters were likely to be hit by painful outages, due to misconfigurations or buggy code. Since then, thanks to engineering refinements and community-crafted operational standards, DNSSEC deployment has come to achieve demonstrably high availability across TLDs. All gTLDs as well as an increasing number of ccTLDs sign their zones, and many TLDs have successfully transitioned to new operators and/or algorithms, while remaining fully signed. And even if validation breaks (and the absence of an attack is confirmed), temporary NTAs (negative trust anchors) can restore basic availability—as done by Cloudflare and other resolver operators during the .de May 2026 incident.

DNSSEC is now considered to be important and stable enough to be a non-negotiable requirement for existing and future gTLDs. This policy-side view is matched by real world uptime records: Two of the world’s largest TLDs, .com and .net operated by Verisign, have long been DNSSEC-enabled, with more than 29 years of uninterrupted DNS resolution uptime. Also spotless is the uptime record of the world’s largest portfolio of TLDs, managed by Identity Digital (previously Afilias) and signed as soon as 2009.

In conclusion, as the facts presented in this article suggest, DNSSEC in 2026 should not be judged by limitations and operational records from its earlier deployment years (i.e., the trouble that triggered publications like the IANIX list and “Against DNSSEC”). Some concerns remain genuine tradeoffs, others have been substantially reduced by protocol evolution, automation, and operational experience.

In short, let’s not get stuck in archives. Instead—recognizing that DNSSEC has been stable and well tested in deployments for nearly two decades and continues to evolve when needed—let’s choose to draw on up-to-date information (such as presented in this article) and check out actual and successfully running implementations (like the DNSSEC automation showcases that will be provided by the third article of this series).

And if after doing so, with your own risk profile in mind, you make the informed decision not to use DNSSEC in your own setting, that’s perfectly fine. But make sure everybody else is also free to make their own choices—and accordingly, if others depend on you for having access to DNSSEC, don’t break their chance to use it, if they wish to.

#10000. Password manager mSecure tells users to change passwords, won't say why

Customers left wondering what's been compromised after vendor advises resetting passwords, 2FA and passkeys

Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed.

In an email sent to customers on November 3, seen by The Register, US-based developer mSeven Software said it launched an investigation after discovering something amiss with its password management application.

"mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company wrote. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist."

The company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information.

Its advice to customers, however, suggests that they should take this seriously.

"Given the potential security implications, mSeven recommends that you immediately take steps to protect all confidential information stored within the mSecure password management application," the email continued. "This may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys."

For anyone with hundreds of passwords stored in mSecure, that's potentially hours of work. And without knowing what happened, customers have no way of telling which credentials they actually need to replace.

The warning has understandably gone down poorly with customers, who have taken to mSecure's support forum demanding answers.

"Please provide more context to your email below advising there has been a security breach," one customer wrote. "It is not acceptable to offer the vague advice 'take steps'. Please state what remedial action is required, and what data was compromised."

Others are wondering whether they're expected to spend the next several days changing every password they've ever saved.

"I have over 800 passwords in mSecure, is the email saying I need to change all of them!" another customer asked.

A separate user, who said they had more than 500 passwords stored in the application, questioned whether the warning applied to every two-factor authentication method and passkey associated with their accounts, or just those used to access mSecure itself.

The confusion has also spilled onto Reddit, where customers have shared copies of the vague notification and questioned what might have happened.

mSeven has yet to respond to The Register's questions, leaving customers to guess whether their data has actually been compromised or the company is simply being cautious. That's not exactly reassuring from a business whose entire purpose is keeping other people's secrets safe.

The company's email concludes: "We regret any inconvenience that this may cause." For customers contemplating hundreds of password resets, "inconvenience" may be putting it mildly. ®

#9998. Profiling in PyTorch (Part 3): Attention is all you profile

This is the third post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:

The series "Profiling in PyTorch" is meant to make you comfortable reading profiler traces and tables. In Part 1 we profiled basic math operations like addition and multiplication. We saw how the profiler table uncovers hotspots, and how the profiler trace shows the order in which an algorithm runs over time.

In Part 2 we wrapped that addition and multiplication into a torch linear layer. We then stacked several linear layers on top of each other (a multilayer perceptron) and profiled that. Along the way we also profiled fused and hand-tuned kernels.

From the perspective of the Transformer architecture, the next logical step for us to profile is yet another fundamental algorithm, attention. While being infamous for its quadratic-time complexity, many clever tricks exist to mitigate that issue and make it fast. Our goal here is not to cover every trick in detail. Instead, we want to see how each one looks different under the profiler.

The scripts for this blog post live here: 04_a_naive_attention.py, 04_b_inplace_ops_attention.py, 04_c_sdpa_attention.py, and 04_d_kernels_attention.py. Like before, it helps to open them in a separate tab and walk through the code as you read. We use an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to set up a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.

Attention works with Queries (q), Keys (k), and Values (v). The interaction between them can be written as a short sequence of steps:

So attention is really a collection of primitive operations. Some of them we already know (the matmuls), and the rest are easy to spot. Let's write a naive attention module in PyTorch and profile it.

Before opening the trace, let's do our usual exercise and guess what we should see. Tracing the forward of this module, we expect:

Figure 1 shows the CPU lane of the profile (the GPU lane is folded so it does not overwhelm us). Inside attn_fwd (our annotated forward call) we can see exactly the operations we guessed. The matmul is an old friend by now, and the new operations are easy to spot:

Now let's unfold the GPU lane and see which kernels were actually launched.

Figure 2 shows the GPU lane next to the CPU lane. Let's zoom into a single attn_fwd block on the GPU lane to look at the kernels one by one.

Figure 3 lets us read off the individual kernels for one profiler step:

Five of these are expected. The memory copy is the odd one out, so where does this come from? The clue is that PyTorch has in-place operations. When you operate on a tensor the ordinary (out-of-place) way, PyTorch often makes a copy, applies the requested operation to it, and returns the copy. Following the sequence of operations, the culprit here is our masked_fill.

What if we replaced this with an in-place operation?

All we change is masked_fill to masked_fill_ (note the trailing underscore, PyTorch's convention for in-place operations), and we run the same script.

Let's look at the trace and see if something changed.

The in-place version (Figure 5) wraps far fewer CPU ops inside the masking step than the out-of-place version (Figure 4). This is an encouraging signal. Let's unfold the GPU lane to confirm what happened there.

On the GPU lane the Memcpy kernel is gone for good (Figures 6 and 7). With a one line change we shaved a whole kernel off each forward pass. This may not look like much on its own, but remember this is a single attention operation. In the context of a transformer based large model (LLMs, Diffusion models, etc.), it repeats once per layer, and there are many layers, so the saving adds up quickly (and if it earns you a raise, sharing at least 10% with us feels only fair).

Out-of-place is PyTorch's default for a reason. To compute gradients, autograd has to remember the tensor values it saw on the forward pass, because many backward formulas reuse them. An in-place operation overwrites those values in memory, so the backward pass would read the wrong numbers. Due to the fact that we run forward under torch.no_grad, in-place is safe for us, with no backward pass and nothing to corrupt. It is also noteworthy that in-place operations do not only save time (like we see in our case) but also memory (due to no extra copy) which is great for large tensors like logits!

We just built attention from primitives, and even shaved off a Memcpy. The good news is that the PyTorch team has done all of this for us, and packaged the whole pipeline into a single function:

This one line replaces our hand written module, and is_causal=True even saves us from building the mask by hand. It is worth pausing to appreciate how much this one call hides. And it hides more than just code lines. Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA) does not have a single implementation. Under the hood it dispatches to one of the several backends and picks the fastest one that supports our inputs (dtype, head dimension, mask, hardware, etc.).

The official SDPA tutorial walks us through this selection, and the backends themselves are listed in the torch.nn.attention.SDPBackend enum:

Normally SDPA chooses for us, but we can pin a specific backend with the torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel context manager. This is what we do in our scripts. This lets us profile each backend on its own and read how differently they show up in the trace. Let's go one at a time.

Before we open anything, let's guess. We have replaced hand written attention (matmul, mul, mask, softmax, matmul) with a single one liner, so we should expect the trace to get simpler and faster. Fewer kernels, less CPU dispatch, maybe even a fused kernel. Let's check the profiler table first.

This is our first surprise, the one liner is 3.7x slower.

Opening the trace (Figure 9) shows why the alarm bells ring, the math backend launches 20 GPU kernels per forward instead of the 5 launched with our naive attention implementation (Figure 8). This is the opposite of what we guessed. Let's figure out why this happens.

In Part 2 we learned to read a kernel name like a fingerprint. Let's use that habit here:

The A100s we used to capture these traces ship with Tensor Cores, specialised hardware for accelerated matmuls that is known to be far faster than the ordinary CUDA cores. To see why that matters here, it helps to know what lives inside a GPU. A Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) is the compute unit of a GPU, and each SM has two kinds of arithmetic units, the CUDA cores and the Tensor Cores. CUDA cores are general purpose and process a handful of elements at a time, while Tensor Cores multiply and accumulate a whole small matrix tile in a single instruction. So the question is simple, "Is each backend actually using the fast path?"

The kernel names answer it. The s16816 in the naive kernel (Figure 10) is the signature of a bfloat16 Tensor Core matmul (the 16x8x16 Tensor Core instruction), so the naive version is on the fast path. sgemm (Figure 11) is the classic single precision (FP32) matmul that runs on the ordinary CUDA cores. In other words, the math backend never touches the Tensor Cores at all: to trade speed for numerical accuracy it upcasts tensors to FP32 (doubling the data moved, even when the inputs are in bf16) and falls back to the slower CUDA cores.

In the naive version we built the causal mask once and reused it. Here we passed is_causal=True and the math backend materialized one for us, on every single call. You can watch it happen on the CPU lane:

On the GPU this shows up as a triu_tril_kernel, several where kernels, and an add_. The convenience flag that let us stop thinking about the mask did not remove the work, it just moved it one layer down, where the mask is rebuilt from scratch every forward.

Our hand written version called plain aten::softmax. The math backend calls aten::_safe_softmax, and the difference is again visible as extra kernels (Figure 13):

A row that is fully masked (every entry -inf) would make an ordinary softmax compute exp(-inf)/sum(exp(-inf)) = 0/0 = NaN. _safe_softmax guards against exactly that. Our naive kernel never bothered, and would have quietly produced NaNs in that corner case.

Put together, the math backend is the reference implementation. It is a straightforward, dtype-safe, NaN-safe decomposition of attention into primitive ATen ops. It is essentially the naive attention we wrote by hand, but more careful. That carefulness is exactly what makes it extremely slow.

Its job is not to be fast, but to always work. This makes it the perfect baseline. Every backend we profile next (flash, efficient, cudnn) is trying to collapse the 20 GPU kernels into essentially one fused kernel that stays in bf16 and never materializes the intermediate matrices at all.

Where the math backend launched 20 kernels across one profiler step, the efficient backend launches only one fmha_cutlassF_bf16_aligned_64x64_rf_sm80 (as seen in Figure 14).

This is the memory efficient attention kernel that grew out of Meta's xformers library and was upstreamed into PyTorch. When people say "the xformers backend," this fmha_cutlassF kernel is what they mean.

The void pytorch_flash kernel (Figure 15) is FlashAttention-2 (Tri Dao's implementation), vendored into PyTorch.

Before we read the trace any further, it is worth answering the question you should be asking by now: why is there a whole backend named "flash", and why does it matter so much?

Let's go back to the math backend for a moment. Its real problem was not the count of 20 kernels, it was what those kernels handed to each other.

Step 1 builds the full score matrix attn = q . k.T, which is [seq, seq] per head. For a sequence length of 4096 that is 4096 x 4096 ≈ 16 million numbers for a single head. That matrix is written out to the HBM (the GPU's main memory), if there is even enough space to do so. Then, it is read back to be scaled, written again for the mask, read again for the softmax, and so on. Attention's cost is dominated by this back and forth traffic to HBM, not by the matmuls themselves.

FlashAttention attacks exactly this. Instead of computing the whole s matrix and only then reducing it, it walks over k and v in tiles, keeps a running softmax as it goes (the "online softmax" trick), and accumulates the output one tile at a time. The full [seq, seq] score matrix is never written to HBM, it only ever lives on-chip. This is the single idea that lets the entire attention pipeline collapse into one fused kernel that stays in bf16 on the Tensor cores.

Here is where flash surprises people who read profiler footprints. It is the fastest backend, yet the profiler reports it with very low occupancy (shown in Figure 16). To see why that is fine, we need three quick definitions.

A GPU kernel is essentially a series of instructions executed by many small execution units. These individual execution units (threads) take care of loading variables, adding them together, storing them back, etc. For each kernel, we launch many, many threads, and to keep track of them, we group them by blocks.

Blocks are scheduled onto Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), the main compute units of a GPU. A block lives entirely on one SM, and an SM can host multiple blocks at once if it has enough resources. Those resources include registers, shared memory, maximum resident threads, and maximum resident warps. So when we say a kernel has low occupancy, we mean each SM has fewer resident warps than it could theoretically support.

If you want to know more about threads, blocks, grids, etc. here is a great resource.

If you click the flash kernel in the trace, its footprint tells the story (Figure 17).

Flash uses a lot of per-thread registers and a large amount of shared memory per block. For example, if a block has 128 threads and each thread uses 255 registers, that block needs 128 × 255 = 32,640 registers. On an Ampere SM with 65,536 registers, only two such blocks fit at once. Each 128-thread block has 128 / 32 = 4 warps, so two blocks give only 8 resident warps. Against a maximum of 64 resident warps, that is roughly 13% occupancy. Flash has low occupancy not because it is poorly optimized, but because each block is deliberately very "heavy" in on-chip resource usage.

And that is the whole point. High occupancy helps hide latency by keeping many warps ready to run, but it does not make the work itself efficient. Flash spends those registers and that shared memory on purpose, to keep attention tiles on-chip, reuse data aggressively, and avoid ever materializing the full attention matrix in global memory.

By now the pattern is familiar. Like flash and efficient, cuDNN gives us one fused, flash-style kernel per forward (Figure 18). So the natural question is: if flash already fuses attention, why does PyTorch ship yet another flash backend? The answer is who writes the kernel and how it is built, and that difference is what makes the trace look different.

Flash and efficient are fixed, pre-compiled kernels vendored into PyTorch. You get the same binary every time. cuDNN is NVIDIA's own deep learning library, and its attention kernel is generated and tuned for the specific problem at hand. It is closer in spirit to torch.compile's codegen than to a fixed cuBLAS binary. You can read that straight off the (very long) kernel name:

That one fact, generated per problem, explains everything else that looks unusual in the trace.

No transposes: The CPU lane goes from _cudnn_attention_forward straight to a couple of aten::empty allocations and then the kernel, with zero aten::transpose (Figures 19, 20 and 21). Flash and efficient each insert four (metadata) transposes to reshape the tensors while cuDNN consumes the native [B, H, S, D] layout directly because its generator emits a kernel for that layout.

It launches through cuLaunchKernelEx, not cudaLaunchKernel: Every other kernel in this whole series went through the runtime API cudaLaunchKernel. cuDNN uses the driver-level extended launch, which carries launch attributes (Figure 22).

The profiler reports 0% achieved occupancy: Do not take that at face value, it is a measurement gap, not a stalled GPU. CUPTI (the profiling backend) cannot attribute occupancy to a driver-API (cuLaunchKernelEx) launch the way it does for cudaLaunchKernel, so the field reads 0. The footprint fills in the truth (Figure 23): 240 registers × 256 threads = 61,440 registers per block against the SM's 65,536, so only one block fits per SM (8 warps ≈ 12.5%), right in line with flash.

The "no transposes" story tempts us to expect cuDNN to be the leanest backend on the CPU. It is the opposite.

Even with zero transpose ops, cuDNN spends about 214 µs per forward on the CPU, more than flash (138) or efficient (117). Almost all of it sits in aten::scaled_dot_product_attention self time (26% of the whole run) and _cudnn_attention_forward. That is cuDNN's runtime engine selecting and preparing the plan (the "knob" search) on every call.

Fewer visible ATen ops did not mean less CPU work, it moved the work into the library, where the profiler can only show it as one fat, opaque bar. When a trace suddenly gets cleaner, the work has not always disappeared, sometimes it has just moved somewhere the profiler cannot break down.

On the GPU, cuDNN (186.3 µs) lands between efficient and flash. On this very flash-friendly shape, hand-written FlashAttention-2 edges it out. cuDNN often wins on other shapes (larger head dimensions, different sequence lengths) precisely because its generator retunes per problem, but that retuning is also what you just paid for on the CPU.

Before we wrap up, here is a single table to review every attention variant we profiled and the one lesson each trace taught us.

If you take away only one thing from the whole series, let it be the habit we repeated before every single trace which is to guess first, then look.

State out loud what you expect the trace to contain, open it, and treat any mismatch as the most interesting thing on the screen. Every real insight in these three posts, the hidden Memcpy, the addmm epilogue, the 20 kernel math backend, flash's "wrong-looking" occupancy, cuDNN's fat CPU bar, came from a guess that did not match the trace.

Profiling is not a separate, intimidating skill reserved for GPU experts. It is just the discipline of looking closely and asking "wait, why is that happening?" until the answer clicks. You now have the vocabulary and the reflexes to do that on your own models. Open a trace, form a guess, and go find the mismatch.

Thanks for reading the Profiling in PyTorch series. Now go profile something. 🤗

#9997. Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice

Fixing the critical PHP flaws is not as simple as clicking "Update." Here's how to assess your risk, and what you can do to protect yourself.

New data shows that organizations aren't moving to patch PHP2Shell as fast as attackers are moving to exploit it. It's understandable, cybersecurity experts say, because updating in this case is especially complicated.

The data began trickling in on Oct. 21, painting a picture of the world's initial response to the new PHP vulnerabilities. The picture wasn't pretty.

Some well-positioned experts picked up on a remarkable volume of threat activity. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince stated that in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed on Oct. 21, his company observed thousands of exploitation attempts. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, late on Oct. 21.

The next day, Check Point Research claimed that attempts at exploitation had already reached 10% of organizations worldwide. On the flip side, only a small percentage of vulnerable organizations have been visibly updating to new PHP releases.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

Using discoverable deployments on Shodan as a sample, Ox Security researchers found that more than 99% of instances were not yet advertising a newly patched version 24 hours after fixed versions were made available. Researchers at Flare piled on, noting that 73% of those instances advertised PHP branches that no longer receive updates from the PHP Foundation. (It also qualified these figures, noting that basic Internet scanning misses some crucial nuances.)

Meanwhile, Cisco Talos estimated, based on open source intelligence (OSINT), that around half of all PHP systems won't receive patches.

On the morning of Oct. 23, Eastern time, Ox informed Dark Reading that its 99% figure had dropped to 97.5%. And Flare told Dark Reading that of the 27% of public records reflecting upstream-supported branches, about 5% have been updated.

Addressing PHP2Shell is often not as simple as clicking "Update," practitioners acknowledge. Still, there are steps that most organizations can take to protect themselves immediately, like diligently looking for PHP deployments across an organization's entire fleet of systems, hunting for signs of compromise, and restricting access to or otherwise taking offline any systems that can't be patched immediately.

In principle, protecting against PHP2Shell should be simple. There are new versions one can update to, which cover the vulnerabilities in question, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. In practice, addressing PHP2Shell will look very different from one organization to the next, and require more or less effort, depending on how, where, and in what ways they use PHP.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

The unanimous first step all cybersecurity experts point to is that organizations should discover and inventory all of the assets they have running PHP. It's easier said than done. As the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) noted in an Oct. 21 security alert, PHP isn't just something that runs websites; it's "often a component of other software and prevalence may not be directly observable."

Flare researchers saw that firsthand when examining the attack surface. "What stood out to me during the research was how much PHP we found outside conventional web hosting," says Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher at Flare. "We identified it in storage devices, physical access-control systems, cameras and remote-access interfaces. If you're only looking at your main websites or limiting an external assessment to ports 80 and 443, you're going to miss some of that."

For organizations with this sort of exposure, he continues, "You generally can't log into a storage appliance or physical access-control unit and independently upgrade its PHP installation. You need the manufacturer to provide updated firmware. If the manufacturer has stopped supporting that product, the organization may have no patch available."

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

Putting edge cases aside, let's assume that an organization has managed to find and list out all of its PHP deployments. From there, remarkably, things only get more complicated.

Publicly available data seems to suggest that most PHP out in the world is running on old branches. "If you’re running an application built around PHP 5 or PHP 7, moving to a current PHP release could mean rewriting parts of the application, replacing dependencies, and testing everything that might break. There’s a good reason why organizations avoid doing that casually, particularly when the application supports something operationally important," Cheek explains.

In these cases, remediation will be a slow process, if organizations choose to pursue it at all. Luckily, and confusingly, old PHP versions aren't always unsavable.

The most common version in public records, 7.4.3, is what shipped with Ubuntu 20.04. As Cheek points out, "Linux distributions frequently retain an older PHP version number while backporting security fixes. So an old version number doesn't automatically mean the software hasn't been patched." Besides operating systems, applications can also backport fixes for the PHP they come packaged with.

Thus, organizations running outdated PHP actually fall into very distinct buckets: Some organizations will need to do the heavy lifting necessary to migrate or replace their applications or products. In the meantime, experts say, they should consider taking their vulnerable systems offline entirely. Cheek also offers one pro tip to mitigate CVE-2026-109619, for those that can reach the PHP configuration.

"The reported attacks run through PHP session upload progress, a feature that is on by default and needs no session_start call in the application. Disabling session.upload_progress.enabled and restarting the PHP workers blocks the confirmed session-upload-progress attack paths without requiring a PHP version upgrade," he explains, with the qualification that it doesn't address the other PHP2Shell flaw, CVE-2026-109618, so it's a temporary measure at best.

Some organizations will be privileged enough to install backported fixes through their vendors. On Oct. 21, Ubuntu developer Canonical published fixes for PHP2Shell for all versions since 14.04. Even these relieved parties will have more accounting work to do, since an OS or application update doesn't necessarily carry a full PHP version upgrade. If one takes advantage of Ubuntu's updates, future scans could continue to show it ostensibly running PHP 7.4.3.

And don't forget, Cheek says: "The restart matters. Installing a corrected PHP package doesn't necessarily replace the interpreter already loaded into running worker processes."

Besides all of the technical details, size will determine a lot about how organizations can respond to PHP2Shell.

As with any urgent cybersecurity vulnerability, small businesses may start off with disadvantages in awareness as well as the resources needed to get themselves cleaned up. Yet after 48 hours of working nonstop to help more than 1,000 organizations with PHP2Shell, OX Security CEO Neatsun Ziv is quicker to point out the advantages in being small. "

At small organizations, you can do whatever you want. You just go in and patch. You wait five hours. Nobody complains about breaking anything," he says.

But larger organizations are different, he says. "They've got a golden image — one server baseline they update," Ziv says. "It's always a downstream model: you deploy a new golden image, this golden image is then being built with new software, this new software goes to production, and nobody can change production. This is the norm in deployments today. Nobody goes to servers and actually patches them. It just becomes unmaintainable in the long term."

And that's to say nothing of just how many people from different teams need to be involved in major updates within a large organization; or of how major organizations run disproportionately significant systems that can't afford to break; or of how prevalent and varied PHP can be even within organizations. As Ziv notes, "Most of the organizations that we work with found hundreds of servers that are running PHP."

Check Point chief security and trust officer Alex Spokoiny adds that even beyond one's own house, organizations also face risk from how all of their suppliers handle PHP2Shell.

"The first step is to engage the relevant suppliers and understand how they are responding. Are they affected? What protections have they put in place? When do they expect remediation to be completed? If you cannot get clear or reasonable answers to those questions, that is itself something you need to factor into your risk assessment and potentially consider alternative options," he advises.

Organizations can also team up, to everyone's benefit. "For example, where technically possible, they may be able to extend their own Web application firewall (WAF) protection to applications operated by third parties, helping reduce exposure while the provider works toward a permanent fix," Spokoiny says.

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9996. Improved asteroid deflection model runs faster, reveals more doomsday worries

“We expected aim to matter ... What surprised us was how much,' says Sandia physicist Nathan Moore

Researchers at Sandia National Laboratories have developed a method to make asteroid deflection modeling faster and more detailed. Their simulations also demonstrated just how much asteroid shape and orientation can complicate efforts to deflect a threatening space rock.

Sandia researchers, led by staff physicist Nathan Moore, were looking for a way to better model how X-rays from a nuclear detonation near an asteroid can change its trajectory, as explained in a recently published research paper.

“Before, the calculations were so time-consuming, one could not do very many of them,” Moore told The Register. “So it was very difficult to explore different scenarios, different asteroids, or different mission concepts.”

The complexity of those calculations forced earlier researchers to make compromises, often modeling asteroids as spheres or simplifying the physics involved.

Perfectly spherical asteroids are rare, and their irregular shapes present an additional challenge for those keeping an eye on the skies to avert a potential asteroid apocalypse.

To overcome the computational problem and enable better modeling of irregular asteroid shapes, Moore and his team combined two high-fidelity simulation codes already in use at Sandia: ALEGRA, which models radiation heating and high-energy material dynamics, and SPARTA, which simulates the behavior of low-density gases.

As Moore explained to us in an email, both codes are good at one particular part of asteroid impact modeling, but bad at the other.

“ALEGRA … can very accurately simulate the vaporization of the rocky surface, but the calculation becomes more inefficient for matter at low densities,” Moore told us. “This is a problem for asteroid deflection simulations, because as the gas expands around the asteroid, the calculation time goes up.”

Earlier asteroid simulations using ALEGRA typically modeled asteroids as spheres to reduce calculation times.

“SPARTA is more efficient at low gas densities,” Moore said. “The problem is, conversely, SPARTA gets more difficult to run at high gas densities. So the key here was using both codes.”

In Moore’s model, ALEGRA handles regions of high gas density, while SPARTA tackles the more dilute regions of an irregular shape. The result is two codes handling the parts of the problem they're best suited to solve, reducing the overall computational burden.

The combined approach is more than 1,600 times faster than earlier methods, Moore said in a Sandia press release, while retaining sufficient accuracy to predict deflection in irregularly shaped asteroids.

The improved simulations reveal just how much asteroid shape and orientation can complicate attempts to calculate the outcome of a nuclear deflection.

“We expected aim to matter,” Moore said. “What surprised us was how much.”

Deflection simulations using detailed models of three well-studied asteroids – Golevka, Bennu, and Itokawa – found that irradiating different sides of the same asteroid with X-rays from a nearby nuclear detonation could produce as much as a fivefold difference in the resulting velocity change. Bennu, the most symmetrical of the three, still showed nearly twofold differences in deflection velocity depending on which side faced the blast.

In other words, we need to be incredibly precise about where we detonate a nuclear device near an asteroid, or we risk giving it a much smaller shove than intended.

With that in mind, the paper points out that we might know little about an incoming asteroid, and might not have enough time to get a good picture of it before attempting to deflect it and prevent life as we know it from ending in a planet-wide conflagration. We also can’t be quite sure an asteroid’s orientation will cooperate once our deflecto-bomb arrives. The team also pointed out that it’s tricky to get an accurate prediction without knowing the composition and internal structure of an asteroid.

One small step for asteroid deflection, one giant heap of new things to worry about, in other words. But hey – at least we’re no longer limited to deflection models that treat asteroids as perfect spheres, even though the real threats are likely to be considerably lumpier.

Let’s just hope we spot an asteroid threat from far enough away that we get a chance to study it first.  ®

#9994. Introducing Real World VoiceEQ: Measuring the human quality of voice AI

Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.

Voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface. From customer support and healthcare to education, entertainment, and personal assistants, speech is increasingly replacing text as the way people interact with AI.

Over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically. Word error rates continue to fall, latency has reached conversational speeds, and many established benchmarks are approaching saturation. Yet anyone who regularly uses voice AI knows something still feels off.

Voice models can sound like different people over the course of a conversation, miss hesitation or uncertainty, and struggle with accents, noise, or emotional speech. Those shortcomings are easy to miss in benchmarks focused on latency and word error rate. People care whether a voice system can truly listen, respond appropriately, and remain natural and reliable in real conversations.

To measure those qualities, we built Real World VoiceEQ—a benchmark designed to evaluate the human quality of voice interaction. It assesses whether voice systems can recognize, produce, and respond to the acoustic information transcripts leave out, from tone and emotion to speaker identity and background context.

Real World VoiceEQ evaluates more than 40 leading proprietary and open-source voice models across 15+ key evaluation dimensions and more than 60 metrics spanning Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and Speech Understanding.

Real World VoiceEQ was developed from more than 1 million individual human ratings collected across different demographics, speaking styles, and acoustic environments. The current benchmark includes 785,000 TTS ratings and 48,000 STS ratings, making it one of the largest human evaluations of voice AI conducted to date.

Every evaluation was conducted using Kairos, our flexible, voice-native evaluation platform. The same infrastructure enables frontier AI labs and enterprises to run custom evaluations tailored to specific use cases, identify granular failure modes in production voice systems, generate human preference data, and continuously improve models through reinforcement learning and human feedback.

The race for a single "best" voice model is giving way to a collection of specialized capabilities.

Today's leading systems optimize for different strengths—including technical accuracy, emotional understanding, conversational intelligence, expressiveness, and robustness. One model that excels at repeating booking reference numbers, bank account details, or complex pharmaceutical names may struggle to produce emotionally expressive speech. Another may sound remarkably natural but be less reliable on precision-oriented tasks.

As voice AI matures, measuring progress increasingly requires evaluating these capabilities independently rather than collapsing them into a single overall score. In our TTS evaluations, no system configuration ranked among the top five across all eight capability groups—underscoring why there is no single "best" voice model.

Speech-to-Speech models showed the widest variation of any category we evaluated. Some systems recognized emotion exceptionally well but struggled to respond naturally. We found that access to audio did not guarantee that agents used the paralinguistic information it contained. Some systems remained largely transcript-driven, relying on the words being spoken while overlooking cues such as tone, pacing, hesitation, emphasis, and volume.

Humans naturally use these cues to infer confidence, uncertainty, frustration, sarcasm, and empathy. Today's models often miss them.

Imagine a banking agent asking whether you recognize a potentially fraudulent transaction. A confident "Yes" and a hesitant "…yes…" may have completely different meanings, even though the transcript is identical. Humans recognize that difference immediately. Many of today's voice models do not.

Many established benchmarks are nearing their limits and don't reflect real-world conditions. Models still struggle with accented speech, overlapping speakers, emotion, background noise, and longer conversations. In our evaluation, performance varies far more across leading open-source and proprietary models than traditional benchmarks suggest. In one example, transcription word error rates on noise-backed speech were roughly four times higher than on music-backed speech, showing how a single background-audio score can hide the real failure mode.

In preliminary research, we found signs that some models may be optimized for established public benchmarks. Several reproduced known errors in reference transcripts, followed arbitrary spelling conventions, and even reconstructed masked words that were not present in the audio.

LLMs are now widely used to evaluate text-based models, but our findings suggest that speech-language models (SLMs) should be used more carefully for voice evaluation. When we compared leading SLMs with trained human raters on text-to-speech assessments, agreement was highest on tasks with clear, verifiable answers, such as pronunciation accuracy.

Agreement declined on more subjective evaluations. SLMs sometimes appeared to infer emotion from text-based contextual cues, and agreement was weakest for open-ended judgments such as whether a voice fit an acting role or maintained a consistent identity. Automated evaluators can be valuable for well-defined tasks, but they are not yet a substitute for human listeners when judgments depend on acoustic-context, perception, and social interpretation.

As voice becomes one of AI's defining interfaces, speed and technical accuracy alone will no longer determine which systems succeed. The models people ultimately choose will be those that can understand, express, and respond like humans—not just under ideal benchmark conditions, but across the complexity of real-world conversation.

For decades, speech AI has advanced by optimizing against quantitative metrics on standardized benchmarks; from WER for transcription accuracy to objective perceptual metrics like PESQ and DNSMOS for speech quality. We hope Real World VoiceEQ can extend this paradigm by providing a human-grounded metric for evaluating the components of synthetic voice interactions.

Read the full technical report and explore the public leaderboards—or get in touch to learn how Hume can evaluate your voice model or agent using Real World VoiceEQ, or design custom evaluations tailored to your specific use case.

#9993. GSMA warns of growing risks to mobile networks from extreme weather

Mobile comms body wants a joined-up approach from governments and regulators to mitigate downtime

The GSMA wants governments and regulators to work more closely with mobile operators to help protect networks against growing risks from extreme weather.

As the global body representing the mobile network industry, the GSMA claims that severe storms and floods already cost operators $1.7 billion annually to repair damage to cell radio sites, and it believes that figure could nearly double to more than $3 billion a year by 2050, under the climate conditions expected then.

The GSMA sets out its findings in a six-part research series, Futureproofing Connectivity: Climate Risk and Resilience in Telecommunications, alongside a separate document outlining its Policy Principles for Mobile Network Resilience.

The report identifies weather-related risks that can affect telecoms networks, along with the associated restoration costs. Towers, masts, and rooftop sites are particularly exposed to wind and storms or lightning, for example, while ground-level equipment at mobile sites can be inundated in flooding incidents.

High temperatures can cause radio equipment to overheat, while heavy rain can degrade wireless signal strength, and infrastructure in coastal locations may be exposed to storm surges.

However, the report fingers the electricity supply as the biggest vulnerability. If that gets knocked out, the network could go offline once any backup power is exhausted, which may take anywhere from a few hours to considerably longer, depending on the site.

Under current climate conditions, the cost of damage to cell sites is estimated at $1 billion associated with severe storms, while river and coastal floods account for $577 million and $124 million, respectively.

Based on projected mid-century climate conditions, the GSMA expects costs due to severe storms to rise significantly to about $2.37 billion, accounting for three-quarters of all damage.

The report asserts that cell network resilience requires a whole ecosystem approach, pointing out that if severe weather impacts power networks, then that also affects the telecoms infrastructure.

The GSMA says that network firms have traditionally managed the operational risks that may affect network availability, but claims they face barriers in conducting full assessments of those associated with climate change.

Some of these barriers are internal, such as lack of shared information between departments. Other barriers are in the different regulatory reporting frameworks, with infrastructure rules tending to focus on service continuity, while climate disclosure frameworks focus on governance, financial exposure, and reporting for investors and other stakeholders.

The report lists separate recommendations for network firms and for policymakers and regulators.

Operators are advised to embed resilience by design, using modeled projections for severe weather and future risk scenarios. They are also told to plan and test resilience across the wider ecosystem, engaging with others such as public authorities.

When it comes to policymakers and regulators, the report asks for resilience frameworks to be developed through consultation with the operators. It also advises coordination among mobile operators, electricity and fuel providers, and emergency services to help maintain vital communications during major disruptions.

And as if that isn't enough to chew over, the separate policy document sets out five principles for governments and regulators. These include avoiding prescriptive regulations and instead promoting outcome-based policies, encouraging dialog and consultation between governments, regulators, and operators, and developing resilience as a cross-sector responsibility.

“Mobile connectivity is essential infrastructure,” says GSMA Foundation president and chief regulatory officer John Giusti.

“Whether responding to extreme weather, power failures or other major disruptions, people, businesses and emergency services depend heavily on mobile networks,” he added.

“Severe weather is already costing the industry billions of dollars, and those costs are set to rise substantially. Building resilience will require a coordinated effort amongst operators, governments and the wider ecosystem.” ®
